abstracts.t: Can Electricity Replace Herbicides in Organic Sorghum?

sc.x: Weed management remains a critical constraint in organic sorghum production, where the absence of synthetic herbicides necessitates intensive cultivation and labor-dependent weed control practices. Electrical Weed Control (EWC) has emerged as a promising non-chemical alternative; however, its efficacy is governed by complex interactions among plant morphology, electrical conductivity, soil moisture, contact duration, and energy transfer. Consequently, significant knowledge gaps remain regarding the optimization and field-scale implementation of EWC in agronomic cropping systems. This research evaluates the potential of EWC as an integrated weed management strategy in organic sorghum production systems in Texas. Specific objectives include: (i) quantifying the influence of soil moisture on plant–soil electrical conductivity and weed injury (ii) determining the effects of EWC on weed reproductive biology, including seed viability and seedbank recruitment potential; (iii) enhancing weed mortality through conductive liquid-mediated optimization of current transfer; and (iv) integrating inter-row EWC with targeted intra-row propane flaming to improve crop selectivity and whole-row weed suppression.Field and laboratory studies will quantify weed control efficacy, crop injury, reproductive suppression, and operational performance. The outcomes will advance understanding of soil–plant–electricity interactions and provide a foundation for integrating electrical and thermal technologies into sustainable reduced-tillage weed management systems for organic sorghum.

I enjoy science because it allows me to transform curiosity into solutions for real-world challenges. Growing up in a farming family, I witnessed how weeds directly affect farmers’ livelihoods. These experiences inspired me to pursue weed science and develop practical, sustainable solutions for agriculture. My research focuses on non-chemical weed management in organic sorghum systems, with an emphasis on Electrical Weed Control and integrated weed management strategies. I am particularly motivated by the growing global demand for organically produced food, feed, and fiber, as well as the urgent need to address herbicide resistance, one of the most significant threats to agricultural sustainability. Farmers need effective weed management tools that maintain productivity while reducing reliance on synthetic herbicides and intensive tillage. I believe my research is important because it explores innovative alternatives to conventional weed control. By improving our understanding of electrical weed control, weed seedbank suppression, and the integration of electrical and thermal technologies, my work aims to provide farmers with practical, scalable, and environmentally responsible weed management solutions. Ultimately, I enjoy science because it creates knowledge that benefits farmers, strengthens agricultural sustainability, and contributes to a safer, more resilient, and chemical free world for food, feed, and fiber production.

abstracts.t: A Smartphone Application to Estimate Sorghum Panicle Traits Using In-Field Imagery

sc.x: Estimating sorghum yield in breeding plots before harvest is labor-intensive and time-consuming, typically requiring panicle removal, manual or machine-based grain counting, or UAV deployment. Smartphones combined with computer vision algorithms offer a promising solution to this bottleneck. Following this rationale, we developed a mobile application to estimate sorghum panicle traits and yield at the plot scale using smartphone imagery, benchmarking performance across more than 80 distinct genotypes, and assessing performance as early as developmental Stage 6. The application can (i) estimate key sorghum panicle traits, (ii) assess panicle population, and (iii) estimate plot-level yield. Five deep learning models were integrated into a React Native mobile application, enabling all estimations to be performed offline. For panicle traits, the application achieved mean absolute errors of 1.22 cm for panicle length, 1.96 cm for panicle diameter, and 280 grains for grain number. At the plot scale, mean absolute percentage errors were 7% for population estimates and 8.5% for yield predictions. This mobile application can be used not only by breeders but also by farmers, crop insurance providers, and agronomists to rapidly estimate grain numbers in sorghum panicles and forecast yields prior to harvest.

I am deeply curious by nature, constantly driven to understand how things work and, more importantly, why they work. This curiosity led me to pursue engineering and, ultimately, to transition into scientific research. Exploring challenges that have not yet been addressed and building solutions from the ground up aligns strongly with me; it is where my technical interests and personal motivation connect, and it consistently brings a level of excitement that fuels my work.
My personal objective is to democratize science and digital agriculture by developing low-cost technologies for the agricultural community. This motivation drives me to focus on research and product development that translates directly into real-world use. Knowing that the tools I develop are not only adopted by researchers but also support farmers and other stakeholders across the production chain gives me a strong sense of purpose and impact.

abstracts.t: Beyond Recalcitrance: Breaking the Bottleneck of Sorghum Genetic Transformation using Developmental Regulators

sc.x:
Efficient transformation and regeneration are critical for crop improvement and functional
genomics. Fortunately, recent breakthroughs in the utilization of developmental regulator (DR)
genes have helped overcome the recalcitrant nature of many monocot species including
sorghum to genetic transformation. However, the underlying transcriptional regulation governing
DR-induced somatic embryogenesis and regeneration competence remains poorly understood. In
this study, we investigate the molecular mechanisms associated with DR-mediated enhancement
of transformation in multiple sorghum types (grain, forage and bioenergy) previously difficult to-transform.
By using DR genes, we successfully performed genetic transformation and regeneration in two previously
untested sorghum genotypes. Our analyses reveal key transcriptional networks and novel candidate
regulators associated with cellular reprogramming, differentiation, and somatic embryogenesis capacity,
including genotype-specific responses to DR expression.
By employing DR genes such as BABY BOOM, WUSCHEL and GIF-GRF, we established robust
Agrobacterium-mediated transformation systems using multiple explant types (leaf and immature
embryo) and expanded transformability to genotypes not previously amenable to regeneration.
Integration of a visual reporter RUBY and AmCYAN expression enabled rapid and efficient identification
of transformed tissues. To dissect the regulatory pathways driving embryogenic reprogramming, we
performed transcriptome profiling during early stages of somatic embryogenesis.
Collectively, this work not only provides practical advances in transformation methodology but, most
importantly provides fundamental insights into the transcriptional regulation underlying DR-mediated
regeneration, offering a framework for discovering novel targets and mechanisms for improving
transformation efficiency in other recalcitrant monocot species

abstracts.t: BEYOND LGS1: DIVERSIFYING STRIGA RESISTANCE IN SORGHUM

sc.x: While loss-of-function LOW GERMINATION STIMULANT 1 (LGS1) gene in sorghum confers resistance, emerging evidence indicates that some Striga ecotypes are sensitive to the altered exudate produced by lgs1 genotypes suggesting that this resistance may not be sufficient to build a Striga resilient system for sorghum in Africa. Therefore for durability, it is imperative to diversify Striga resistance in sorghum. This study aims to leverage pedigree information to untangle pre- and post-attachment resistance components in SRN39 by hypothesizing that a genomic locus independent of the LGS1 locus in SRN39 underlies post-attachment resistance. A mapping population developed from SEPON-82, and SRN39, was initiated and advanced to the F4 generation. To disentangle the effects of pre-attachment resistance and enable targeted investigation of post-attachment resistance, in the F2 and F3 generations, marker-assisted selection was conducted using lgs1-1 KASP markers to select for only LGS1 lines for advancement to the next generation. Phenotyping of the population will be done across Africa, data taken on post-attachment indicators, and leaf tissues collected for Bulked Segregant Analysis for QTL mapping. Elucidating the post-attachment resistance locus in SRN39 will improve understanding of multilayer resistance and support the development of more durable Striga resistant sorghum varieties.

Science heightens my inquisitiveness, leading to practical solutions for real-world problems. The process of discovery—making observations, designing experiments, analyzing data, and gradually uncovering answers that can make a difference beyond the laboratory—excites me the most. As a plant breeding researcher, I am especially motivated by the opportunity to improve crops that contribute to alleviating food insecurity. Toward building a more biotic resilient sorghum production system in Africa, my research focuses on post-germination resistance to Striga, a parasitic weed that severely constrains sorghum production across sub-Saharan Africa. Host plant resistance offers an efficient and effective approach to biotic stress management; however, while some resistance mechanisms have been studied previously, post-germination resistance remains less understood. My work aims to identify the genetic regions responsible for this resistance for incorporation into breeding programs. I believe this research is important because developing resistant crops with diverse resistance sources offers a sustainable, durable, and affordable solution for farmers who may not have access to costly chemical control methods.

abstracts.t: Genome-Wide Association Study Identifies Consistent Genomic Loci for Yield and Nutritional Quality in Ethiopian Sorghum Landraces

sc.x: Identifying genomic regions linked to yield and quality is crucial for sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.) improvement, but limited studies on its genome and diversity hinder breeding efforts. This study aimed to identify phenotypic variance and common quantitative trait nucleotides (QTNs) associated genomic regions linked with grain yield and quality traits. The experiment was conducted during the 2020 and 2021 growing seasons across three Ethiopian agroecological zones—wet intermediate (Jimma), dry lowland irrigated (Melkassa), and natural drought-prone lowland (Miesso)—using a diverse panel of 358 Ethiopian sorghum landraces. Grain yield reflected both genetic and environmental effects, while the other traits were mainly under genetic control. A multi-locus genome-wide association study (ML-GWAS) was conducted using 209,572 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) markers. A total of 27 stable QTNs were identified across six environments using multiple ML-GWAS models. Five QTNs were associated with grain yield, nine with protein content, seven with thousand seed weight, and six with amylopectin. Two QTNs S01_65245223 and S09_50940522 were notable in grain yield, with candidate genes encoding a universal stress protein (Sobic.001G363100) and an E3 ubiquitin ligase (Sobic.009G153100), involved in stress response and protein turnover. For protein content, S01_1332500 and S05_53371984 localized with genes encoding EMC2 (Sobic.001G014800) and HVA22-like storage proteins (Sobic.005G121200 and Sobic.005G121300), key for protein folding and accumulation. Thousand seed weight, QTNs S03_3571908 and S01_73998261 were linked to a phospholipase A1 (Sobic.003G038000) and a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase/E3 ligase (Sobic.001G466700), supporting seed filling and growth regulation. For amylopectin, S04_62662803 and S08_53120256 corresponded to GBSSI/SSIIa (Sobic.004G284400) and APS reductase (Sobic.008G118900), central to starch biosynthesis and redox regulation. Multi-locus GWAS revealed stable QTNs for yield and grain quality in sorghum, validating known and novel loci as targets for breeding resilient, biofortified cultivars.

Science, particularly plant genetics and breeding, fascinates me because it provides practical solutions to one of humanity’s most fundamental challenges: food security under changing climates. I enjoy science because it connects curiosity with impact—transforming questions about genetic variation into tangible improvements in crop productivity, resilience, and nutritional quality. Ultimately, I am motivated by the possibility that scientific discoveries can move beyond laboratories and fields into farmers’ hands, improving livelihoods and strengthening agricultural systems in vulnerable regions.

abstracts.t: Leveraging Community-Generated Phenotypic Data to Study Pleiotropy in Sorghum

sc.x: Pleiotropy, where a single genetic locus influences multiple traits, is a fundamental feature of genetic architecture. While large human biobank studies have revealed widespread pleiotropy, studies in plants have largely been limited to single-gene analyses due to the lack of large, reusable multi-trait datasets. The Sorghum Association Panel (SAP) provides a unique opportunity to address this limitation, as it consists of genetically identical inbred lines repeatedly phenotyped across diverse environments and years. In this study, we compiled and harmonized an expanded SAP phenotypic resource spanning 2008 to 2025, increasing the number of analyzed traits to 724. Using a meta-analytic framework, we leveraged this longitudinal dataset to investigate patterns of pleiotropy across agronomic, developmental, and physiological traits without requiring all phenotypes to be measured in a single experiment. As a case study, we examined the pleiotropic effects of the major plant height locus Dw1 and found that genetic variation at this locus influences numerous traits beyond plant height. Our results demonstrate the value of long-term, community-generated datasets for dissecting pleiotropy and uncovering complex genetic relationships in crop species.

I enjoy science because it allows me to explore questions that initially seem impossibly complex and gradually uncover the biological principles that connect them. What excites me most about research is the process of discovery itself the realization that within large genomic, transcriptomic, and phenotypic datasets there are patterns waiting to be understood. I find immense satisfaction in integrating different layers of biological information and uncovering how genes, environments, and regulatory networks interact to shape plant traits.My research focuses exclusively on sorghum, a crop that I believe represents both a fascinating biological system and an important resource for global agriculture. I am particularly interested in understanding the genetic architecture of complex traits, including pleiotropy, gene regulation, genotype-by-environment interactions, and stress responses. I enjoy asking questions such as how a single genetic variant can influence multiple traits, how environmental conditions reshape gene expression networks, and how plants balance adaptation with productivity. The ability to combine genomics, transcriptomics, and large-scale phenotypic datasets to answer these questions is what motivates me every day.I believe this research is important because improving our understanding of sorghum biology will contribute to the development of more resilient and sustainable cropping systems. As climate variability increases worldwide, generating knowledge that can support crop improvement and food security gives both purpose and urgency to my scientific work.

abstracts.t: Redesigning Sorghum Starch for the Food Industry

sc.x: Starch biosynthesis genes are well-characterized in major cereals like maize, rice, and wheat, enabling targeted breeding for specific food and feed properties. However, this knowledge is largely lacking for sorghum, despite starch comprising 70% to 75% of its grain and driving crucial traits like cooking quality, digestibility, and processing performance. Because the starch pathway is conserved across cereals, known genes from other crops offer a blueprint for sorghum research. To date, only three starch biosynthetic genes with unique phenotypes have been characterized in sorghum: GBSS (waxy), SBEIIb (amylose extender), and SSIIa (sugary). Our lab previously identified SBEIIb and SSIIa using EMS mutagenesis and whole-genome sequencing. Concurrently, a screen of 840 diverse sorghum accessions revealed similar starch phenotypes within the standing genetic variation, specifically in landraces from India and Africa. Ongoing genetic studies aim to determine whether these natural traits are driven by the three known genes or novel mechanisms. My thesis research focuses on identifying potentially novel genes and alleles for starch metabolism by genetic mapping in biparental populations, complementation testing, and detailed composition analysis. Successfully uncovering new genes and alleles will provide new genetic donors to improve sorghum grain quality for industrial, food, and feed applications.

Although still a young scientist, I have developed a deep academic and technical understanding of agricultural research. I completed my academic studies in botany in my home country of India while serving as a Senior Research Technician for 12 years at CIMMYT-Asia, based in Hyderabad, India. At CIMMYT, I primarily worked on maize heat and drought tolerance programs that contributed to the release of 20 hybrids now grown across South Asia. I transitioned to graduate school at Purdue University because I wanted to learn how genetics and biochemistry contribute to the trait variation I had observed in breeding programs. Pursuing my M.S. in Plant Breeding and Genetics has given me that opportunity. I enjoy science because it turns observation into explanation, and explanation into tools that breeders can use. My research is important because sorghum is a staple food for millions of people, yet breeders currently have very few characterized genes to work with for improving grain quality. Identifying new genetic targets for starch modification could expand the use of sorghum in food markets across the Americas, Africa, and Asia, where this crop plays a critical role in food security and agricultural economies.

abstracts.t: Tissue Culture Free Sorghum Transformation May Shrink Genetic Modification Timeline

sc.x: Sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] is a globally important food and bioenergy crop, ranking fifth in world cereal production. Despite the global importance of sorghum, there is no simple and efficient transformation system, which limits the implementation of new biotechnology in elite sorghum cultivars and slows the discovery of genes within the sorghum genome. Tissue culture is the primary challenge in sorghum transformation systems, and while morphogenic regulators have increased the tissues and genotypes that can be transformed, tissue culture remains a resource, skill, and time intensive process. An in planta transformation system could circumvent these challenges by bypassing tissue culture altogether. A new in planta transformation method for Agrobacterium-mediated transformation that targets developing embryos has shown success in wheat and other cereal crops and appears to be genotype independent. The aim of this research is to develop and optimize a similar method in sorghum, ultimately creating an easy, efficient, and genotype independent transformation pipeline that is singificnalty faster than state-of-the-art methods. Positive transformants have been identified in the T0 and T1 generations by PCR screening in sorghum genotypes Tx430 and Tx623. If successful, this can be combined with a CRISPR gene editing system for systemaic gene discovery in sorghum.

My interest in crop science began with my backyard garden while growing up where I developed a passion for gardening and an interest in how plants grow and function. Later in high school, I was able to attend the Global Youth Institute (GYI) hosted by the World Food Prize. This program selects 200 students from around the world to attend the Borlaug Dialogue and the World Food Prize presentation. Before this, I considered agriculture as a hobby instead of a science, but during the GYI, I got to meet and learn from scientists, activists, and politicians who were working to address global food insecurity. The final factor that developed my passion for crop science was learning about new gene editing and modification technologies like plant transformation and CRISPR gene editing. Studying these cutting edge technologies can give us a glimpse into the foundation of life and how it is regulated and controlled. My current research closely aligns with my passions for science and global food security. Moreover, my research will enable scientists to more efficiently gain understanding of the genetic basis of sorghum's incredible abiotic stress tolerance and apply this understanding to other C4 grasses such as maize and sugarcane.

abstracts.t: Sorghum Tolerance to Mesotrione-Based Formulations Applied Preemergence

sc.x: Forage sorghum producers have fewer herbicide options compared to traditional grain sorghum producers. Moreover, many of the new herbicide-tolerant technologies are not widely available or approved for forage-type sorghum. However, there is interest in adding forage sorghum to current herbicide labels. One preemergence herbicide of interest is mesotrione, an HPPD-inhibiting WSSA Group 27 herbicide. A research trial was conducted in 2026 at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in Halfway, TX, to examine crop response of two forage sorghums and two grain sorghum cultivars. Treatments consisted of S-metolachlor + mesotrione at a 1X (0.604 + 0.0608 kg ai ha-1) and 2X (1.201 + 0.121 kg ai ha-1 ) rate and S-metolachlor + atrazine + mesotrione at a 1X (0.753 + 0.276 + 0.0753 kg ai ha-1) and 2X (1.51 + 0.554 + 0.151 kg ai ha-1) rate. Crop response will be collected at various rating times after application. Overall, these results will aid in determining future use of mesotrione in forage sorghum.

Growing up on a farm in Ohio sparked my passion for agriculture at a young age, and my passion for scientific research grew from the desire to help growers to improve their operations through the chemistry used in their fields. In any agricultural system, weeds are present and when not managed properly could lead to herbicide resistance, an issue that is recurring, across many modes of action. My research is important for expanding the tools available in forage-type sorghum for early season weed control. Building up and maintaining a broad catalog of herbicides ensures dynamic options for weed control, especially when managing persistent and troublesome weeds. Diversification of weed management programs reduce risk in the development of herbicide resistance. Being involved in scientific research allows me the opportunity to understand new products coming to market, and I can help ease the minds of growers when introducing products into their weed management programs. Maintaining clean, weed-free fields allows growers to maintain growth, sustaining their operation for generations to come.

abstracts.t: Better Sorghum, Better Feed: Integrating Field Traits, DNA Markers, and Gene Editing

sc.x: The U.S. cattle feed market is growing, but reliance on water-intensive corn silage is threatened by Ogallala Aquifer depletion. Forage sorghum offers a drought-tolerant, high-biomass alternative, but improvement is limited by few dedicated breeding programs and limited use of modern molecular tools. My research addresses this gap by integrating field evaluation, marker-assisted selection, breeding, and gene editing. First, we evaluated 16 commercial and research sorghum silage lines to understand how traits such as brown midrib, dhurrin content, high protein digestibility, and waxy grain influence yield and quality. Because biomass production is also strongly influenced by flowering time, we developed KASP markers for key forage-related traits such as Ma5 maturity locus to enable early selection of photoperiod-sensitive, high-biomass genotypes without relying only on season-long field phenotyping. These trait and marker insights then guide our third goal: developing forage sorghum lines, grain sorghum-derived forage lines, and early test hybrids, generating a practical breeding foundation for evaluation and cultivar improvement. Finally, to improve forage quality more precisely, we are utilizing CRISPR/Cas gene editing to target bmr6 for enhanced digestibility. Together, these goals connect field evaluation, DNA-based selection, breeding, and gene editing to advance water-efficient, high-quality forage sorghum.

As a first-generation student from India, science has been a path that allows me to learn, ask questions, and contribute to real-world agricultural challenges. I enjoy science because it connects curiosity with practical impact. During my master’s research, I evaluated pearl millet germplasm for drought tolerance in western Kansas using association mapping. While working on this project, I had the opportunity to speak face-to-face with farmers during a field day. Hearing their concerns about drought and crop production made me realize how important it is for research to be practical and useful to society in some way. That experience inspired me to continue working on research that can directly support producers. My current project on forage sorghum builds on that motivation. Drought is a recurring challenge in western Kansas, and forage sorghum offers a promising alternative because of its drought tolerance, biomass potential, and value as livestock feed. Through my research, I am evaluating sorghum lines for yield and feed quality, developing molecular markers for important traits such as flowering time, and exploring gene editing to improve digestibility. I hope my research can contribute to more sustainable and resilient forage systems.

abstracts.t: Identifying natural variants impacting grain iron content and localization in sorghum

sc.x: Iron and zinc are micronutrients essential for proper growth, maintenance, and immune function. Supplementation programs and fortification strategies have been implemented in many countries to combat micronutrient deficiencies, however in rural regions or places of government and economic instability, these options may not be accessible. Micronutrient biofortification is underway in most staple crops and has been tested and employed in several countries. Biofortification of sorghum grain iron and zinc can be accelerated in breeding programs with the deployment of marker assisted selection (MAS), however identification of quantitative trait loci (QTL) and casual genes is needed in order to develop effective markers to use for selection. Through a reverse genetics pipeline, we have identified several putative causative variants in candidate genes derived from literature that may affect grain iron content. Additionally these targets are being assessed on their effect of iron localization in the grain to prevent iron losses from processing. These variants have been turned into genetic markers in the process of validation and testing. These markers have potential to assist breeders in MAS of lines to accelerate the nutritional improvement of sorghum.

Science is the process of understanding the world around us, and allows for the development of power through knowledge. I strongly believe that understanding the problems people face can allow them to overcome them through knowledge. Food security and malnutrition are some of the biggest challenges our global society faces, where it helps perpetuate cycles of poverty and stunts development of people and nations. I believe that access to nutritious food and the ability to grow it is a human right, where we can reselect the nutrient content in crops to improve their nutritional value. I feel that I found my role as a plant geneticist in the global vision of improving food security through my mission of improving the food people are already eating through leveraging natural variation. I enjoy using the knowledge I gain through scientific understanding of crop genetics and nutrition to give power to people over their health and destiny.

abstracts.t: AMMI and GGE Analysis of GxE and Yield Stability of Early Maturing Sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] Genotypes in Dry Lowland Areas of Ethiopia

sc.x: In spite of biotic and abiotic stress, the yield performance of crop varieties is highly affected by GxE, which is the major concern to plant breeders while developing improved varieties. In Ethiopia, high yielding and stable varieties that withstand drought in the dry lowland areas are limited. Therefore, the yield performance of 59 early maturing Sorghum genotypes and one standard check were tested at five locations with the objectives of estimating the magnitude of GxE for grain yield and to identify high yielder and stable genotypes across locations. The experiment was conducted using with Row Column design and three replications. The REML combined analysis of variance across locations showed very highly significant difference among locations and significant among genotypes and highly significant among interactions for grain yield studied. Genotype 28, Genotype 56, Genotype 20 and Genotype 21 were the best yielders and stable ones. AMMI and GGE biplot are also revealed that the ideal genotype and ideal environment are Genotype 34 and Shoarobit, respectively. Hence, Genotype 56 and Genotype 28, were selected as a high yielder. Generally, this study showed the importance of testing early maturing Sorghum genotypes for their yield and stability across diverse dry lowland areas of Ethiopia.

I like science because it ask questions and find answers that make peoples lives better. Science is a way to come up with ideas and I think it is really cool how it can make farming better and more sustainable. I am very curious about how plants made and how they interact with the environment so I want to do research that helps us understand how to make farming work better in real life.

I am working on a project that looks at how different types of sorghum grow in different environments. This is especially important for places in Ethiopia where it's dry and hard to grow crops. Sorghum is a food source for a lot of people but it is hard to grow when there is not enough water and the weather is bad.

My research shows that I am committed to using science to solve problems. I want to make sure that people who depend on sorghum have access. Science is a tool that can help us make peoples lives better and I want to use it to make a difference.

abstracts.t: Strong stem, stable yield

sc.x: Stem lodging is a major problem in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench), especially under drought. Drought stress during the post-flowering phase can lead to mechanical failure of the sorghum stalks and induce lodging which leads to severe losses in both yield and grain quality. Lodging is mainly determined by the stem strength but measuring it accurately in the field is challenging. In this research, a novel field-based device called DARLING (device for assessing resistance to lodging in grain crops) was used to measure stem strength in diverse sorghum genotypes grown under both well-watered and water-limited conditions. Alongside this, stem geometry, mechanical properties, and tissue characteristics, was also evaluated to understand what truly determines stem strength. Our results showed that stem strength is not just about material properties but largely regulated by structural design how the plant distributes its mass along the stem. In most cases, plants deviate from its optimal structure, making them more susceptible to failure under stress. This means that improving lodging resistance is not just about selecting stronger stems, but about designing better plant architecture. Optimizing stem structure offers a promising strategy to reduce lodging losses, helping farmers maintain both yield and crop stability under drought conditions.

I enjoy science because it allows me to ask questions that directly connect to real-world problems and then work toward meaningful solutions. What excites me most is the process starting with a simple observation in the field and uncovering the mechanisms behind it through experiments and analysis. There is always a sense of curiosity in understanding how complex biological systems work. My research focuses on stem lodging in sorghum, which may seem like a simple problem, but it has imposed serious economic burden for farmers in the region where water is the limiting factor. What makes this work important to me is that it bridges fundamental principle of physics and practical application. By understanding how stem structure and mechanical properties contribute to plant stability, we can develop better strategies to improve crop resilience. Improving lodging resistance is not just about scientific advancement it contributes to improving yields, reducing economic losses, and supporting farmers dealing with unpredictable climate conditions. Being able to work on a problem that is both scientifically challenging and socially relevant is what drives my interest in science.

abstracts.t: Extrusion processing and hydrocolloids: Nutritional and sensory properties of biscuits made of precooked whole sorghum flours as well as sorghum rolled flour

sc.x: Pregelatinized sorghum flour produced through single‑screw extrusion was evaluated in two studies. The first examined composite flours for biscuits, blending wheat with extruded sorghum, fonio, and millet at 30%, 50%, and 70%. Biochemical analysis showed moisture contents of 9–9.43%, protein 7.8–12.77%, ash 1.45–1.90%, fat 11.86–24.85%, and carbohydrates 54.74–68.78%. Sensory evaluation revealed that acceptability declined as incorporation increased, with 30% sorghum biscuits achieving the best scores, indicating that moderate substitution balances nutrition and consumer preference. The second study focused on pre‑cooked rolled sorghum flours enriched with Arabic gum or maltodextrin. Compared with the non‑extruded control, extrusion produced granules with slightly higher carbohydrate (79.8–80.39%) and ash (0.79–1.18%) contents, while starch decreased sharply (32.32% vs. 68.08%). Arabic gum notably enhanced mineral levels, including iron, calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, and phosphorus. Sensory evaluation of porridges prepared from these granules showed improved acceptability compared with traditional sorghum porridge, with higher scores for color, aroma, taste, mouthfeel, and overall appeal. Together, the findings highlight extrusion technology as a promising method to improve sorghum’s nutritional and sensory qualities. Biscuits benefit from partial incorporation of extruded sorghum flour, while porridges made from gum‑enriched granules offer superior taste, texture, and mineral content. These results confirm the potential of pregelatinized sorghum products as convenient, health‑enhancing alternatives to traditional cereal foods.

I enjoy science because it allows me to explore how everyday materials can be transformed into healthier, more sustainable options through innovation. Science is not just about discovery—it is about solving real problems and improving lives. Working with cereals like sorghum, fonio, and millet through extrusion technology shows how traditional crops can be reimagined into modern, convenient foods without losing their cultural and nutritional value. This research is important because it demonstrates practical ways to enhance food quality, diversify diets, and address nutritional challenges, especially in regions where these grains are staples. By improving protein, mineral content, and sensory appeal, sorghum‑based products can provide affordable, accessible alternatives to wheat, while also supporting local agriculture and food security. The findings highlight how extrusion technology can bridge tradition and innovation, creating products that are both nutritious and acceptable to consumers. For me, science is meaningful when it connects laboratory work to everyday needs, and this research embodies that connection—transforming underutilized grains into health‑enhancing foods that can contribute to better nutrition and sustainable development.

abstracts.t: Cultivation Techniques for Sorghum: Effects of Variety, Seeding Density and Row Spacing on Yield and Forage Quality under Swiss Conditions
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: Agroscope, Zurich, Switzerland
Agroscope, Zurich, Switzerland
Agroscope, Zurich, Switzerland
Agroscope, Zurich, Switzerland

sc.x: Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench is still a minor crop in Switzerland, with approximately 400 ha currently under cultivation. Agronomic recommendations for temperate environments are therefore still limited. As a drought-adapted C4 species with high biomass potential, sorghum may contribute to climate-resilient cropping systems and serve as an alternative to maize, particularly in regions where forage production is challenging.

A three-year field trial (2022-2024) was conducted in Zurich (Switzerland). Four sorghum varieties (CSSH-45, ES Athena, ES Biomass, KWS Zerberus), one maize variety (P8834) and a maize-sorghum mixture were evaluated at three row spacings (37.5, 50, and 75 cm) and three seeding densities. Agronomic performance was assessed using multiple traits, including lodging, dry matter (DM) yield, net energy for lactation (NEL) and digestibility of organic matter (DOM).

Variety was the main factor influencing both DM yield and forage quality. ES Biomass and KWS Zerberus achieved higher DM yields, whereas CSSH-45 and ES Athena showed superior NEL and DOM values. Overall, sorghum reached energy yields comparable to maize, although distinct varietal differences were observed in the balance between biomass production and forage quality. Increasing seeding density significantly increased DM yield but partially increased lodging. Row spacing significantly affected DM yield, with the highest yields observed at 50 cm, whereas no consistent effect on forage quality parameters was detected.

These findings highlight the importance of varietal selection and planting configuration for optimizing sorghum production under temperate Swiss conditions. While higher plant populations increased DM yield, they were also associated with greater lodging risk, whereas forage quality was mainly determined by varietal differences.

abstracts.t: Capacity Building in AI driven research and Education in UAS Application in Precision Agriculture
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

sc.x: This study investigates the concept of combining artificial intelligence (AI) and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to develop precision agriculture plans for growing sorghum under different climatic conditions. The major objectives are to calculate the correlation patterns in the CC%-DAP curves with grain yield and biomass accumulation, creating an AI-based growth monitoring product in sorghum, and precision phenotyping in drought-tolerance genotypes.

The study was conducted at the USDA-ARS Conservation and Production Research Laboratory in Bushland, Texas. This study investigates the concept of combining artificial intelligence (AI) and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) to develop precision agriculture plans for growing sorghum under different irrigation conditions. In order to create genotype-specific canopy growth curves, UAS data is used to collect high-resolution RGB images of the canopy during the growing period. These images are then processed using softwares like PiX4D mapper and QGIS. Canopy Cover Percentage (CC%) and Days After Planting (DAP), two measures of plant growth and development, are given particular consideration. Vegetation indicators such as Excessive greenness index were calculated to enhance the detection of green vegetation and improve canopy segmentation from RGB imagery and canopy height model was calculated to estimate the plant height and spatial variability across the field.

This project will enhance the effectiveness of crop surveillance, enable more prudent irrigation regulation, and enhance breeding sorghum under conditions of high productivity and stress resistance through the use of UAS imagery, AI analysis, and breeding of stress-tolerant and high-yield varieties. The outcomes lead to sustainable water management and development of digital applications in crop enhancement in resource-limited environments.

sc.x: The development of resilient, energy-dense biomass feedstocks is required to meet the escalating global demand for bioenergy, especially for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable bioproducts. While massive biomass potential is offered by C4 grasses like sorghum, significant lipid accumulation in vegetative tissues such as leaves and stems is naturally absent. To overcome this biological bottleneck, the objective of this study was to engineer both grain (Tx430) and sweet (Ramada) genotypes of sorghum to accumulate triacylglycerols (TAG) in their vegetative tissues.

Unprecedented success was demonstrated under field conditions. The top-performing engineered Tx430 lines accumulated TAG up to 5.5% and 3.5% of dry weight in leaves and stems, respectively. This represents staggering 78-fold and 58-fold increases in vegetative lipid content compared to wild-type (WT) plants. Furthermore, multi-location trials confirmed that this robust TAG accumulation trait is highly stable across different environments. Crucially, the engineered oil sorghum lines consistently maintained dry biomass yields and fundamental tissue composition comparable to their WT counterparts.

A synergistic 'push-pull-protect' metabolic engineering strategy was utilized, involving the coordinated co-expression of the transcription factor WRINKLED1 (to push carbon into fatty acid synthesis), diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT; to pull fatty acids into TAG), and oleosin (to protect TAG within lipid droplets). Following initial lab-to-field development, multi-year, multi-location agronomic evaluations across the US Midwest were conducted to assess crop viability and trait stability across diverse agricultural settings prior to downstream bioprocessing.

By demonstrating that the hyperaccumulation of vegetative oil can be achieved without a biomass penalty, and with bioprocessing optimization for TAG recovery currently underway, engineered oil sorghum is validated by these findings as a highly scalable, commercially viable platform for next-generation bioeconomy applications.

sc.x: Anthracnose, caused by the fungus Colletotrichum sublineola, is a significant disease that limits production of sorghum in humid environments. A recombinant inbred (RI) population was created by single seed descent from the cross of SC173 by N98. While these two parental lines were mostly resistant to anthracnose in Tifton, GA, segregation for anthracnose response was observed in the RI population.

Disease data were collected from field experiments for two seasons at Tifton, GA (2023 and 2024) and one season at Isabella, PR (2025). The population was genotyped using a new mid-density SNP panel developed by AgriPlex Genomics in cooperation with the sorghum genetics community. Using R/qtl, a genetic map was constructed with 1,046 polymorphic markers forming 10 linkage groups, with a map length of 1,311.9 cM.

In Georgia, 2023, there were 61 susceptible and 62 resistant, which suggests one major gene is involved, whereas in Georgia, 2024, there were 29 susceptible and 92 resistant, which suggests two genes. R/qtl identified two significant complementary quantitative trait loci (QTL) in both Georgia environments. Resistance was associated with the SC173 allele of a locus on Chromosome 5, whereas resistance was associated with the N98 allele on Chromosome 9. In Puerto Rico, there were 16 susceptible and 107 resistant, suggesting three genes (chi square = 0.029, p = 0.865), but no significant QTL were detected, likely because of the small population size and lack of statistical power.

The utility of the mid-density SNP panel for QTL mapping was validated. Two loci for anthracnose resistance were identified in this population, and they overlap with previously mapped QTL. The anthracnose pathogen is highly diverse and can overcome a single resistance gene. The 32 RI lines carrying both resistant QTL identified here could be utilized in breeding sorghum lines with durable resistance.

sc.x: Sorghum cultivation is expanding rapidly in Brazil, with production projected to reach 6.7 million tons in the 2025/26 season. However, anthracnose (Colletotrichum sublineolum) remains a primary biotic constraint. This study evaluated the efficacy of six fungicide programs across six commercial grain sorghum hybrids with varying levels of resistance

The trial was conducted at Embrapa Maize and Sorghum (Sete Lagoas, MG) during the 2025 second crop season using a randomized complete block design (RCBD) in a 6x6 factorial scheme. Hybrids were categorized as Highly Susceptible (HS), Susceptible (S), Moderately Resistant (MR), and Resistant (R). Management programs (M1–M6) involved two alternating applications of triazoles, strobilurins, multi-site (mancozeb) mixtures, and thiophanate-methyl. Program M6 included an amino acid supplement in the first application. Assessments included the Area Under the Disease Progress Curve (AUDPC) and grain yield (kg/ha).

Significant interactions (p < 0.05) occurred between hybrids and fungicide programs. Resistant hybrids maintained the lowest AUDPC (47.72–78.83) regardless of treatment; for these, fungicide efficacy was negligible (< 46%), chemical control can be dispensed with. Conversely, intermediate and susceptible hybrids showed control efficiencies exceeding 75%. For HS hybrids, disease pressure remained critical (AUDPC 1597.33) with efficacy (only 46%), failing to provide viable protection. Notably, the "Amino acid + Fungicide" provided superior yield protection for susceptible hybrids. A negative correlation between AUDPC and yield was confirmed for HS (minimum de 4.409 kg/ha and maximum de 6.315 kg/ha.

Anthracnose management must be hybrid-specific. While fungicide programs are highly effective for hybrids with intermediate resistance, they do not achieve sufficient efficacy to anthracnose for highly susceptible genotypes when only two applications are used. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) should prioritize the selection of resistant or moderately resistant hybrids, utilizing fungicides as a tactical tool to maximize yield stability. sc.x: The growth of the plant-based food market drives the search for sustainable, nutritious, and technologically viable ingredients. Sorghum, a resilient and gluten-free cereal, combined with cowpea protein isolate, represents a promising alternative for the development of meat analogues. Both sorghum and cowpea have high levels of phenolic compounds, and complementary amino acids, resulting in better protein quality in the final product. Furthermore, sorghum has a neutral flavor and lower production costs compared to soybean, which is the primary ingredient used in meat analogues. Thus, this study aimed to evaluate the sensory acceptability of plant-based burgers made with whole sorghum grain and cowpea protein isolate.

The TS and TFS formulations showed an Acceptability Index (AI) above 80% for overall impression, color, aroma, and flavor, and both were considered accepted for these sensory attributes. There was no difference among samples for aroma (p>0.05). For color, TS did not differ from CO. The flavor of TS showed intermediate performance, not differing from CO, demonstrating that the presence of tannins did not compromise the sensory acceptability of the final product. Texture was the main limiting factor, with mean scores lower than CO (p≤0.05).

Two formulations containing cooked sorghum, with tannins (TS) or tannin-free (TFS), added with cowpea protein isolate (1.6:1, w/w) and seasonings, both with 19% protein, were developed and compared to a commercial product (CO). Sensory analysis was conducted with 99 untrained consumers using a nine-point hedonic scale. Data were analyzed by ANOVA and Tukey’s test (5%). Acceptability was considered satisfactory when ≥70% of the scores were ≥6.0.

These results highlight sorghum as a viable ingredient for plant-based meat analogues, particularly due to its functional and sensory potential. This work was supported by the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPq) - Brazil.

sc.x: Hybrid seed production in sorghum currently depends on cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)-based three-line systems, which restrict parental diversity and increase breeding costs and timelines. To overcome these constraints, we are developing a humidity-sensitive genic male sterility (HGMS)-based two-line breeding system that enables conditional and reversible male sterility for efficient hybrid seed production. This project aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying humidity-sensitive male sterility and translate this knowledge into practical breeding tools.

The mutant exhibited reduced pollen release and seed set under moderate relative humidity (30–60%) but restored fertility under high humidity (>80%), without visible structural defects in anthers or pollen surfaces. These findings demonstrate environmentally responsive and reversible male sterility suitable for two-line hybrid breeding.

We isolated and validated an EMS-induced sorghum mutant carrying a recessive mutation in a pollen cell wall-associated gene that confers an HGMS phenotype. Transcriptome analyses identified four additional anther-enriched candidate genes involved in pollen coat lipid metabolism and cuticular wax biosynthesis. Functional genomics, genome editing, and breeding approaches are being integrated to validate candidate genes and develop HGMS germplasm.

Expected outcomes include identification and functional validation of key HGMS genes, development of genome-edited and near-isogenic germplasm carrying HGMS alleles, and establishment of a robust two-line hybrid seed production platform. This research will deliver the first environmentally responsive male sterility system in sorghum, enhancing hybrid breeding efficiency, broadening the genetic base of parental lines, and reducing seed production costs.

sc.x: Sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] is a globally important food and bioenergy crop, ranking fifth in world cereal production. Native to Africa, it is a C4 grass adapted to environments with high levels of abiotic stress and low fertility, making it a productive and increasingly popular crop due to climate change. Despite the global importance of sorghum, there is no simple and efficient transformation system, which limits the implementation of new biotechnology in elite sorghum cultivars and slows the discovery of new genes within the sorghum genome that could be applied in breeding programs. Tissue culture is the primary challenge in sorghum transformation systems due to the high level of recalcitrance expressed by sorghum. While morphogenic regulators have increased the tissues and genotypes that can be successfully transformed, tissue culture remains a resource, skill, and time intensive process. An in planta transformation system could circumvent these challenges by bypassing tissue culture altogether.

The aim of this research is to develop and optimize a similar method in sorghum, ultimately creating an easy, efficient, and genotype independent transformation pipeline. Currently, positive transformants have been identified in the T0 and T1 generations by PCR screening in sorghum genotypes Tx430 and Tx623.

A new in planta transformation method for Agrobacterium-mediated transformation that targets developing embryos has shown success in wheat and other cereal crops and appears to be genotype independent. This technique delivers agrobacterium to immature developing embryos by wounding, which are left to mature on the plant before being germinated to grow into chimeric transformed plants.

If this technique is confirmed to be successful, it can be combined with a CRISPR gene editing system, making it a powerful tool for gene discovery in both sorghum and other C4 grasses in addition to enabling efficient introduction of agronomically important traits into commercial production lines.

sc.x: Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is a drought-tolerant ancient cereal and gluten-free crop with diverse end uses in food, feed, forage, biofuel, sugar, and alcoholic beverage production. Despite its importance, the regulatory networks underlying natural variation in grain quality traits remain poorly understood.

We generated integrated biophysical, transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets across five developmental stages in 12 Multi-Parent Advanced Generation Intercross (MAGIC) lines, including six parental lines and six derived progeny exhibiting diverse grain quality phenotypes. The MAGIC population captures substantial phenotypic diversity for starch, protein, and oil content within relatively similar genetic backgrounds, providing a powerful framework for association analysis and high-confidence network construction. Kernel samples display considerable variation in hardness, diameter, and weight, with a strong positive correlation between kernel diameter and weight. Comparative gene and metabolites expression network analyses between genotypes with contrasting levels of starch, protein, and oil accumulation are enabling the identification of key regulatory genes and allelic variants that drive grain compositional differences.
To address this knowledge gap, we are applying a systems biology approach to dissect gene regulatory networks controlling starch, protein, and oil biosynthesis during sorghum seed development.

This work will generate a comprehensive gene network framework for sorghum grain development, providing molecular targets and allele combinations to support precision breeding strategies tailored to diverse market and nutritional demands within the sorghum industry.

sc.x: Based on USDA data, North Carolina and South Carolina respectively had the 5<sup>th</sup> and 7<sup>th</sup> lowest 2-year maize yield average of 32 reporting states (approximately 8,200 kg ha<sup>-1</sup> combined). For reference, the top four Midwest states (IL, IA, IN, and OH) had a collective yield average of 12,436 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>. Less than 10% of farmland in the Carolinas is irrigated. Southeast states receive relatively high precipitation, but the issue with regional rainfall is its sporadic timing that is combined with sandy soils that have low water holding capacity. Further, frequent rains and high humidity generate ideal conditions for the spread of fungal diseases like anthracnose that can reduce yields.

For the past decade, the Clemson University sorghum breeding program has advanced parent lines for resistance to anthracnose and desirable agronomic characteristics. The program integrated genomic prediction to assist with testcross parent selection while maintaining three field selection cycles from F<sub>2</sub>-F<sub>4</sub>, typically under heavy disease pressure. Development and testing of 400-500 F<sub>1</sub> testcross hybrids annually from 2016-2025 generated a dataset of more than 2,000 hybrids with genotyped parents to examine genomic prediction accuracy using cross-validation.

Genomic prediction accuracy was high for plant height and moderate for grain yield, anthracnose resistance, days to anthesis, and test weight. Independent culling using genomic prediction values was implemented to cull F5 lines based on plant height and anthracnose thresholds resulted in one or more progeny from ~50% of families advancing to testcrossing. In a validation set, culled hybrids (n=381) had a significantly lower grain yield than the 514 retained hybrids. Moderate anthracnose resistance was needed to achieve high grain yield.

Early generation field selection followed by genomic selection of parents to testcross is effective in a reciprocal recurrent selection scheme for sorghum hybrid development for the eastern United States.

abstracts.t: Mechanistic Insights into Sorghum Adaptation to Environmental Challenges
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: China Agricultural University, Beijing, China

sc.x: In recent years, intensifying global climate change and frequent extreme weather events have posed severe challenges to crop yield stability. Traditional stress tolerance studies have largely focused on single stress factors, which can no longer meet the practical demands for breeding crops with multiple stress resistance under complex environmental conditions. China has approximately 1.5 billion mu of saline‑alkali land, of which about 500 million mu of moderately and lightly saline‑alkali land is suitable for agricultural utilization. Saline‑alkali soils are often accompanied by not only high salt and high pH, but also drought stress, nutrient deficiency, and other associated constraints. As the world’s fifth major staple crop, sorghum possesses strong tolerance to salinity, alkalinity, drought, waterlogging, low fertility, and high temperature, and is therefore regarded as a “camel plant”. Accordingly, sorghum serves as an ideal model crop for dissecting the molecular mechanisms underlying plant adaptation to complex environmental stresses.

We previously identified the key alkali‑tolerance gene AT1 in sorghum and validated its conserved function in rice, maize, wheat, and other cereals (Science, 2023), which greatly facilitated the cultivation of rice variety Zhongkefa 5 in the soda saline‑alkali regions of northern China. We also discovered a phosphorus‑deficiency induced strigolactone efflux transporter and proposed a new strategy to control parasitic weeds by reducing strigolactone exudation (Cell, 2025). In addition, we have systematically established a sorghum functional genomics platform and developed elite sorghum germplasm resources (Mol Plant, 2025).

Over the past five years, the corresponding author has published 16 papers in journals including Science and Cell. These findings have been highlighted by more than 10 journals such as Nature Biotechnology and were awarded as one of the Top 10 Scientific Advances in China 2023.

sc.x: Phenomic selection has recently gained popularity as a complementary or even alternative method to genomic selection. The use of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) allows for relatively cheap and non-destructive high-throughput data collection. This could be especially relevant for breeding programs that lack the funds or infrastructure to implement genomic selection. The objective is to evaluate the potential of spectral data aquired from Sorghum seeds to predict seed quality (germinability), yield performance and traits related to frost, cold and drought tolerance.

Within the SorBOOM project (2024-2028), a NIRS based phenomics framework is being established which benefits from the vast amount of phenotype data generated in both multi-environment filed trials (comprising n=200 experimental F1 hybrids and their parentals per year) and controlled abiotic stress experiments. Spectral datasets are processed using standardized preprocessing procedures. Predictive models are currently being developed to relate the spectral variation to the phenotypic reference data. Several approaches of phenomic selection will be tested: 1 Prediction of line per se performance; 2 Prediction of hybrid performance based on parental seeds; 3 Prediction of hybrid performance based on F1 seeds. The accuracy of approaches 1 & 2 will be compared with genomic prediction models conducted on the same dataset. Further, we aim at the development of combined phenomic prediction models, which are likely to increase the accuracy (Roscher-Ehrig et al. 2024).

At the current project stage, the focus still lies on data generation, quality assessment, and the establishment of robust analysis pipelines, rather than on final model performance. The presented work therefore represents an early-stage evaluation of NIRS based phenomics in Sorghum.

sc.x: Plant height and flowering time are key agronomic traits that influence planting density, breeding efficiency, and experimental throughput in crop research. Compact, rapid-cycling crop models have proven highly valuable for accelerating both basic research and breeding, as demonstrated by the development of mini-fast flowering maize. However, a comparable platform has not yet been established for sorghum. To address this gap, this project aims to develop and genetically characterize a compact, early-flowering sorghum ideotype that enhances the efficiency of both functional genomics and breeding applications.

We identified genetic alleles associated with reduced plant stature and early flowering and are combining these traits through targeted breeding. A miniaturized early-flowering sorghum accession is being backcrossed with the mini-1 mutant in the BTx623 background to generate compact, rapid-cycling lines. The reduced-height phenotype in mini-1 has previously been mapped to a locus encoding a Never in Mitosis A (NIMA)-related kinase (NEK), suggesting a role in regulating cell division and stem elongation. In parallel, early flowering in the diversity accession is hypothesized to involve variation in photoreceptor-mediated signaling pathways that regulate developmental timing. Segregating populations derived from the mini-1 × early-flowering cross are being phenotypically and physiologically characterized to dissect the genetic interaction between plant architecture and flowering pathways. Additional crosses with diverse sorghum accessions are underway to introgress compact architecture into multiple genetic backgrounds and evaluate trait stability.

By elucidating the genetic and molecular basis of reduced height and early flowering, this work will establish a mini-fast flowering sorghum platform that accelerates breeding cycles, facilitates dense planting systems, and enhances sorghum as a model for functional genomics and crop improvement.

abstracts.t: Multi-Environment and Multi-Year Evaluation of Commercial Sorghum Hybrids for Biomass Yield, Forage Quality, and Biofuel Potential in California
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, University of California, Merced, Parlier, United States

sc.x: Increasing pressure on water resources and rising demand for livestock feed from California’s dairy industry underscore the need for alternative crops that maintain productivity under challenging conditions. However, most sorghum breeding research has focused on the U.S. Midwest rather than California, where growing environments differ substantially. This study evaluated commercial sorghum hybrids across multiple locations and years in California to identify hybrids with high biomass yield, stable performance, good forage quality, and favorable traits for bioenergy production.

Significant effects of genotype, environment, and genotype × environment interactions were observed for most traits, emphasizing the importance of multi-environment testing. Eight hybrids exhibited consistently high and stable biomass yields across locations and years. Forage quality traits varied among hybrids, with higher starch and fat concentrations positively associated with greater milk yield per ton, while lower fiber fractions (ADF and NDF) improved Relative Feed Quality (RFQ). A multi-trait stability index identified nine hybrids that combined high biomass yield with superior RFQ and milk/ton, making them suitable for dairy forage systems. Additionally, several hybrids showed promising nutritional profiles for starch-based and fiber-based biofuel production pathways.

This study assessed 59 forage commercial hybrids (27 non-BMR forage, 20 BMR, 9 PS, and 3 PS-BMR) from 2019 to 2023 at three Central Valley sites: Parlier, Five Points, and Davis. The experiment used a randomized complete block design with four-row plots on 30-inch raised beds. Forage was harvested 100–120 days after planting, and subsamples were analyzed for nutritional composition; hybrid performance was estimated using BLUP from mixed models, and stability across environments was assessed using the WAASB method.
Superior sorghum hybrids with high biomass, stable performance, and favorable feed and biofuel traits were identified, supporting resilient and sustainable production systems.

sc.x: Ethiopia is a center of origin and diversity for sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L). Moench] possesses a rich genetic pool vital for sorghum improvement programs. This study aimed to identify genomic regions and candidate genes associated with key agronomic traits through a genome-wide association study of 329 diverse sorghum landraces evaluated in four environments over cropping seasons in Ethiopia.
Agronomic data were analyzed using the BLINK and FarmCPU models based on 83,861 high-quality SNPs generated through genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS).

The results revealed high phenotypic variation, with broad-sense heritability ranging from 0.46 to 0.90. Population structure analysis identified six genetic groups, while linkage disequilibrium (LD) analysis showed LD decay of 9−21 kb across 10 chromosomes, extending up to 45 kb at background levels. The GWAS identified 62 SNPs mapped to different loci, of which 54 loci were fully annotated and encoded various putative proteins. These loci included both novel regions and those previously linked to quantitative trait loci (QTLs). Marker-trait associations (MTAs) identified two major hotspots on chromosome 7 (Sobic. 007G153700 and Sobic.007G135000), located near the dwarfing genes Dw3 and qHT7.1. A significant peak on chromosome 2 (Sobic. 002G372100) was detected near the well-characterized maturity gene Ma2. Additionally, the gene Sobic. 003G270200, which encodes dehydrin protein and shows high expression in dry seed at grain maturity, was associated with thousand-grain weight. Several major effect SNP loci were also identified, including S01_77782180 (PVE = 13.2%) for internode length, S02_77050836 (PVE = 35.1 %) for maturity, S04_4026982 (PVE = 18.5%) for number of leaves, S05_70650422 (PVE = 10.1%) for panicle length, S05_66970432 (PVE = 11.5%) for panicle weight, S08_59054818 (PVE = 12.9%) for panicle yield.

Overall, following validation of the identified SNP loci and candidate genes regulating grain yield and related agronomic traits, these markers can be utilized in marker-assisted selection for sorghum breeding programs

sc.x: Drought stress during grain filling is a major constraint to sorghum productivity in semi-arid regions. To determine the genetic basis of post-flowering drought tolerance, we conducted a QTL mapping study using a backcross-derived population developed from the drought-tolerant donor parent B35 (a known stay-green source) and three elite recipient varieties Nganda, Golobe, and Darou.

A total of 240 BC-derived lines were evaluated under well-watered and water-stressed field conditions in Senegal across two growing seasons. Genotyping was carried out using SNP markers, and a mid-density linkage map was constructed. Phenotypic data were collected for key drought-related traits, including stay-green score, plant height, thousand grain weight (TGrW), and stress tolerance index (STI).

Several stable QTLs associated with stay- green expression, TGrW, and STI under drought stress were identified on chromosomes 1, 2, 5, and 10. Notably, QTLs such as snpSB00098, snpSB00103, and snpSB00468, previously reported for delayed senescence, showed pleiotropic effects and stability across multiple environments. Further analysis revealed environment-specific QTLs (e.g., S2_70398364, S1_55816748, S6_55263696, S2_66955986) with phenotypic variation explained (PVE) ranging from 17% to 31%, highlighting significant genotype × environment interactions. Gene annotation within QTL regions S2_72113870, S3_62340030, S8_31765612, and S9_3314960 uncovered candidate genes including SORBI_3002G245800, SORBI_3002G034700, SORBI_3003G291200, SORBI_3009G123300, SORBI_3009G123900 and others involved in drought response, chloroplast and mitochondrial function, and abiotic stress regulation.
These findings provide valuable genomic regions and candidate markers for marker-assisted selection and the development of drought-resilient sorghum cultivars for semi-arid environments.

sc.x: Understanding the genetic basis of drought-adaptive and yield-related traits is critical for accelerating sorghum improvement in water-limited environments. This study aimed to evaluate genetic performance and identify stable genomic regions associated with key drought-adaptive and productivity traits in lowland sorghum.

A panel of 338 advanced F5 sorghum lines was evaluated across two drought-prone lowland environments in Ethiopia (Kobo and Meiso). Phenotypic data were analyzed for variability, heritability, and genotypic variance. Multi-locus genome-wide association studies (ML-GWAS) were conducted to detect stable marker trait associations across environments and models.

Substantial phenotypic variation, high heritability, and predominance of genotypic variance were observed for most traits, indicating strong genetic control. Genotypes ETSC17184-8-1, ETSC17240-8-1, and ETSC17129-8-4 outperformed checks by >19% in grain yield and exhibited superior stay-green performance, highlighting their value as drought-adaptive donor lines. ML-GWAS identified 43 stable markers associated with flowering time (12), maturity (11), plant height (10), stay-green (2), grain yield (3), and grain filling rate (5). Among these, 12 QTNs (28%) were novel, while others co-localized with previously reported loci. A major locus on chromosome 7 explained 18% of phenotypic variance for plant height and co-localized with the known Dw3 region. Grain yield-associated markers exhibited pleiotropic effects and overlapped with loci controlling yield-related traits. Several loci also showed combined effects on phenology and productivity traits, indicating shared genetic regulation.

The identified stable and biologically relevant loci provide robust genomic targets for marker-assisted selection and genomic breeding. In parallel, superior genotypes with combined high yield and stay-green performance were identified as valuable donor parents. Together, these findings enable the simultaneous improvement of phenology, stay-green, and grain yield, thereby enhancing drought adaptation in lowland sorghum breeding programs.

sc.x: Stay-green (SG) is a key drought-adaptation trait in sorghum that delays leaf senescence, maintains photosynthetic activity during grain filling, and improves yield stability under terminal drought stress. However, SG and lodging resistance are complex quantitative traits influenced by multiple genes and environmental interactions. Genomic prediction offers a powerful approach to estimate the performance of these traits using genome-wide marker information. The objectives of this study were to evaluate the predictive ability of genomic prediction for SG, lodging, and plant height to assess its potential for improving selection efficiency in hybrid breeding programs.

A collaborative sorghum hybrid population was developed among three public breeding programs (USDA-ARS, Texas A&M University, and Kansas State University) and one private breeding program. Each program contributed 12 elite pollinators and 12 elite seed parents, generating approximately 1200 hybrids through a partial factorial mating design (48 × 48). Hybrid performance was evaluated across six drought-prone environments in West Texas and Central Kansas, resulting in approximately 4000 field plots, with about 600 hybrids phenotyped visually and using UAVs during the 2024–2025 season. Genomic prediction models were evaluated using repeated cross-validation.

Preliminary analyses indicated moderate predictive ability for the evaluated traits. Predictive ability ranged from 0.30–0.40 for SG, 0.31–0.37 for lodging, and 0.54–0.57 for plant height, reflecting differences in trait heritability and genetic architecture. Estimated heritability values were 0.64 for SG, 0.57 for lodging, and 0.79 for plant height. Selection of the top 20% of hybrids based on genomic predictions consistently identified genotypes with improved SG and reduced lodging.

These results demonstrate that genomic prediction can achieve moderate accuracy for complex drought-adaptive traits in sorghum hybrids. The integration of genomic prediction into sorghum breeding pipelines has strong potential to accelerate hybrid selection, improve drought resilience, and enhance breeding efficiency across diverse environments.

sc.x: Sorghum has a superior tolerance to abiotic stress and high optimal temperature for photosynthesis among major cereal crops. However, its reproductive tissues are still highly sensitive to thermal stress. Episodes of extreme heat during key developmental windows can severely reduce pollination efficiency, seed set and seed size, causing significant reductions in harvestable grain yield.

To address this vulnerability, we performed both field and controlled experiments to quantify the effects of high temperatures on sorghum panicle development from pre-booting through hard dough stages.

These experiments revealed stage-specific disruptions in reproductive tissue development and function under heat stress. In parallel, we isolated and characterized a diverse set of sorghum mutants exhibiting altered panicle heat tolerance traits, offering new genetic resources for understanding the physiological and molecular mechanisms that underlie reproductive resilience.

Collectively, this work advances a more detailed framework for improving heat resilience in reproductive biology and support ongoing efforts to develop enhanced resilient sorghum lines through targeted breeding and genetic improvement.

sc.x: Lodging is a constraint to yield stability in sorghum, particularly under water stress during grain filling, when carbon remobilisation weakens stalks. Breeding for lodging resistance is challenging because field scoring is labour-intensive and timing-sensitive, while lodging is inconsistent across environments and years and often confounded by trade-offs with grain yield. This study aimed to: (1) develop a framework to predict plot-level lodging severity in sorghum using UAV-based photogrammetric height data; (2) validate model performance at independent sites and compare UAV predictions with manual measurements for selection decisions; and (3) evaluate the utility of time-series lodging phenotypes derived from UAVs relative to standard phenotypes for genomic prediction in breeding trials.

The ensemble naïve model achieved strong performance (r = 0.80, RMSE = 17.5-18.75), explaining 67% of the variation in lodging counts. Genetic correlations (0.78-0.96) between UAV-based and manual measurements indicated consistency. Selection of the top 10% lodging-resistant candidates identified more than 75% of the same candidates using both methods. The standard UAV-based approach from a single site showed moderate ability (r = 0.55) to predict average performance across five sites, whereas time-series deviations showed higher prediction accuracy

The framework used two sites, each with two trial series and plot-level lodging counts recorded before harvest. UAV images were captured at maximum crop height, at flowering, and at lodging assessment. Height percentiles derived from image-based point clouds quantified plot height changes between flights and were used as predictors in parametric, non-parametric, and ensemble models. Reliability of UAV-predicted lodging was assessed against manual measurements using univariate and multivariate analyses. Linear deviations derived from time-series information were used to predict average individual performance from historical trials and were compared with the standard genomic prediction approach
Phenomic and genomic prediction are cost-effective tools to improve selection of lodging-resistant genotypes in sorghum breeding programs and, ultimately, yield

abstracts.t: Optimizing leaf architecture to unlock yield potential in sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench]
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Clemson University, Florence, SC, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a major cereal crop valued for its adaptability to drought-prone and marginal environments. Despite its agronomic importance, yield gains have lagged behind crops such as maize and rice. To meet rising food and bioenergy demands, sorghum productivity must be enhanced through innovative breeding strategies. Canopy architecture, particularly leaf angle, remains underutilized in breeding despite evidence from other crops showing that erect leaves improve light interception and productivity under high-density systems. This study evaluates the role of leaf angle in shaping canopy structure, photosynthetic performance, and yield across contrasting environments.

Ninety sorghum hybrids were evaluated in 2025 across three environments under irrigated (high-input) and dryland (low-input) systems using a randomized complete block design. Traits measured included yield, leaf angle (MultispeQ), intercepted PAR (iPAR) and leaf area index (LAI) using a ceptometer, and photosynthetic parameters (ΦII, LEF, qL, NPQt, SPAD). Data were collected during early grain filling in upper and lower canopy layers.

Yield and leaf angle exhibited high heritability (H<sup>2</sup> = 0.68 and 92, respectively). Dryland outyielded irrigated conditions by 648 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>, likely reflecting heat stress and irrigation interruptions. Leaf angle was stable across canopy layers (r = 0.88) and positively associated with yield, LAI, and iPAR. Dryland conditions showed higher LAI and iPAR, which were strongly correlated with yield (r = 0.58 and 0.47). Photosynthetic traits had low heritability and limited environmental effects, although irrigated conditions showed stress responses (lower LEF, higher NPQt). Multivariate analyses indicated that erect-leaf hybrids consistently formed denser canopies with improved light interception and productivity.

Sorghum yield is primarily driven by canopy architecture, where erect leaf angle enhances LAI and radiation capture. Photochemical efficiency plays a secondary role, becoming more relevant under stress. Erect-leaf hybrids represent a promising, heritable target for improving sorghum productivity across management systems.
