sc.x: Sorghum is a vital crop that is grown for food, feed, and biofuel. It thrives in water-scarce regions with high average temperatures. Although sorghum is generally considered drought and heat tolerant, its productivity can still decline under severe or prolonged stress conditions. In addition, significant variation exists among sorghum genotypes, with some lines possessing desirable agronomic traits such as grain quality, but remaining sensitive to these stresses. Understanding of bacterially mediated molecular mechanisms, with reference to rhizospheric bacteria in crop responses to drought or heat stress is limited, particularly in sorghum subjected to combined drought and heat stress.

The tolerant genotype’s rhizosphere hosted a higher abundance of bacteria associated with nitrogen cycling, including nitrification and denitrification. It also maintained arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi under drought and combined stress, supporting improved water and nutrient uptake. In contrast, the sensitive genotype’s rhizosphere was dominated by saprotrophic fungi such as Talaromyces, with functional profiles shifting toward organic matter decomposition.

This study investigated the role of soil microbes in the differential drought and heat tolerance of two contrasting sorghum genotypes. Amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene (bacteria) and ITS region (fungi) was conducted using Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing. Reads were processed with Mothur (v1.48.0) and analyzed in R using the microeco package. Taxonomic classification was performed using the SILVA v138.1 database for bacteria and the UNITE v10 database for fungi. Functional predictions were assigned using FAPROTAX for bacteria and FUNGuild and FungalTraits for fungi. Differences in taxonomic abundance and functional profiles between genotypes were evaluated using two-way ANOVA.

These findings reveal key rhizospheric microbial mechanisms associated with sorghum tolerance to drought and heat stress. Furthermore, understanding the complexity of bacterially mediated molecular mechanisms that enhance sorghum tolerance to combined drought and heat stress provides valuable insights for improving sorghum resilience under changing climatic conditions.

sc.x: The global energy transition necessitates identifying efficient alternative raw materials for thermal energy production. This study aimed to develop and validate agro-industrial processes for cultivating and using biomass sorghum (hybrid BRS 716) as a fuel source for high-pressure boilers.

Results indicated a green matter productivity of 36.27 t/ha with 55.79% of moisture. Boiler performance remained stable across all tested proportions, demonstrating the material's industrial compatibility. A significant negative correlation was observed between biomass moisture and steam production, underscoring the critical importance of moisture control for process efficiency. The most energy-efficient results were obtained with mixtures containing 58% of sorghum and 42% wood chips, which achieved steam flow increments of up to 68.7 t/h and an average energy generation of 26.6 MW.

The experimental research was conducted in a 125-hectare pilot area in Terra Rica, Paraná, Brazil. Phytotechnical management was fully mechanized, featuring a plant population of 120,000 plants/ha and glyphosate desiccation post-flowering to reduce moisture content. The harvested biomass was fragmented into 5 cm particles to ensure complete suspension burning and maximize heat release during combustion. Industrial burning tests were performed over four days, evaluating mixtures of biomass sorghum and eucalyptus wood chips in proportions ranging from 49% to 71% sorghum. Statistical analysis was performed using ANOVA and Tukey’s test (5%).

These values showed no significant difference compared to the use of 100% wood chips, confirming the high potential of the BRS 716. In conclusion, biomass sorghum is a technically viable and highly efficient alternative for large-scale energy cogeneration in modern industrial plants.

abstracts.t: LAMBDA - glutathione transferases, mystery enzymes in sorghum abiotic stress response
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: University of Copenhagen, Frederiksberg C, Denmark
University of Copenhagen, Frederiksberg C, Denmark

sc.x: Plant glutathione transferase (GST) remain poorly understood enzymes, which canonical role is detoxification of harmful metabolites and mitigation of stress. Several studies report drought-induced upregulations of GST genes in crops, and enhanced stress tolerance in model plants overexpressing them, yet the mechanisms, substrates, and in vivo functions of most GSTs remain elusive. Lambda GSTs (GSTLs) respond strongly to abiotic stress, and abiotic stress-induced oxidative stress and redox (reduction-oxidation) imbalance damages cellular proteins and metabolism. GSTLs display antioxidant activities in vitro, and their closest human homologs, omega GSTs (GSTOs), also possess antioxidant and protein-protective functions in vivo. Our research group has knockouts for all GSTL genes in sorghum, and preliminary data reveal drought-sensitive phenotypes in at least one sorghum gstl mutants. Given the strong stress responsiveness of GSTLs, the LAMBDA project aims to identify roles and functions of GSTLs in drought resilience and contributions to redox homeostasis in plants. Although GSTLs clearly respond to abiotic stress, their roles in helping plants withstand such conditions are still unresolved. This knowledge gap is especially critical given that drought is the leading cause of global crop yield losses. Understanding the physiological and molecular basis for drought resilience is essential for identifying breeding targets to achieve food security and sustainable agriculture under climate change. Even for the highly drought tolerant Sorghum bicolor, the molecular mechanisms enabling their resilience remain unclear. Using interdisciplinary approaches in redox biology, analytical chemistry, proteomics, microscopy, and enzymology, we will test the hypotheses of LAMBDA and define how GSTLs contribute to drought resilience. We will phenotype sorghum and Arabidopsis gstl mutants under drought and perform analyses of antioxidant levels, cellular redox state, oxidative protein modifications, and GSTL enzymatic functions. This work will provide new insight into plant drought tolerance mechanisms and inform breeding strategies to future‑proof crops against climate change.

abstracts.t: Strengthening the sorghum value chain from farm to fork through start-ups and incubation: A replicable model by ICAR–IIMR.
abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

a: ICAR-Indian Institute of Millets Research, Hyderabad, India

sc.x: Sorghum is a climate-resilient, nutrient-dense cereal with strong potential to address food security, malnutrition, and climate change. However, its commercialization has been limited by fragmented value chains, inadequate processing, and weak market linkages. ICAR-Indian Institute of Millets Research developed a holistic farm-to-fork model integrating production, processing, nutrition, health validation, marketing, entrepreneurship, and policy support.

The integrated interventions enhanced productivity and improved grain quality through targeted scientific cultivation practices. Advancements in processing technologies, including milling, extrusion, flaking, puffing, baking, and fermentation, enabled the development of diverse ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook sorghum-based products with improved shelf life and consumer acceptability. A total of 55 technologies were developed and commercialized at ICAR-IIMR. Nutritional and clinical evaluations demonstrated low glycemic index/load, reduced HbA1c levels, and improved micronutrient status in children, supporting their role in managing lifestyle-related diseases and enhancing nutritional security. Market adoption was strengthened through branding, labelling, packaging, and consumer awareness initiatives, including the launch of IIMR’s own brand, Eatrite. Entrepreneurship promotion through Nutrihub, Technology Business Incubator, supported over 200 sorghum-based startups through incubation, training, and technology licensing. Strategic collaborations with state governments and leading food companies such as PepsiCo, Nestle, Britannia Industries, and ITC Limited further accelerated product innovation and market expansion.

A decade-long R&D approach strengthened the sorghum value chain by linking stakeholders from farmers to consumers. Interventions included end-product-specific agronomic practices, advanced processing technologies (milling, extrusion, flaking, puffing, baking, and fermentation), and nutritional and clinical evaluation of sorghum-based foods, along with market strategies such as branding, packaging, consumer awareness, and entrepreneurship development through incubation and technology transfer.

The ICAR-IIMR model demonstrates a scalable and replicable framework for strengthening sorghum value chains globally. By integrating agriculture, technology, nutrition, and markets, it enhances farmer livelihoods, promotes climate-resilient crops, and supports sustainable, healthy food systems.

abstracts.t: Development and Optimization of High-Protein Extruded Foods from Sorghum–Soy Blends
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: ICAR-Indian Institute of Millets Research, Hyderabad, India

sc.x: The growing demand for high-protein, plant-based foods has driven the use of cereal–legume blends in extruded products. Sorghum, a climate-resilient cereal, combined with defatted soybean flour, provides a balanced composition rich in protein and dietary fiber. Low-moisture extrusion is widely used to produce shelf-stable, high-protein products with desirable texture and functionality.

A sorghum–soy blend (20% sorghum flour and 80% defatted soybean flour) was prepared and analyzed for physical and proximate properties before extrusion. Eight treatments (T1–T8) were developed under low-moisture conditions by varying barrel temperatures (65–140°C), screw speeds (26 and 28 Hz), and feed moisture levels (28% and 30%). The extrudates were evaluated for physical, functional, structural, textural, and sensory properties to identify optimal processing conditions.

Among the treatments, T8 processed at 70°C, 110°C, and 140°C in Zones 1, 2, and 3, respectively, with 30% feed moisture and a screw speed of 28 Hz, exhibited the most desirable properties. The extrudates showed favorable functional characteristics, including a water absorption index of 0.23%, a water solubility index of 0.21%, an expansion ratio of 8.1, a bulk density of 1.48 g/cm³, and a tapped density of 1.55 g/cm³. Textural analysis revealed hardness (69.97 N), fracturability (28.45 N), chewiness (11.75 N), gumminess (17.80 N), springiness (0.44), and cohesiveness (0.42), indicating a firm and structured product. Nutritionally, the optimized extrudates showed an increase in protein content from 51.96% to 56.47% and dietary fiber from 8.49% to 13.54%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the sorghum–soy blend in enhancing product quality.

The study confirmed that a sorghum–soy blend can be effectively used to produce high-protein extruded products with desirable functional, structural, and nutritional properties. The optimized condition (T8) showed superior characteristics, highlighting its potential for commercial plant-based applications.

sc.x: The brown midrib (bmr) mutants of sorghum and other C4 grasses have a visible red to brown leaf midrib in contrast to green or white midribs observed in wild-type plants. This phenotype has long been associated with reduced lignin content and altered lignin composition, which has allowed it to be used to increase forage digestibility for ruminant livestock and potential applications for conversion of biomass to biofuels and renewable chemicals. The BMR forage hybrids sold commercially contain bmr6 or bmr12 alleles, which encode loss of function mutations in cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD) and caffeic acid-O-methyltransferase (COMT) genes, respectively.

However, there are 5 other bmr loci in sorghum, bmr2, bmr19, bmr29, bmr30 and bmr31. Studies have shown the bmr plants from these five loci have modest reductions in lignin concentration as compared to bmr6 or 12 plants. Given the incremental impact of the 5 other bmr loci on lignin concentration, combining bmr alleles from different loci to create double mutants represents a potential strategy to reduce lignin concentration further and increase forage digestibility.

These studies are being conducted currently, and some combinations have shown promising preliminary results, reducing lignin further without adversely affecting plant growth. However, combinations involving bmr2 have resulted in stunted plants. Further analyses of these plants indicate the lignin concentration was not reduced beyond bmr6 bmr12 double mutant combination, which suggests alterations to the metabolic network and not a lower limit of lignin concentrations within cell walls are responsible for these growth defects. Further studies are underway to address this question.

The bmr6 and 12 mutations are proven tools to manipulate lignin synthesis in sorghum. This research addresses the challenge of cutting lignin levels further to improve forage and bioenergy feedstocks.

sc.x: Although sorghum is a promising feedstock, particularly in regions that experience drought stress and water limitations, little is known about how drought conditions impact the ease of downstream conversion to fuels and fuel products. This study is therefore designed to evaluate the environmental impact of drought stress on biomass yield, biomass quality and fermentability of three types of Sorghum in two California locations using three water regimes (postflowering drought, preflowering drought, control).

Multiple drought treatments are compared to the control, as the timing (pre-flowering versus post-flowering) of drought stress elicits different survival strategies and corresponding impacts on yield and composition. Forage type sorghum maintained the highest biomass yields across all irrigation conditions and locations. Glucose and xylose yields resulting from ionic liquid pretreatment and enzymatic saccharification were not significantly impacted by irrigation treatments but differed by location and genotype. However, Rhodosporidium toruloides grown on the resulting plant hydrolysates unexpectedly produced higher titers of bisabolene for drought-stressed sorghum samples regardless of genotype.

This study combines agronomic field trials with a high-throughput experimental pipeline to explore the field performance and liquid biofuel (bisabolene) yields resulting from three sorghum types (photosensitive forage sorghum, optimized grain sorghum and drought resistant grain sorghum) grown under pre- and post-flowering water limitations in two different California locations.

The presented study serves as both an exploration of drought’s effects on biomass convertibility to sugars and bioproducts, as well as a demonstration of the strengths and drawbacks of an end-to-end experimental pipeline.

abstracts.t: Composition and Nutritional Analysis of Nine Sorghum Cultivars from the Southern High Plains (Sorghum bicolor L.) for Human Consumption

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is a drought-tolerant cereal grain traditionally grown in arid regions of Africa and Asia and later introduced to the United States for syrup production and animal feed. Today, sorghum is gaining attention due to its sustainability, nutritional value, and versatility as a food ingredient.

Proximate analysis was conducted to develop nutritional profiles for nine sorghum cultivars grown in the Southern High Plains. Statistical analysis using Tukey’s pairwise comparison test identified significant nutritional differences among certain cultivars (p ≤ 0.05).

Nine cultivars of Sorghum bicolor grown in the Southern High Plains were analyzed to determine their nutritional composition, functional properties, and antioxidant potential. The cultivars evaluated in this study were 3401, 3489, 3480, 3372, MARCIA, 64S5BT, TS684G, BTMO5J0, and TX-430. Samples were obtained from a local West Texas producer and ground into a fine flour prior to analysis to ensure uniformity and accuracy in testing procedures.

Sorghum cultivars grown in the Southern High Plains show nutritional variability but consistently provide beneficial nutrients, including fiber, protein, and antioxidants. Darker cultivars contained higher phenolic content. Overall, sorghum demonstrates strong potential as a sustainable, gluten-free grain that can contribute to improved human nutrition, food security, and agricultural sustainability.

sc.x: Stem lodging is a major constraint in grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) production, particularly in dryland systems where post-anthesis drought accelerates senescence and weakens stem integrity. While lodging resistance is influenced by structural, compositional, and physiological traits, the specific biomechanical and geometric factors governing stalk stability under drought stress remain poorly understood.

Water-deficit conditions significantly affected the stem mechanical properties through smaller diameter, increased slenderness ratio, and lower integrated puncture score compared to the well-watered condition. Section modulus and moment of inertia were strong predictors of bending strength across treatments, and the apical internode was disproportionately vulnerable to mechanical failure. Structural optimization analysis showed that only 24.3% of stalks exhibited optimal material distribution along their length. Accelerated senescence under water-deficit conditions correlated negatively with bending strength, suggesting that premature carbon remobilization compromises stem integrity. Principal component analysis indicated that geometric traits, particularly stalk diameter, section modulus, and integrated puncture score, collectively explained bending strength more strongly.

Thirty-three diverse sorghum genotypes were evaluated under well-watered and water-deficit conditions across two growing seasons. Stem bending strength was measured under field conditions using the DARLING-lite. Rind penetration strength and integrated puncture score (IPS) were determined using an Instron universal testing system to quantify tissue mechanical properties. Biomechanical parameters, including slenderness ratio, moment of inertia, and section modulus, were calculated using engineering beam theory assuming elliptical stem geometry. Stem compositional analysis of selected genotypes was conducted using standard NREL (National renewable energy laboratory) protocols to quantify structural carbohydrates and lignin.

Geometric traits, particularly section modulus and stem diameter, are key determinants of sorghum stem strength, while compositional traits play a limited role. The vulnerability of the apical internode underscores the need for improved structural optimization to enhance lodging resistance under water-deficit conditions.

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is a water-efficient and drought-tolerant alternative to maize for silage production in semi-arid regions. However, its broader adoption as a high-quality silage crop is constrained by relatively low protein and starch digestibility. To overcome this limitation, we are pyramiding high protein digestibility (HPD) and waxy (low amylose) alleles to develop nutritionally enhanced silage sorghum. Using an EMS mutant population, we have identified the causative alleles underlying the two traits and developed molecular markers.

Subsequent backcrossing and selfing will produce homozygous double-recessive lines, which will be systematically evaluated for grain composition, digestibility, seed development, biomass yield, and overall agronomic performance. By integrating targeted allele stacking with elite germplasm improvement, this project aims to deliver high-biomass, nutrient-enriched sorghum cultivars that enhance feed efficiency and livestock productivity.

Our breeding utilizes marker-assisted backcrossing to introgress these two recessive alleles into five elite silage sorghum backgrounds, enabling precise allele tracking while minimizing reliance on labor-intensive biochemical assays. Initial crosses between F1 donor plants carrying both alleles and elite silage lines have been completed, launching the introgression pipeline.
These improved silage varieties will strengthen sorghum’s role as a resilient forage crop for water-limited production systems worldwide.

sc.x: Panicle morphology is a key determinant of grain yield, plant architecture, and environmental adaptation in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench). This study used genome-wide association analysis to investigate the genetic basis of panicle length in the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP).

Significant associations for panicle length were identified across multiple chromosomes, indicating a polygenic genetic architecture. A major and consistent locus was identified on chromosome 5 within a 200 kb interval (60.856–61.056 Mb). The lead SNP S5_60955807, was supported across GWAS analyses and was located within SORBI_3005G144600, suggesting it as a strong positional candidate gene for panicle length. Additional associated regions on chromosomes 1, 2, and 6 further supported the complex inheritance of the trait.

A total of 288 PI accessions were evaluated in 2023 and 347 PI accessions in 2025 at Fort Valley, Georgia, using a randomized complete block design with two replications. Genotypic data consisting 191,738 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers generated through genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) were analyzed. Panicle length was manually measured using a scale, and phenotype values were processed prior to association analysis. For marker-trait association (MTA) analyses, Mixed Linear Model (MLM), Bayesian-information and linkage-disequilibrium iteratively nested keyway (BLINK), and Settlement of MLM Under Progressively Exclusive Relationship (SUPER) models were used.

Beyond applications for marker-assisted breeding, these findings provide insights into how selection on panicle traits can balance yield potential, disease resistance, and environmental adaptation. The ecological and evolutionary implications highlight how panicle architecture contributes to sorghum’s diversification, domestication, and resilience across various agroecological zones, ultimately informing the development of next-generation cultivars for sustainable agriculture.

sc.x: Efficient transformation and regeneration are critical for crop improvement and functional genomics. Fortunately, recent breakthroughs in the utilization of developmental regulator (DR) genes have helped overcome the recalcitrant nature of many monocot species including sorghum to genetic transformation. However, the underlying transcriptional regulation governing DR-induced somatic embryogenesis and regeneration competence remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the molecular mechanisms associated with DR-mediated enhancement of transformation in multiple sorghum types (grain, forage and bioenergy) previously difficult-to-transform.

By leveraging DR genes, we successfully achieved genetic transformation and regeneration in two previously untested sorghum genotypes. Comparative transcriptome analysis following DR-mediated transformation of these genotypes revealed key transcriptional networks underlying the process. Furthermore, we identified sorghum-specific novel candidate regulators associated with cellular reprogramming, differentiation, and somatic embryogenesis capacity, which may contribute to the development of more efficient and genotype-independent sorghum transformation systems.

By employing DR genes such as BABY BOOM, WUSCHEL and GIF-GRF, we established robust Agrobacterium-mediated transformation systems using multiple explant types (leaf and immature embryo) and expanded transformability to genotypes not previously amenable to regeneration. Integration of a visual reporter RUBY and AmCYAN expression enabled rapid and efficient identification of transformed tissues. To dissect the regulatory pathways driving embryogenic reprogramming, we performed transcriptome profiling during early stages of somatic embryogenesis.

Collectively, this work not only provides practical advances in transformation methodology but, most importantly provides fundamental insights into the transcriptional regulation underlying DR-mediated regeneration, offering a framework for discovering novel targets and mechanisms for improving transformation efficiency in other recalcitrant monocot species.

sc.x: Water scarcity in arid and semi-arid regions necessitates the exploration of alternative irrigation sources to sustain agricultural productivity. Global oil and gas extraction generates substantial volumes of produced water (PW), with the United States contributing 32%, a significant share of global PW output. The Permian Basin alone is among the most prolific sources, where produced water is generated in volumes that far exceed oil production with water-to-oil ratio typically being 4:1 depending on reservoir age and formation characteristics. This disproportionate ratio underscores the scale of PW presenting as an environmental liability and an underutilized water resource. Following polishing and desalination treatment, Polished Desalinated Produced Water (PDPW) has the potential to serve as a viable substitute for conventional freshwater for irrigating sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.). This study evaluated the agronomic feasibility and biological implications of using PDPW for sorghum production through a multi-scale assessment integrating water quality characterization, plant physiology, tissue chemistry, and rhizosphere soil and plant microbial dynamics. Initial irrigation suitability of PDPW was established through comprehensive water quality profiling with comparative benchmarking against local groundwater.

Controlled environment and field-scale irrigation experiments were conducted with grain sorghum. Morphometric parameters such as plant emergence, plant height, biomass and physiological parameters included transpiration rate, chlorophyll content, water use efficiency, and assimilate rate(A) were recorded. Plant tissue chemical analysis including macro and micronutrient uptake and heavy metal accumulation was performed to assess the extent of contaminant transfer from irrigation water to plant biomass. Soil and plant microbial community structure and function were characterized using amplicon sequencing (16S rRNA and ITS) to evaluate shifts in bacterial and fungal diversity under PDPW irrigation relative to groundwater.

Overall, this research helped explore the environmental and agronomic viability of PDPW reuse, supporting options for sustainable water-management strategies in energy-producing regions such as the Permian Basin.

sc.x: Photoperiod-sensitive (PS) sorghum can maintain vegetative growth for a longer period. As such, PS sorghum has potential to produce high biomass either for biofuel or forage purposes. In the U.S. Southern Great Plains, water is a major limiting factor affecting sorghum production. Therefore, developing sorghum genotypes with improved drought tolerance is critical for sustainable production. The objective of this study was to better understand physiological responses of PS sorghum genotypes to drought stress and identify important plant traits related to biomass production.

A two-year (2018 and 2019) field study was conducted in two locations in the Southern Great Plains (Colby, KS and Bushland, TX). Six PS sorghum genotypes (TAM08001, TAM17500, TAM17600, TAM17650, TAM17800, TAM18000) were grown at three water levels (dryland, irrigation at 50% and 100% ET requirements). During the growing season, agronomic and physiological measurements were taken, including plant height, leaf traits, stem traits, and aboveground biomass.

Sorghum biomass is largely determined by soil water at Bushland, TX. Plant growth and biomass accumulation were significantly reduced under dryland conditions due to drought stress. In contrast, the variation of plant biomass was smaller at Colby, KS, and differences in plant parameters were generally not significant between the two irrigation treatments. For most of the plant parameters, genotypic differences were significant regardless of soil water regime. Among the six genotypes, TAM08001, TAM17650 and TAM17800 consistently performed better than other genotypes, particualy under water limited conditions. The greater biomass was positively related to several plant traits such as leaf area, leaf dry weight, stem diameter, stem dry weight and specific leaf area.

High biomass can be achieved under dryland conditions in western Kansas but requires limited irrigation in Texas High Plains. The plant traits related to greater biomass can be used for developing new sorghum hybrids.

abstracts.t: Deciphering Root Adaptations and Water-Use Strategies in Sorghum Under Drought and Well-Watered Conditions

a: ICAR- INDIAN INSTITUTE OF MILLETS RESEARCH, Hyderabad, India

sc.x: Sorghum, a C4 crop and one of the world’s major cereals, is predominantly cultivated in semi-arid regions where water scarcity is a recurring constraint. Climate change–induced increases in drought frequency, intensity, and duration are further threatening sorghum productivity, causing yield losses of up to 30%. Given sorghum’s emerging role as a climate-resilient crop, there is a need to better understand adaptive traits that sustain yield under water-limited conditions. This study focuses on root system architecture, transpiration behavior, and water-use efficiency as critical determinants of drought adaptation. The objective was to evaluate how sorghum genotypes modulate root traits and water-use strategies under contrasting moisture regimes to identify key traits that can be targeted for improving drought tolerance and yield stability.

To elucidate genotypic variation in root traits and their relationship with water component traits and above-ground performance, post-rainy (rabi) sorghum genotypes were evaluated under well-watered (WW) and water-stressed (WS) conditions using a lysimeter-based phenotyping system. Root architectural traits such as crown root number, nodal root angle, root length, depth, and root length density, were quantified using a mesocosm fabricated for sorghum, along with water use, transpiration efficiency (TE), and biomass productivity. Root anatomical traits such as xylem vessel diameter, number, and cortical cell area were characterized through microtome cross-sections to assess structural plasticity under drought.

Significant genotypic differences were observed in root growth patterns and anatomical modifications under WS conditions. Genotypes with deeper and denser roots exhibited enhanced water extraction and higher TE, while narrower xylem vessels and thicker cortical layers were associated with improved water conservation. Correlation and principal component analyses revealed strong associations between root depth, TE, and drought tolerance indices.

These findings highlight the importance of integrative root and water-use traits in identifying physiologically superior sorghum genotypes & breeding drought-resilient Rabi sorghum adapted to rainfed production systems.

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) is a promising C4 bioenergy crop valued for its high biomass yield and drought tolerance. Stem lodging poses a critical challenge, compromising mechanical harvestability and feedstock quality. This study was aimed to dissect the genetic architecture of stem structural integrity traits bending strength (BS), force applied (FA), and average stem diameter (ASD) in bioenergy sorghum using genome-wide association analysis (GWAS).

Significant marker–trait associations were detected across multiple chromosomes. Chromosomes 1, 3, 5, and 7 showed associations with BS and FA, while chromosomes 2, 7, and 9 were linked to ASD. Chromosomes 5 and 7 exhibited the strongest and most consistent signals, with chromosome 7 suggesting pleiotropic effects influencing multiple traits simultaneously. These co-localizations point to shared genomic regions governing stem mechanical properties.

A total of 345 accessions from the Bioenergy Association Panel (BAP), obtained from the USDA gene bank, were evaluated during the 2025 growing season at Fort Valley State University in a randomized complete block design with two replications. Stem mechanical traits such as BS and FA were measured using the DARLING ( Device for Assessing Resistance to Lodging In Grains) instrument and ASD was manually measured using Vernier caliper. GWAS was performed using a Mixed Linear Model (MLM) via the GAPIT package in R, with principal component analysis, kinship, and population structure matrices incorporated to minimize confounding effects.

This study identified key genomic loci associated with stem mechanical and morphological traits in bioenergy sorghum. The findings provide a solid foundation for marker-assisted breeding strategies aimed at improving lodging resistance and biomass productivity.

abstracts.t: Leveraging Translational Genomics to Enhance Sorghum Starch Quality
abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

a: Purdue University, Department of Agronomy, West Lafayette, United States
Purdue University, Department of Agronomy, West Lafayette, United States

sc.x: Sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] is an important cereal crop for food and feed production worldwide. Starch is the largest component of the grain and contributes directly to cooking quality, digestibility, and end-use functionality. In recent years, genes controlling starch structure and composition have been identified, including granule-bound starch synthase (waxy), starch branching enzyme IIb (amylose extender), and soluble starch synthase IIa (sugary). These genes are known to play critical roles in starch quality in cereal crops like maize and rice.

We are using chemically induced and naturally occurring genetic variation in these starch biosynthesis genes to characterize their effects on grain quality through translational genomics. Genetic analyses include complementation testing, segregation analysis, and molecular mapping of both EMS-induced mutants and native variants from exotic sorghum germplasm. Starch composition is being evaluated through amylose content analysis, gelatinization testing, and gel consistency measurements to link specific genetic variants to functional starch properties.

We have identified at least three genes that play important roles in starch gelatinization and composition in sorghum. Induced mutations in waxy, starch branching enzyme IIb, and soluble starch synthase IIa produce distinct starch profiles with altered amylose content and gelatinization properties. Additionally, native variants from exotic germplasm sources exhibit novel starch phenotypes that do not correspond to previously characterized induced mutations, suggesting the presence of new alleles or additional genes influencing starch quality.

Both induced and native genetic variants in starch biosynthesis genes are being used to develop food-grade sorghum with novel starch characteristics. By introgressing these genes into elite breeding lines, we aim to create varieties with improved digestibility, cooking quality, and end-use functionality. This translational genomics approach creates new opportunities for expanding food-grade sorghum utilization and strengthening the competitiveness of sorghum in domestic and international markets.

sc.x: The utility and value of sorghum lignocellulosic can be improved by reducing lignin content and by producing value-added coproducts. Engineered sorghum lines that accumulate protocatechuate (DHBA) and 4-hydroxybenzoate (4HBA) were obtained via the expression of bacterial QsuB and UbiC genes, respectively. The goal of this study is to generate hybrids between these engineered lines and brown midrib (BMR) varieties to stack coproduct and low-lignin traits.

Hybrids were generated by crossing in the greenhouse and field-tested at two locations in California (Kearney -KARE- and UC Davis -UCD-). Biomass from plants harvested at the soft dough stage was used for yield measurement, compositional analysis, and coproduct quantification.

Two BMR hybrid lines with coproduct accumulation were successfully created. The BMR x QsuB hybrid showed higher amounts of DHBA in stover biomass at both locations. Lignin content was reduced and higher amount of glucose and xylose were released after biomass pretreatment and saccharification. Similar reductions of biomass were observed between the hybrid and BMR parent at both sites, but the hybrid produced more biomass at the KARE site. The BMR x UbiC hybrid showed significant 4-HBA accumulation at both locations. Lignin reduction was greater at the KARE site. A reduction of biomass yields was observed at both sites, which was stronger than that of the BMR parent at the KARE site.

Expression of QsuB in BMR mutant does not impact further biomass yield. For the BMR x Qsub hybrid, KARE appears to be a better site to supply DHBA and fermentable sugars. However, expressing UbiC in BMR background further reduces biomass yield at the KARE site. Thus, the UCD site is preferred to supply 4HBA and fermentable sugars for this hybrid. The BMR trait appears variable under different soil types and field testing at additional locations is needed to validate hybrids performance.

sc.x: Due to increasing summer drought associated with climate change, multi-cut Sorghum bicolor is being discussed as a potential complement for summer forage production in Switzerland. However, only limited data are available on yield performance, forage quality, and the potential release of hydrogen cyanide (HCN) of the varieties available on the market. The aim of this study was therefore to evaluate multi-cut sorghum varieties for forage production under Swiss cultivation conditions.

Seven sorghum varieties were evaluated in field trials conducted at two sites in Switzerland (Zurich: 2019–2020; Posieux: 2023). The trials were arranged in randomized complete block designs with four replicates and managed under site-specific conditions, aiming for three cuts per season. Measurements included yield, forage quality parameters, and plant height. Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) potential was determined in selected .

The achieved yields, showed an average total production over three cuts of 106±20 dt DM ha⁻¹, with the first cut having the highest yield (41±12 dt DM ha⁻¹) and the other cuts showing decreasing yields. Raw protein averaged 135±36.0 g kg⁻¹ DM, digestible organic matter 67.5±5.3%, and net energy for lactation (NEL) 5.5±0.6 MJ kg⁻¹ DM per cut across varieties. The varieties differed significantly in total biomass and yield per cut, but not in forage quality parameters, except for NEL. The measured HCN potential were predominantly within a non-critical range (<500 mg HCN kg<sup>-1</sup> DM), although one sample exceeded this threshold.

Overall, yield and, to a lesser extent, forage quality were influenced by variety choice, while HCN potential levels were generally within a safe range, but highlight the importance of careful management. However, further trials are required to allow a more precise differentiation between varieties, particularly across a wider range of sites, in order to strengthen general recommendations for Switzerland.

sc.x: Sorghum originates from Africa but adapts well to temperate climates. The crop requires little water, is drought tolerant, and shows resistance to major maize pests such as the European corn borer and the western corn rootworm. Due to its moderate nitrogen demand and robustness, sorghum is considered a promising option for crop diversification and climate-resilient farming systems. In Switzerland, sorghum is currently grown on approximately 400 ha, mainly as a forage crop, and can generally be cultivated in regions suitable for maize production. Sugar sorghum (Sorghum bicolor var. saccharatum) accumulates high concentrations of fermentable sugars in its stems, comparable to sugarcane, suggesting potential for the production of regional spirits. This study evaluated the suitability of sugar sorghum varieties for distillation under Swiss conditions.

Distillates produced from concentrated sorghum juice showed an aromatic profile similar to white rum while retaining a distinctive regional character. In contrast, distillates obtained from raw juice exhibited more pronounced herbal and vegetal notes. These results demonstrate that sugar sorghum can produce spirits with diverse aromatic profiles depending on processing methods.

Field trials with several sugar sorghum varieties were conducted in Zurich (Switzerland) from 2022 to 2024. Juice extracted from the sorghum stems was fermented either directly as raw juice or after concentration and subsequent re-dilution. The fermented mash was then distilled, and the resulting spirits were evaluated through sensory analysis. Aromatic profiles were compared with established spirit categories such as rum, grain spirits and baijiu.

Sugar sorghum shows promising potential as a raw material for the production of innovative regional spirits in Switzerland. Cultivating sugar-rich sorghum varieties could offer new opportunities for local distilleries while supporting crop diversification and climate-resilient agriculture. However, further trials are needed to confirm these preliminary results and optimize production processes.

sc.x: Understanding the genetic control of growth rate will facilitate the development of improved forage sorghums with superior biomass accumulation. A prior Genome Wide Association Study (GWAS) using a photoperiod-sensitive panel (PSP) mapped loci associated with growth rate, but narrowing causal candidate genes is challenging due to the high linkage disequilibrium (LD) in sorghum. In this study, we aim to conduct a Transcriptome Wide Association Study (TWAS), which in conjunction with previously associated genomic regions, will facilitate the identification of candidate genes controlling growth rates for further functional validation.

Integration of TWAS results with previously identified genomic regions reduced the number of candidate genes within the high-LD regions while identifying new novel expression-associated genes. These results enhanced mapping resolution relative to GWAS alone and prioritized candidate genes responsible for growth rate variation in photoperiod sensitive sorghum.

Growth rate was estimated using leaf, stem and total biomass weights obtained over the growing season and parameters derived from a beta growth model. Bulk RNA-seq data was obtained from vegetative meristematic tissue because of its biological role in plant growth and development. Sequencing reads were processed through a bioinformatic pipeline, and read counts were normalized using Transcripts Per Million (TPM) and the R package, DESeq. The normalized values were subsequently transformed to a scale of 0 to 2 for analysis with the Compressed Linear Mixed Model in the R package GAPIT.

This approach provides a framework for refining genomic regions in high-LD crops and prioritizing candidate genes contributing to biomass accumulation. The use of meristematic tissue further establishes a resource that could be leveraged to investigate the genetic architecture of additional traits in sorghum.

sc.x: Sorghum is a cornerstone forage crop in semi-arid agriculture, yet its adoption is persistently limited by dhurrin-derived hydrogen cyanide toxicity, particularly under drought and other abiotic stresses. The recent development of prussic acid-free (PF) sorghum, achieved through disruption of the first committed step in dhurrin biosynthesis, represents a major breakthrough for forage safety. However, eliminating a central defensive metabolite raises a fundamental question: how does sorghum compensate metabolically, and does this come at a cost under stress? At present, the metabolic plasticity and stress robustness of PF genotypes remain largely unknown. To address this gap, we evaluated PF and non-PF sorghum hybrids across field and controlled environments.

Field-based untargeted metabolomics revealed reprogramming in PF-sorghum, with a shift away from cyanogenic metabolism toward phenylpropanoid and flavonoid pathways, alongside enrichment of stress-associated signaling compounds. To test the robustness of these responses, independent PF and non-PF hybrids were subjected to salt, drought, and combined stress under greenhouse conditions. Measurements included chlorophyll content (SPAD), biomass accumulation, forage quality parameters, expression profiling of drought- and salinity-responsive genes (qRT-PCR), and metabolomic profiling at at vegetative and soft-dough stage.

Our preliminary results demonstrate that PF sorghum is not merely a safer forage option but exhibits adaptive metabolic rewiring that supports performance under stress. This work provides the first integrated framework linking cyanogenic pathway disruption to whole-plant resilience, advancing PF sorghum as a viable solution for climate-resilient and livestock-safe agriculture.

sc.x: Stomatal regulation controls the balance between carbon gain and water loss, but its use in sorghum breeding is limited due to a poor understanding of its genetic basis and a lack of scalable phenotyping tools.

Analysis of 311 diverse sorghum accessions (~12,000 leaf images) revealed strong genetic variation in stomatal traits. Genome-wide association mapping identified 71 loci controlling stomatal density and size, including 38 environment-specific loci, indicating both genetic control and environmental plasticity. Stomatal density and size showed a consistent inverse relationship, suggesting coordinated regulation. Haplotype variation influenced photosynthesis, stomatal conductance, transpiration, and intrinsic water-use efficiency, supporting their functional relevance. To overcome phenotyping limitations, a field-deployable platform combining handheld microscopy and machine learning was developed, enabling rapid and accurate trait measurement (R² ≈ 0.97) and supporting large-scale, multi-environment data collection. This data was integrated into genomic selection models using 200 high-yielding hybrids. The models captured additive, dominance, and genotype × environment effects, achieving moderate prediction accuracy and improved hybrid prediction. This approach enables efficient selection while reducing reliance on labor-intensive phenotyping. Across environments, stomatal density was positively associated with yield, whereas stomatal conductance showed a negative relationship, indicating that productivity depends on coordinated structural and functional traits.
This study develops a trait-based breeding framework by integrating genetic analysis, high-throughput phenotyping, and genomic selection.

Overall, the results support an ideotype with higher stomatal density and smaller, more efficient stomata. This study establishes stomatal traits as practical targets for improving water-use efficiency and yield stability in sorghum.

abstracts.t: Grain Sorghum Grazing Systems For Livestock Utilization in Late Summer and Winter
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: University of Missouri, Columbia, United States
University of Missouri, Columbia, United States

sc.x: Feed costs represent the largest expense in livestock production systems, with winter feeding accounting for a substantial portion of annual inputs. A potential strategy to reduce these costs is the use of standing grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.) as a winter grazing resource, allowing livestock to harvest feed directly and reduce reliance on harvested forages.

Field experiments were conducted at the University of Missouri Bradford Research Center (38.9° N, 92.2° W) during the 2022 and 2023 growing seasons to evaluate the nutritional quality of grain sorghum forage and grain under winter grazing conditions. Grain sorghum was planted in 30-inch (76-cm) rows at a seeding rate of 120,000 seeds per acre (297,000 seeds ha⁻¹).

Results from 2022 and 2023 indicated that whole-plant grain sorghum averaged 7.1% crude protein (CP) and 72% total digestible nutrients (TDN) during December, demonstrating suitability as an energy-dense winter feed. Subsequent experiments in 2024 and 2025 evaluated temporal changes in forage quality and biomass accumulation from late summer through winter. Whole-plant quality in August averaged 9.8% CP and 58.6% TDN, while September values declined to 6.2% CP and increased to 69.1% TDN. These changes correspond with plant maturation and the allocation of resources toward grain development, increasing starch concentration in the seed head. Dry matter production increased substantially from 7,164 lb acre<sup>-1</sup> (8,024 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>) in August to 14,021 lb acre<sup>-1</sup> (15,704 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>) in September. Forage quality and total dry matter remained relatively consistent from November through February with 68% TDN and 6.2% CP, indicating minimal deterioration of standing grain sorghum during the winter grazing period.

These results demonstrate that grain sorghum can provide a high-yielding, nutritionally adequate forage source for winter grazing, offering producers an opportunity to reduce feed costs while maintaining livestock performance.

sc.x: Recombination is a fundamental meiotic process that generates genetic diversity and underpins plant breeding by creating novel allele combinations and breaking unfavourable linkages. However, crossovers are unevenly distributed along chromosomes, largely confined to sub‑telomeric regions, leaving much of the genome under‑recombined. In sorghum, recombination variation across diverse genetic backgrounds remains poorly understood. This study aimed to systematically characterise recombination variability across multiple sorghum populations and develop a framework that moves beyond traditional consensus mapping approaches to capture population‑specific recombination landscapes.

High‑quality linkage maps were constructed for 18 F₂ populations derived from crosses among 13 racially diverse sorghum parental lines. A scalable, continuously updatable framework was developed to integrate multiple genetic maps. Novel statistical approaches, incorporating splines within mixed models, were applied to quantify regional variation in recombination rates along chromosomes and to characterise recombination landscapes within each population.

Substantial fine‑scale variation in recombination was detected among populations. Certain genomic regions exhibited elevated recombination in specific genetic backgrounds while showing reduced or absent recombination in others, revealing pronounced population‑specific patterns. In contrast, some regions displayed consistently low variability across populations, suggesting conserved recombination landscapes. As additional populations were integrated, the consensus recombination landscape became progressively refined, with total map length decreasing from 1,620.2 cM (three populations) to 1,532.8 cM (fifteen populations), indicating increasing stability and representativeness.

The mixed‑model spline framework developed here offers a scalable and dynamic approach to integrating genetic linkage maps while preserving population‑specific recombination variation. Anchored to physical genome coordinates, it enables seamless updating of consensus recombination landscapes and can be readily adapted to alternative assemblies or pan‑genome references. Taken together, this framework provides a robust resource for informed breeding decisions with direct relevance to sorghum genetics and breeding.

sc.x: Drought limits sorghum productivity in dryland systems. While above-ground traits are well studied, below-ground processes-including root architecture, rhizosphere microbiome dynamics, and metabolic regulation-remain poorly understood. In sorghum–legume intercropping, these interactions are shaped by nitrogen transfer and microbial activity. Brassinosteroid signalling regulates phenylpropanoid metabolism, influencing lignin and flavonoid accumulation. This study investigates flavonoids as key drivers of root structure, barrier formation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress responses.

Experimental systems have been established under both field and controlled conditions. Preliminary results show genotype-dependent variation in root architecture, water uptake, and metabolic profiles. Ongoing analyses are expected to reveal coordinated shifts in rhizosphere microbiomes, carbon and nitrogen allocation, and phenylpropanoid metabolism, influencing root barrier formation and microbial recruitment under drought stress. Complementary field trials by EIAR and UQ assess diverse sorghum intercropping systems, capturing genotype × environment × management interactions, with root traits and soil water dynamics analysed using electromagnetic induction (EMI)-based phenotyping.

Stable isotope (¹³C and ¹⁵N) labelling is used to trace carbon and nitrogen fluxes between Vigna unguiculata and Sorghum bicolor intercop or sole crops under drought stress in pot experiments. Nutrient dynamics are analysed using ICP-based methods, and root–rhizosphere samples are subjected to microbiome and multi-omics analyses. In parallel, S. bicolor wild type and brassinosteroid receptor mutants are tested under PEG-induced drought, with or without methyl jasmonate. Root tissues are examined for lignin and suberin deposition, alongside gene expression and omics analyses to link hormonal regulation with rhizosphere processes.

This study provides a systems-level understanding of drought resilience by linking root traits, microbiome dynamics, nutrient fluxes, and hormone-regulated metabolism. Integrating field and mechanistic insights of below-ground traits and molecular pathways to improve sorghum performance and adaptive responses. These findings will support breeding strategies and development of resilient sorghum–legume systems under changing climate stress conditions.

sc.x: Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) yield components are sensitive to canopy and stand reductions caused by hail and severe weather, yet responses may have shifted with advances in genetics and management.

Field experiments conducted in Burleson County, TX (2022–2024) evaluated timing and severity of leaf area reduction (0, 33, 66, 100%) imposed at GS2 (6-leaf), GS4 (flag leaf), GS6 (flowering), and GS7 (soft dough) using a randomized complete block design with five replications. Complementary trials conducted from 2017–2020 in College Station, TX and Manhattan, KS evaluated stand reductions (0, 25, 50, 75, 90%) applied at GS2, GS5, and GS7 at two seeding rates in a split-plot randomized block design with four replications.

Across environments, yield response depended strongly on growth stage severity of canopy or plant stand loss. Leaf area peaked near GS4, and reductions at GS4 and GS6 significantly decreased grain yield through reductions in seeds per head and kernel size. Leaf loss at GS2 showed substantial recovery via subsequent leaf development, while GS7 defoliation resulted in minimal yield reduction. Similarly, stand reduction experiments demonstrated that early-season plant loss allowed compensation through tillering and maintenance of panicle density, sustaining yield up to 50% stand loss at GS2 in Kansas and comparable levels in Texas. Compensation at GS5 was primarily associated with increased grain number per panicle, while GS7 reductions resulted in substantial yield losses, exceeding 85% at severe stand reductions.

Machine learning approaches, including gradient boosting, improved prediction of yield loss relative to traditional regression methods, achieving prediction errors near 10–11%. Results demonstrate that sorghum maintains substantial plasticity to early-season canopy and stand loss, while late-season damage substantially limits yield potential, informing improved decision support following hail events.

sc.x: Sorghum is the fifth largest cereal crop in the world and is used as staple food, animal feed and for other industrial purposes. With climate change and an increasing world population, the demand for improved sorghum varieties and more basic and industrial sorghum research is increasing. The latest biotechnologies have facilitated sorghum research already over the recent years, however development in grain yield is still limited compared to other crops such as barley and rice. New genetic variation can be introduced by applying gene editing or classical mutagenesis with chemicals or radiation.

Here we applied Ethyl Methanesulfonate (EMS) to create a sorghum library consisting of seeds harvested from 150.000 M1 Sorghum bicolor (BTx623) plants. This is the largest sorghum mutant resource to date and is estimated to provide around 240% coverage of all potential EMS mutation sites. Whole-genome sequencing of M3 plants showed a positive correlation between EMS concentration and mutation load, with 50 to 400 non-synonymous mutations in gene coding sequences per plant. These mutations can rapidly and efficiently be screened for with FIND-IT (Fast Identification of Nucleotide variants by droplet DigITal PCR), allowing identification of new genetic variants of interest within days. Over 70 different genetic variants have been identified from this library so far, and the latest developments will showcase the strength of this library in combination with FIND-IT, including engineering sorghum plants to replace fossil carbon.
Since the methodology is GMO free, the newly identified genetic variants can directly be used in breeding programs worldwide, thereby rapidly improving sorghum grain yield or stress resilience.

sc.x: Grain sorghum is major crop in the U.S. Southern Great Plains. Accurate quantification of leaf appearance and phenological development is important for crop management. The objective of this study was to investigate leaf appearance and major phenological stages in grain sorghum hybrids with differing maturity classes in the Texas High Plains.

A two-year (2024 & 2025) field study was conducted at Bushland, TX. Four hybrids (two short maturity, one medium maturity and one medium-full maturity) were grown in two planting dates (PD1 and PD2). The experiment was arranged as a split-plot design with the planting date as main plot and hybrid as sub-plot. The two planting dates were May 22 (PD1) and June 5 (PD2) in 2024, and June 13 (PD1) and June 30 (PD2) in 2025, respectively. Major phenological stages from emergence to maturity, and total (TLN) and fully expanded leaves (FEL) on main stem were recorded. Growing degree days (GDD) was calculated using daily maximum and minimum temperatures. The leaf appearance rate (LAR) was calculated as the slope of linear regression between FEL and GDDs.

In 2024, plants in PD2 had less GDDs at the major phenological stages. However, plants in both planting dates had similar GDDs for major phenological stages in 2025. In general, short matuiry hybrids required less GDDs to reach major stages than longer maturity hybrids. The effects of planting date and hybrid on LAR were minimal. The variation of plants among planting dates and hybrids was mainly contributed by the total number of leaves on main stem, and plants in early planting in 2024 and longer maturity hybrids had more main stem leaves.
The data from this study are important for timing and modeling leaf appearance and major phenological stages in grain sorghum in the Texas High Plains.

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is the fifth most important cereal crop globally and is widely used for food, feed, and biofuel production. This study aimed to identify genetic variations associated with yield-related seed traits in a diverse sorghum panel.

MLM identified significant SNP associated with the weight, seed count, yield per panicle count on chromosomes 1,4 and 8. Manhattan plots showed strong peaks above the significance threshold(p=10<sup>-6</sup>) revealed strong SNP associations for the traits. Correlation analysis revealed that 1000 seed weight showed a significant positive association with kernel length and width, while the kernel length -to-width ratio exhibited a positive correlation with the seed weight and kernel size trait, highlighting their contribution to yield variation.

A total of 288 PI accessions from the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP) were obtained from the USDA Plant Genetic Resources Conservation Unit in Griffin, Georgia. The experiment was conducted in a randomized complete block design with two replications during 2023 growing season at Fort Valley, Georgia. Seeds were phenotype using the QM3i Vibe high-throughput imaging system to measure seed length, width, area, perimeter, and 1000-seed weight, which enables rapid and automated acquisition of large-scale phenotypic data across numerous samples improving the efficiency and accuracy of the trait measurement Genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) data were analyzed along with these phenotypic traits using TASSEL for genome-wide association studies (GWAS).

These results demonstrate that GWAS, combined with high-throughput phenotyping, can identify genetic loci underlying key agronomic traits, providing insights into the genetic basis of yield traits in sorghum and can support future crop improvement efforts.

abstracts.t: High-Throughput Quantification of Midrib Color Reveals Allelic Series at Dry and Regulatory Networks of Cell Wall Biosynthesis in Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, United States

sc.x: Plant cell walls, composed primarily of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, are central to plant structure and biomass utilization. In sorghum, lignin content directly affects forage digestibility and biofuel conversion efficiency, making cell wall composition a key target for crop improvement. Classical mutants such as brown midrib (BMR) and variation at the Dry locus show that lignin biosynthesis can be visually reflected in midrib coloration. However, these traits are typically assessed qualitatively, limiting the ability to capture continuous variation and fully exploit natural diversity for genetic discovery.

Genome-wide association analysis in 888 individuals with 6.4 million markers identified strong associations between midrib brightness traits and a locus on chromosome 6 corresponding to Dry, a NAC transcription factor. Fine-mapping using pySuSiE resolved this signal into two credible sets in repulsion linkage disequilibrium, consistent with independently derived loss-of-function alleles. These allelic classes define functionally distinct haplotypes that generate quantitative variation in midrib color. Integration of population-scale RNA-seq data showed that genes involved in secondary cell wall biosynthesis were consistently downregulated in loss-of-function genotypes.

To address this, we developed a high-throughput image analysis pipeline to quantitatively measure midrib color across a sorghum diversity panel. Using ~10,000 field images from three environments, the pipeline applies computer vision methods to isolate midrib tissue under variable conditions, including anthracnose pressure. Color features extracted in HSV and RGB space enabled precise, continuous phenotyping at population scale.

This work demonstrates that high-throughput phenotyping can serve as a scalable tool to dissect gene function and regulatory networks using natural diversity, providing new opportunities to accelerate genetic improvement of biomass-related traits in sorghum.

sc.x: Lodging is a constraint to yield stability in sorghum, particularly under water stress during grain filling, when carbon remobilisation weakens stalks. Breeding for lodging resistance is challenging because field scoring is labour-intensive and timing-sensitive, while lodging is inconsistent across environments and years and often confounded by trade-offs with grain yield. This study aimed to: (1) develop a framework to predict plot-level lodging severity in sorghum using UAV-based photogrammetric height data; (2) validate model performance at independent sites and compare UAV predictions with manual measurements for selection decisions; and (3) evaluate the utility of time-series lodging phenotypes derived from UAVs relative to standard phenotypes for genomic prediction in breeding trials

The framework used two sites, each with two trial series and plot-level lodging counts recorded before harvest. UAV images were captured at maximum crop height, at flowering, and at lodging assessment. Height percentiles derived from image-based point clouds quantified plot height changes between flights and were used as predictors in parametric, non-parametric, and ensemble models. Reliability of UAV-predicted lodging was assessed against manual measurements using univariate and multivariate analyses. Linear deviations derived from time-series information were used to predict average individual performance from historical trials and were compared with the standard genomic prediction approach

The ensemble naïve model achieved strong performance (r = 0.80, RMSE = 17.5-18.75), explaining 67% of the variation in lodging counts. Genetic correlations (0.78-0.96) between UAV-based and manual measurements indicated consistency. Selection of the top 10% lodging-resistant candidates identified more than 75% of the same candidates using both methods. The standard UAV-based approach from a single site showed moderate ability (r = 0.55) to predict average performance across five sites, whereas time-series deviations showed higher prediction accuracy
Phenomic and genomic prediction are cost-effective tools to improve selection of lodging-resistant genotypes in sorghum breeding programs and, ultimately, yield

abstracts.t: Integrated Micro-Dosing of Diammonium Phosphate and Sesame Seeds for Sustainable Control of Striga and Yield Improvement in Sorghum under Dryland Conditions in Niger
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: INRAN, NIGER, Niger

sc.x: Sorghum is a key staple crop in sub-Saharan Africa, valued for its resilience to harsh conditions. However, its production in Niger is constrained by climate change, poor soil fertility, and Striga hermonthica infestation, which causes severe yield losses. Although several control methods exist, their adoption remains limited among smallholder farmers. Integrated, low-cost strategies such as fertilizer micro-dosing (DAP) and sesame use show promising potential for reducing Striga impact and improving sorghum productivity.

Nitrogen and phosphorus deficiencies play a major role in increasing Striga hermonthica infestation in sorghum systems. This study evaluated the effects of DAP micro-dosing (0, 2, and 5 g) and sesame seed application (0, 0.5, and 1.5 g) on Striga infestation and sorghum performance. The results showed that DAP at 2 g significantly reduced Striga emergence and improved plant vigor, while sesame at 1.5 g also effectively decreased Striga infestation. The combined application of DAP and sesame produced a synergistic effect, leading to greater suppression of Striga and a significant increase in sorghum grain yield.

The study was conducted at the Konni research station (Tahoua, Niger), a major sorghum-growing area with 500–600 mm annual rainfall and high Striga pressure. A 3 × 3 factorial design with three replications tested DAP (0, 2, 5 g) and sesame seed doses (0, 0.5, 1.5 g), resulting in nine treatments. The field was ploughed and artificially infested with 1 g of Striga seeds per hill. Sorghum was sown at 0.80 m spacing with 5–6 seeds per hill, later thinned to three plants per planting hole

DAP micro-dosing at 2 g significantly reduced Striga emergence and distribution, while sesame application at 1.5 g also lowered infestation levels. Their combined use showed a synergistic effect, effectively suppressing Striga and significantly improving sorghum grain yield.

sc.x: Sorghum aphid (Melanaphis sorghi) remains a major constraint to sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) production, reducing plant vigor, biomass, and grain yield across diverse environments. Improving host-plant resistance is therefore a priority for sustaining sorghum as a resource-conserving, climate-resilient crop. Although the RMES1 locus on chromosome 6 has been strongly associated with aphid resistance, the broader genomic basis of tolerance across diverse germplasm remains incompletely understood. In particular, it is unclear whether tolerant accessions share conserved resistance haplotypes, structural variants, or differences in disease-resistance gene content that can be translated into breeding tools.

To address this, we developed a comparative genomics framework integrating 14 PacBio-based sorghum genome assemblies, chromosome-scale synteny analysis, and phenotype-guided prioritization of accessions differing in aphid response. Candidate lines were selected from greenhouse and field datasets, with emphasis on accessions showing reproducible tolerance under aphid pressure. As a foundation for downstream analyses, we generated and evaluated eight chromosome-scale sorghum genome assemblies. In parallel, we performed full-length mRNA sequencing of whole seedlings from sorghum lines to capture transcript isoform diversity and improve gene model resolution across prioritized accessions.

All assemblies resolved 10 chromosome-like pseudomolecules and exhibited high gene space completeness (99.6–99.7% BUSCO). Assembly continuity was strong, with contig N50 values ranging from ~72 to 128 Mb, and genome fractions approaching ~90% relative to the BTx623 v5.1 reference. Synteny analyses further supported high structural concordance among the best-performing assemblies.

These transcriptomic resources complement the genome assemblies and provide a framework for identifying structural and regulatory variation associated with aphid tolerance in known genetic regions. Ongoing analyses integrate whole-genome alignment, pan-gene comparison, and evaluation of NLR/NBS-LRR gene families across tolerant and susceptible lines. This work provides a scalable foundation for identifying candidate resistance haplotypes and developing diagnostic markers, including KASP-compatible assays, to support sorghum breeding and crop improvement.

sc.x:
Conventional energy and material production systems are carbon-intensive, driving the need for sustainable alternative solutions. Agricultural feedstocks, specifically sorghum stubble, an abundant agricultural residue generating (~47.35 MMT globally; 6.63 MMT in the U.S.), are often underutilised and disposed of through open burning, leading to environmental pollution and resource loss. It contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, which can be converted into high-value products such as paper, textiles, platform chemicals, fermentable sugars, adhesives, and asphalt binders, offering a sustainable pathway for biomass valorisation.

The goal of the research is to develop low-energy, environmentally sustainable biorefining strategies for the efficient fractionation of sorghum stubble, to maximise the recovery of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin through integrated multi-parametric and multi-objective optimisation approaches.”

Sorghum stubble was pretreated under controlled conditions to fractionate cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Recovery yields and physicochemical properties were optimised using response surface methodology. Recovered polymers were linked to potential applications as illustrated in the figure: cellulose → paper/textiles; hemicellulose → platform chemicals/fermentable sugars; lignin → adhesives/asphalt binders.

This study developed low-energy, green biorefining strategies, comparing microwave-assisted and hydrothermal pretreatments (150–190 °C, 10–30 min). Microwave pretreatment achieved superior hemicellulose recoveries (96–97 %) and fermentable sugar yields (27.16 % for sorghum) versus hydrothermal (82–85 % recovery; 23.8 %). It enhanced cellulose crystallinity, surface area, and energy efficiency while reducing particle size. Sorghum carbohydrates are promising materials for biofuel, textile and pul and paper production, whereas lignin-based materials are utilised for adhesives, asphalt binder and energy generation. Microwave-assisted fractionation is thus highly effective for sustainable biopolymer production.

Sorghum stubble is a highly promising feedstock for sustainable biopolymer production. Low-energy, optimised fractionation enhances the simultaneous recovery of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, supporting their conversion into diverse high-value applications and advancing circular bioeconomy strategies.

sc.x: Background: Grain sorghum stubble is an abundant, underutilised semi-arid agricultural residue, often left in fields or burned, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. Hemicellulose, a major polysaccharide in sorghum, has potential applications in biofuels, biochemicals, and biomaterials, but its extraction is challenging due to its complex association with cellulose and lignin. Conventional chemical and thermal pretreatments often degrade hemicellulose and generate undesirable by-products. Objective: This study aimed to optimise microwave-assisted extraction (MAE) to maximise hemicellulose recovery from grain sorghum stubble, quantify mono-, oligo-, and polysaccharides in the hydrolysate, assess degradation by-products, and evaluate residual solid composition.

Hemicellulose extraction efficiency (ηh) increased with both temperature and time, peaking at 96.9% at 190 °C for 30 min, with a total carbohydrate yield (Yc) of 23.4%, representing ~84% of the initial hemicellulose. Monosaccharides accounted for 40% of the sugars in the hydrolysate, indicating extensive depolymerisation. By-products, including furfural, formic acid, and acetic acid, represented ~5% of total sugars. Sorghum’s higher ash content accelerated microwave-induced autohydrolysis compared to woody biomass. Regression models were robust (R² ≥ 0.94) with significant temperature-time interactions (p < 0.05), enabling precise prediction of hemicellulose yields.

Dried, ground sorghum stubble (0.42 mm) was soaked in water and subjected to MAE at 150–190 °C for 10–30 min under controlled pulse cycles. Hemicellulose yields were analysed using HPLC-RID for monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and degradation products. Solid residues were characterised for cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. A central composite design under response surface methodology modelled extraction efficiency and optimised MAE parameters.

MAE is a highly efficient, low-energy, and environmentally friendly strategy for extracting hemicellulose from grain sorghum stubble. Optimised conditions achieved >95% hemicellulose recovery, with tunable mono- and polysaccharide outputs, supporting its valorisation for biofuel and biomaterial production and advancing sustainable biorefinery approaches for herbaceous residues.

sc.x: Sudden temperature flips, especially from warm to cold temperatures during late spring, increasingly threaten chilling-sensitive crops such as sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), impairing early seedling establishment and physiological function. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a lignin-derived molecular heater, digeranyl sinapoyl malate (DGSM), applied exogenously to enhance plant resilience to sudden cold spells.

DGSM-treated plants maintained leaf temperatures approximately 3 °C higher than untreated cold-stressed sorghum plants, indicating improved thermal regulation. Photosynthetic efficiency was significantly enhanced, with DGSM-treated plants showing 18–35% higher photosynthetic activity compared to untreated cold-stressed plants. Electrolyte leakage decreased by 50% following DGSM treatment, demonstrating improved membrane stability and reduced cellular damage. These physiological improvements were associated with reduced oxidative stress and enhanced cellular protection.
DGSM was applied as a foliar treatment to 20-day-older plants one day before cold exposure, followed by one week of chilling stress at 10°C in the growth chamber.

Overall, DGSM functions as a molecular thermal protectant, preserving membrane integrity, maintaining photosynthetic function, and enhancing cold tolerance during sudden cold events that occur during seedling establishment. This lignin-based strategy offers a promising, sustainable approach to enhancing crop resilience under unpredictable temperature stress. Future studies will focus on validating the efficacy of DGSM under field conditions and in large-scale agricultural systems.

sc.x: The availability of a sustainably produced biomass feedstock will determine the size of the US bioeconomy. According to the USDOE Billion-Ton Report, our country has the potential to sustainably produce more than a billion tons of biomass feedstock under adequate market conditions. Agricultural lands will be responsible for providing over 600 million tons of feedstocks, and purpose-grown energy crops will be a major player. Purpose-grown energy crops are becoming more vital as renewable biomass sources for biofuel and bio-based production, because they can generate large amounts of biomass with minimal inputs. High-biomass sorghum is a versatile energy crop with broad adaptability, capable of fitting into various cropping systems and integrating with winter crops.

The Lee Lab is dedicated to sustainable agriculture and energy production by implementing agronomic management practices that increase yields of various energy crops while maximizing ecosystem service benefits. The Lee Lab has conducted extensive field experiments to quantify biomass yield across environments, optimize nitrogen management, identify superior hybrids in the Midwest, evaluate cover cropping systems and associated ecosystem services, and assess the agronomic performance of oil sorghum with enhanced TAG accumulation. Currently, the lab focuses on oil-enhanced lines of high-biomass sorghum that provide a dual-purpose system by producing high oil content in vegetative tissues while supplying lignocellulosic biomass for sustainable aviation fuel feedstock.

This presentation will highlight recent advances in agronomic management for sustainable biomass production and ecosystem services of high-biomass sorghum and will also outline the characteristics of an ideal sorghum system for future bioenergy production. Topics include large-scale production systems, the optimization of management practices, and hybrid selection to enhance productivity and ecosystem services.
