sc.x: SorghumBase serves as a foundational resource for the global sorghum community, facilitating the collective mission to enhance crop resilience and productivity through advanced genomics and breeding. To ensure broad and active participation, we engage consistently with sorghum researchers across multiple fronts. Specifically, we 1) highlight their published research and discoveries through dedicated blog posts, 2) actively support the curation and standardization of their newly generated data for appropriate public repository submission, 3) educate platform users through tutorials and documentation on the advanced features of SorghumBase, and 4) gather continuous community feedback, which is crucial for guiding the ongoing prioritization and development of the platform. Our commitment to growth is demonstrated by significant platform milestones achieved over the last two years. SorghumBase now hosts an extensive collection of over 100 high-quality sorghum genomes, alongside an expanded set of genetic variation and gene expression data resources. Furthermore, we have improved the overall usability and intuitiveness of the website interface. These accomplishments are augmented by our collaborative projects, including spearheading the development of a large-scale genotyping platform with Twist, supporting the curation of the critical GRIN seed collection, and leveraging powerful genotype-to-phenotype tools from DeltaBreed to accelerate breeding efforts. The team aims to provide a useful integrated resource that adheres to the FAIR guiding principles for data stewardship. Data that are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) benefit the community as a whole by maximizing the impact of research investment and contributing directly to advancing our shared goals of sustainable agriculture. We are enthusiastic about future collaborations and look forward to working together to integrate your valuable research data seamlessly with the advanced tools in the platform, which will ultimately better support the entire sorghum research and breeding community. SorghumBase is funded by USDA ARS 8062-21000-041-00D.

sc.x: The establishment of stable, interoperable variant identifiers is critical for advancing crop genomics and accelerating molecular breeding. Inspired by the success of reference SNP cluster IDs (rsIDs) in human genetics, we have integrated standardized rsIDs from the European Variation Archive (EVA) into SorghumBase. Starting with 45 million identifiers from EVA Release 5, we developed a strategy to propagate these IDs from the original reference genome (BTx623 NCBIv3) across diverse assemblies using the Ensembl Variant Remapping pipeline. Our mapping results demonstrate high stability, with a 99% success rate between BTx623 versions (v3 to v5). Across the 100+ pangenomes hosted in SorghumBase, mapping rates range from 20% to 90%, correlating with assembly quality and phylogenetic proximity to the reference. These stable identifiers are now accessible via the SorghumBase genome browser as searchable tracks and gene-level annotations, facilitating seamless cross-assembly comparisons and translational research. Complementing this informatics framework, we developed and validated a community-driven, mid-density PlexSeq™ NGS genotyping array. This platform features 2,421 SNPs strategically distributed across all ten chromosomes, incorporating trait-associated and quality-control markers prioritized by global stakeholders. Validation of 2,726 diverse accessions yielded high call rates and population structure resolution consistent with whole-genome datasets. Notably, genomic prediction accuracy for key agronomic traits matched that of high-density genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) platforms, offering a more cost-effective alternative. As of March 2026, we are synchronizing SorghumBase with EVA Release 8, which includes 55.7 million total rsIDs. While the growth of new variants has plateaued since Release 6, our ongoing efforts focus on maintaining data integrity by reconciling merged or deprecated identifiers. Together, these standardized rsID resources and targeted genotyping tools provide a FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) infrastructure to empower germplasm management and genomic-assisted breeding in sorghum.

sc.x: Iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) are essential micronutrients that limit sorghum productivity in marginal soils, yet genetic variation for micronutrient use efficiency remains underexploited in breeding programs. This study combined physiological evaluation and multi-omics analysis to identify genes, regulatory networks, and traits associated with Fe and Zn stress tolerance in sorghum. The Fe stress studies were further expanded to evaluate responses including four founders of the Carbon Partitioning Nested Association Mapping population (Grassl, Leoti, Pink Kafir, and IS13633).

We conducted transcriptomics and ionomics analyses on Sorghum bicolor BTx623, grown under Fe and Zn limited and excess conditions over a 21-day period in hydroponic growth system with temperature settings of 21–27°C in a greenhouse.

Transcriptomic profiling across 180 RNA-seq libraries revealed dynamic, time-dependent regulation of genes involved in both reduction-based (Strategy I) and chelation-based (Strategy II) micronutrient acquisition pathways. Fe limitation and Zn excess induced the strongest transcriptional responses in roots and leaves. Gene regulatory network analysis identified hub genes including homologs of SbFIT, SbPYE, and SbBTS that coordinate uptake, chloroplast development, Fe–S cluster assembly, and reactive oxygen species detoxification. Clear phenotypic variation was observed among genotypes. Under Fe limitation, most lines developed chlorosis, while Leoti maintained green pigmentation and relatively higher tissue Fe concentrations.

The co-regulation of Fe- and Zn-responsive networks indicates significant micronutrient crosstalk, suggesting that selection for improved Fe efficiency may simultaneously enhance Zn uptake. The flexibility in acquisition strategies across genotypes points to multiple genetic mechanisms breeders can target. Leoti's sustained performance under Fe deficiency makes it a valuable donor parent for nutrient efficiency traits. This study provides actionable breeding targets, including candidate genes for marker development and donor lines with demonstrated Fe stress tolerance, supporting the development of nutrient-efficient sorghum varieties for production in micronutrient-limited environments.

sc.x: High winds are an important but understudied abiotic stressor causing stalk lodging and yield losses in crops such as sorghum. Despite its global importance, the genetic and biomechanical mechanisms underlying wind resistance in sorghum remain poorly understood. Our research aims to elucidate how stem structure, development, and genetics interact to confer mechanical resilience under wind stress and to define an optimal stalk ideotype.

A diverse panel of grain and forage sorghum are analyzed using a multiscale approach. Phenotypic and biomechanical characterization include whole-stem mechanical testing, nanoscale assays, histological imaging, and chemical profiling to link structural and compositional traits with mechanical performance. A computational modeling framework incorporating AI and interpretable machine learning is used to simulate stalk behavior under wind loads and guide ideotype design. Genome-wide and transcriptome-wide association analyses are conducted to identify genetic determinants of key traits, followed by functional validation using virus-induced gene silencing.

This integrative approach will generate a comprehensive dataset connecting genomic variation with stem structure and mechanical function. Modeling efforts facilitate the identification of critical traits across scales that enhance lodging resistance, while AI-driven optimization will predict ideotypes balancing strength and physiological performance. Genetic analyses reveal candidate genes and regulatory networks controlling tissue differentiation and structural reinforcement.

This research advances our understanding of how multiscale biological processes contribute to mechanical stability in sorghum stems. By integrating biomechanics, genomics, and computational modeling, it provides predictive tools and targets for improving lodging resistance. These insights will support the development of more resilient crop varieties under increasing climate variability and contribute broadly to plant biology and crop improvement efforts.

sc.x: Nitrogen (N) management is critical for sorghum forage systems, where excess fertilization can cause nitrate accumulation in plant tissues, increasing livestock poisoning risk and environmental pollution. Improving nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) while reducing nitrate toxicity is a key breeding target. This study combined physiological evaluation of diverse sorghum forage lines under variable N conditions with cross-species gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis to identify candidate genes and regulatory modules for NUE improvement.

Transcriptome analysis revealed strong genotypic variation in expression of nitrate transport, nitrate reduction, and photosynthetic regulation genes, with line-specific profiles corresponding to observed differences in nitrate accumulation. In parallel, a sorghum NUE regulatory network (spNUEGRN) was projected from a maize network comprising 1,625 protein–DNA interactions identified through enhanced yeast one-hybrid assays. Comparative analysis detected 23,864 differentially expressed genes in sorghum under nitrogen stress, with 638 conserved feed-forward loop motifs and approximately 18% regulatory interaction conservation with Arabidopsis, particularly in nitrate uptake and assimilation pathways.

Four male-sterile A-lines (ATx645, ATx3408, A.11022, A.07258bst) with contrasting nitrate accumulation profiles and reference line BTx623 were grown under standard (1 mM) and high (20 mM) ammonium nitrate treatments.

Line-specific expression patterns indicate that certain genotypes possess enhanced nitrogen assimilation capacity, reducing leaf nitrate accumulation. Conserved regulatory motifs across maize, sorghum, and Arabidopsis validate core NUE circuits, while key transcription factor hubs such as bZIP18 and bZIP30 homologs represent actionable targets for marker-assisted selection. This study identifies candidate genes, conserved regulatory networks, and characterized low-nitrate donor lines for breeding forage sorghum varieties with improved NUE, reduced nitrate toxicity risk, and enhanced environmental sustainability.

sc.x: Genomic mapping has yielded extensive catalogs of quantitative trait loci underlying agronomic traits, yet translating these discoveries into breeding gains remains slow and inefficient. Here, we introduce Flywheel Genomics, a framework that integrates trait discovery and translation directly within a highly intercrossed, rapid cycling breeding population.

We show that rapid cycling maintains sufficient genetic diversity, effective population size, and recombination to support ongoing genetic mapping while driving rapid genetic gain. We show that such a population has ideal mapping characteristics as compared to established sorghum mapping populations such as the NAM or SAP. We demonstrate that such a population can generate large, segregating mapping populations and produce near-isogenic lines suitable for locus validation. Simulation analyses further reveal that rapid cycling breeding strategies may outperform conventional pure line approaches for both genetic gain and as platforms for trait discovery.

A highly intermated sorghum breeding population was developed for sorghum production in Haiti (referred to as the Haitian breeding population). Phenotypes for yield, height, stay-green, and heading time were measured and analyzed across environments. Genotypes were obtained using DArTAg and KASP markers, and PCA and LD analyses characterized population structure. Near-isogenic lines were identified for locus validation. Forward-time simulations were conducted to compare different crossing schemes and their effects on genetic gain, allele frequencies, effective population size, and QTL detection.

By embracing the dynamic genetic architecture of traits under selection, Flywheel Genomics reframes breeding programs as self-reinforcing engines of both crop improvement and biological insight, closing the gap between genetics and breeding.

abstracts.t: Development of an MS8-based Nuclear Male Sterility System for Two-line Hybrid Breeding in Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, United States

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is a resilient crop with strong potential as a grain, forage, and bioenergy resource due to its tolerance to abiotic stresses and adaptation to marginal environments. Hybrid breeding is a key strategy for improving crop performance; however, current sorghum hybrid production relies exclusively on cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)-based three-line systems, which constrain genetic diversity and limit breeding efficiency. In contrast, Nuclear Male Sterility (NMS)-based two-line systems developed in crops such as rice offer a more flexible and efficient approach to hybrid seed production.

Here, we report the development of a novel NMS-based two-line breeding system in sorghum using the ms8 mutant and its causal gene, MS8, which encodes a basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor essential for anther development and pollen formation. The ms8 mutant exhibits stable, complete male sterility without affecting vegetative growth. To enable propagation of male sterile lines, we engineered a three-component (3C) transgenic bridge system containing (i) the wild-type MS8 gene to restore fertility, (ii) a pollen-disruption gene to selectively devitalize transgenic pollen, and (iii) a fluorescent seed marker to distinguish transgenic and nontransgenic seeds. Through genetic transformation and strategic crossing, we established bridge plants that produce a 1:1 ratio of transgenic fertile and nontransgenic male sterile seeds, enabling efficient propagation and selection. Critically, cross-pollination between these bridge plants and ms8 mutant plants yields 100% nontransgenic male sterile progeny suitable for hybrid seed production.

Our MS8-based NMS system represents a major advance over current CMS-based sorghum breeding by overcoming its key limitations. This strategy enhances breeding efficiency and genetic diversity in sorghum and provides a generalizable framework for two-line hybrid breeding systems in other crops.

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is a resilient, climate-smart crop that contributes significantly to food and nutrition security in Ethiopia's drought-prone regions. Despite extensive research and development efforts, sorghum production and productivity in Ethiopia remain far below their potential and have recently stagnated. This paper investigates challenges across the crop value chain that hinder progress.

The study utilized both published and unpublished data to analyze production dynamics, commercialization patterns, and medium-term supply and demand. Time-series data were employed to evaluate trends and project future requirements.

Results reveal that while numerous improved varieties have been released, the area planted with certified sorghum seed remains less than 1%. Furthermore, fertilizer application is substantially below recommended levels. These findings suggest that sorghum exists in a low-input, low-productivity equilibrium, reinforced by the limited adoption of major production packages—specifically certified seed and fertilizer—due to a lack of commercialization incentives. Projections indicate that annual production will fall short of demand, resulting in a structural supply deficit of approximately 250,000 tons; annual production is expected to stabilize at 4.96 million tons, while demand is projected to reach 5.21 million tons.

Consequently, both technical and institutional innovations are required. Developing a feasible seed production and supply chain—integrated with grain, feed, and food markets—could catalyze performance across the entire value chain, breaking the low-productivity cycle and allowing sorghum to reach its full economic and yield potential.

sc.x: Chilling stress limits sorghum seedling establishment and yield in temperate environments, particularly under early planting conditions. Improving hybrid performance under chilling stress requires effective prediction approaches for accelerated hybrid breeding.

These models achieved moderate to high prediction accuracy for both seedling and GY traits, with EI showed the highest prediction accuracy among seedling traits. Growth chamber seedling traits were positively associated with field seedling traits, indicating that growth chamber phenotypes can be used to predict field seedling traits. Incorporating growth chamber seedling traits as additional environments improved prediction accuracy field seedling traits, whereas including growth chamber traits as covariates did not improve prediction accuracy. Prediction accuracy for GY using genomic information alone ranged from 0.51 to 0.54 across cross-validation schemes. Incorporating field EP as covariates substantially improved prediction accuracy, increasing prediction ability to 0.66–0.69. Multi-trait models that jointly modeled emergence percentage and grain yield also improved prediction accuracy compared with genomic-only models, with prediction accuracies ranging from 0.62 to 0.64.

In this study, we integrate genomic information of 57 parental lines from multiple public and private breeding programs and their 215 hybrids phenotypic information across environments. Seedling traits: emergence percentage (EP), emergence index (EI), seedling biomass (SB), and grain yield (GY) were measured from experiments growth chamber and early-planted (end of April to first week of May) four field environments conducted at the Kansas State University, Agricultural Research Center, Hays, Kansas. The prediction model: general and specific combining ability (GCA–SCA) and genotype-by-environment (GxE) interaction kernels and its prediction ability was assessed using five leave-parent-out cross-validation schemes.

Overall, these results demonstrate that integrating growth chamber phenotypes and field-evaluated seedling traits with genomic prediction models can significantly improve prediction of hybrid performance under chilling stress and enhance selection efficiency in sorghum hybrid breeding programs targeting early planting environments.

sc.x: Grain sorghum has strong potencial for dryland systems in the Northern Great Plains (NGP), but early planting can expose crops to low temperatures that limit establishment and nitrogen (N) uptake. Information on how N fertilization performs across planting windows remains limited. This study evaluated early-season growth responses and nitrogen responsiveness of grain sorghum to N rates under simulated early and optimal planting conditions.

A growth chamber experiment was conducted at South Dakota State University using a randomized complete block design with four replications. Treatments consisted of four nitrogen rates (0, 56, 112, and 168 kg N ha⁻¹) applied as urea under two regimes simulating early and optimal planting windows. Plants were evaluated at the five-leaf stage (V5) to assess early-season growth responses, including plant height, chlorophyll content (SPAD), and biomass accumulation.

Nitrogen application increased plant height, chlorophyll content, and biomass accumulation across both planting conditions. However, responses were more consistent and greater under optimal planting conditions. Under optimal conditions, plants were taller, produced more biomass, and exhibited higher SPAD values than those under early planting. In contrast, early planting resulted in more variable and generally reduced growth and SPAD responses, indicating limitations in nitrogen uptake and early-season nitrogen status. These results demonstrate that early planting reduced sorghum growth and altered nitrogen uptake during early development.

Early planting conditions reduced sorghum growth and altered responsiveness to nitrogen fertilization during early development, highlighting the importance of aligning N management with planting timing. Adjusting nitrogen strategies to early-season conditions may improve early growth and nitrogen use efficiency in sorghum systems.

sc.x: Plant height (PH) is a crucial agronomic trait associated with cereal and biomass yields. ‘Tentaka (MS79A × 74LH3213)’, a forage sorghum hybrid developed in Japan, exceeds four meters in height, whereas its parental lines are approximately 1.2 meters tall. We previously demonstrated that this heterosis is controlled by six genes (SbPhyB, SbGhd7, SbPRR37, Dw1, Dw3 and qHT7.1/Dw7a). However, another hybrid, ‘Kazetachi (MS138A × 74LH3213)’, is approximately one meter shorter than Tentaka, despite differing only in the female parental line. This reduced PH confers lodging tolerance, making Kazetachi more suitable for regions affected by typhoons, such as Japan. This study aimed to elucidate the genetic basis of heterosis in Kazetachi and to identify factors contributing to lodging tolerance.

QTL analyses for culm length (CL) were conducted using two F₂ populations derived from MS138B × 74LH3213 and MS79B × MS138B. Candidate gene sequences within the detected QTL regions were compared among the three parental lines.

Five QTLs for CL were detected on chromosomes 1 (qCL-1), 6 (qCL-6a and qCL-6b), 7 (qCL-7a), and 9 (qCL-9) in the MS138B × 74LH3213 F2 population, while a major QTL (qCL-7b), explaining >58% of the phenotypic variance, was identified on chromosome 7 in the MS79B × MS138B F2 population. The two QTLs detected on chromosome 7 (qCL-7a and qCL-7b) were distinct based on their loci, and Dw3 was identified as a candidate gene for qCL-7b. Sequence analysis revealed that the MS138B allele contains three tandem repeats of 882 bp in exon 5, suggesting a loss-of-function allele.

The difference in PH between Tentaka and Kazetachi is primarily attributable to Dw3 function. The heterosis of Kazetachi can be explained by five genes excluding Dw3, while the loss-of-function allele of Dw3 likely contributes to lodging tolerance.

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), a C₄ grass adapted to hot semi-arid environments, depends on reinforced xylem vessels to maintain hydraulic conductance under high evaporative demand. During protoxylem differentiation, coordinated microtubule and actin dynamics guide secondary cell wall (SCW) deposition; however, whether actin-based motors regulate vascular architecture and hydraulic performance has remained unknown

Here, we showed that HS1, a previously uncharacterized myosin VIII with a grass-specific N-terminal extension and lineage-specific features in the motor domain, is essential for protoxylem integrity and water transport. The hs1 mutant exhibited severe leaf scorching and pronounced protoxylem defects, including vessel collapse, reduced lumen area, and weakened lignified secondary cell walls, leading to impaired hydraulic conductance and reduced whole-plant water use. Mechanistically, HS1 promoted lignin-associated secondary cell wall biosynthesis during protoxylem differentiation and showed strong cell-type specificity in developing xylem, functionally linking actin-based motor activity to wall reinforcement and vascular function.

Combining genetic analysis, phylogenetic and population genomic analyses, cellular and anatomical analyses, single-cell and bulk transcriptomics, and physiological measurements, we investigated how the actin-based motor protein HEAT-SENSITIVE 1 (HS1) regulates xylem development and hydraulic function in sorghum.

Together, these findings provide the first direct evidence that a motor protein can regulate plant hydraulic conductance, establishing a new regulatory layer for the control of plant hydraulic function by cytoskeletal motor proteins, with potential implications for improving water-use efficiency and stress resilience in grass crops.

sc.x: Effective control of grass weeds after crop emergence in grain sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] remains constrained by the limited availability of selective herbicide options. The 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD)-inhibiting herbicides mesotrione and tembotrione provide broad-spectrum weed control; however, mesotrione is currently restricted to pre-emergence use in sorghum, and tembotrione is not registered due to crop injury. This study characterized the dose-response of tolerant, susceptible, and U.S. elite sorghum genotypes to both herbicides and developed Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP) markers for tembotrione tolerance quantitative trait loci (QTLs).

For mesotrione, sorghum lines G-10 and G-1 showed 3.85- and 3.46-fold greater tolerance than the susceptible cultivar S-1, respectively. U.S. elite lines showed moderate sensitivity to mesotrione (GR₅₀ = 112.1-190.02 g ai ha⁻¹). For tembotrione, line G-200 was the most tolerant (GR₅₀ = 236.27 g ai ha⁻¹), showing the lowest visual injury and highest chlorophyll content among all genotypes, followed by G-350 (GR₅₀ = 185.60 g ai ha⁻¹), while S-1 was the most susceptible (GR₅₀ = 44.18 g ai ha⁻¹). KASP markers targeting G-200-specific SNPs within QTL regions on chromosomes 2, 4, and 8 were developed and reliably distinguished tolerant, susceptible, and heterozygous genotypes. Notably, mesotrione tolerant accessions (G-1 and G-10) carried susceptible alleles at all tembotrione-linked markers, indicating tolerance to these herbicides is controlled by distinct genetic loci.
Eight genotypes per herbicide were evaluated in greenhouse dose-response assays. Visual injury, chlorophyll content, and dry biomass were measured up to 3 weeks after treatment (WAT).

These results demonstrate the potential of KASP markers for efficient marker-assisted introgression of tembotrione tolerance into elite U.S. sorghum germplasm and support the pyramiding of tolerance to multiple HPPD-inhibiting herbicides.

sc.x: Sorghum is a tropical short-day species un-adapted to flower in temperate growing regions. Adaptation of diverse exotic sorghum germplasm for U.S. grain production (Sorghum Conversion Program, 1963 – 2000s) was accomplished by repeated backcrossing of photoperiod sensitive landraces to daylength in-sensitive donor parents and selection for daylength insensitive flowering and short stature. The maturity genes PRR37 (Ma1) and GHD7 (Ma6) were identified as key regulatory components controlling the developmental transition from vegetative to reproductive growth. Here, an accelerated breeding method for converting daylength sensitive sorghum using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to mutate maturity genes is proposed for germplasm conversion in temperate growing regions.

Preliminary greenhouse data from T<sub>0</sub> edited lines grown under long days (16 hours light/8 hours night) show plants with high knock-out probabilities in either gene flower in 62 to 85 days, relative to wild type controls that do not transition from the vegetative stage. A final experiment to phenotype selected T<sub>1</sub> homozygous edited lines to assess maturity, grain yield and plant height is planned for 2026.

CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing was used to create single or double knock outs in the PRR37 (Sobic.006G057866) and GHD7 (Sobic.006G004400) genes. Agrobacterium mediated transformation of Ethiopian landraces IS12661 and IS12610 with editing constructs was accomplished using transient expression of the BBM and WUS2 developmental genes and Zea mays codon-optimized Cas9.

Overall, sorghum gene editing takes ~12-14 months compared to traditional conversion which requires 3+ years and significantly more resources. Importantly, gene editing can introduce mutations to specific target genes without recombination that may break linkage groups for important traits such as stress tolerance. This initial proof of concept demonstrates the utility of CRISPR for accelerated pre-breeding and offers a path to adapt diverse germplasm with quality and agronomic breeding value from the USDA sorghum germplasm collection.

sc.x: Leaf rust, caused by the obligate fungal pathogen Puccinia purpurea, poses a serious threat to sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] production, leading to significant yield losses and undermining its value as renewable fuel crop.

The analysis identified 18 and 19 accessions with rust resistant from NPGS-Sudan and SAP, respectively, among which 14 showed no rust pustules on the leaves across years. Genome-wide association analysis for the NPGS-Sudan led to the identification of a 57 Kb genomic region on chromosome 8 that encompasses a cluster of five homologous R genes, indicating that this cluster might be acting as a single locus named Rp2. Comparative genome analysis found that the orthologous of Rp2 locus in maize (Zm00001d023311) is associated with the resistance response to Puccinia polysora, the causal agent of southern corn rust, and in rice (Os12G29690), with resistance to the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens). Genome-wide association analysis for the SAP led to the identification of major locus in chromosomes 8. This locus encompasses a cluster of four BURP domains homologous genes located across a 33 Kb genomic region named hereafter as Rp3 locus. An allele frequency analysis found that both Rp2 and Rp3 resistance alleles are present in SAP, but the frequency of Rp2 is too low to be detected through GWAS.

In this study, the USDA-ARS, National Plant Germplasm System Sudan core collection (NPGS-Sudan) and the sorghum association panel (SAP) were evaluated for rust resistance response across multiple tropical environments.

A total of five accessions that enclose resistance alleles for both Rp2 and Rp3 resistance loci can be immediately integrated into breeding programs for the development of new resistant varieties or hybrids.

sc.x: Sorghum is a key crop in Australian dryland farming systems, valued for its resilience under water-limited conditions. However, increasing climate variability, including rising temperatures and more erratic rainfall, is intensifying atmospheric demand and constraining productivity. Improving transpiration efficiency (TE), defined as biomass produced per unit water transpired, is therefore critical for sustaining yield in these environments. At the leaf level, TE emerges from the balance between CO₂ assimilation and water loss through stomata, regulated by stomatal conductance (gₛ). While stomatal architecture, including size, density, and pore dimensions, sets an upper limit on conductance, its role in determining realised gas-exchange under variable atmospheric demand remains unclear.This study aims to identify a robust stomatal phenotyping framework by quantifying variation in stomatal architecture and conductance across leaf positions and surfaces.

Preliminary observations indicate significant variation in stomatal architecture across leaf positions and surfaces, with implications for conductance estimates. Variation in sampling position introduces uncertainty in linking anatomical traits to functional gas exchange.

Stomatal architecture was quantified using non-destructive, high-resolution microscopy (Dino-Lite Edge AM7515) across multiple canopy positions, including lower (leaf 6), middle (leaves 8–11), and upper leaves (leaves 15, 16, and flag leaf). Both adaxial and abaxial surfaces were imaged to capture variation in stomatal distribution and structure. A computer vision-based machine learning pipeline has been developed to automate trait extraction from images, improving throughput and consistency. Concurrently, stomatal conductance was measured using a porometer (LI-600, LI-COR).

Identifying a representative leaf position for stomatal phenotyping can reduce variability and improve physiological interpretation. This integrated approach enables more reliable linkage between stomatal architecture and function, supporting trait-based strategies for improving drought adaptation in sorghum.

sc.x: Recombination is a fundamental meiotic process that generates genetic diversity and underpins plant breeding by creating novel allele combinations and breaking unfavourable linkages. However, crossovers are unevenly distributed along chromosomes, largely confined to sub‑telomeric regions, leaving much of the genome under‑recombined. In sorghum, recombination variation across diverse genetic backgrounds remains poorly understood. This study aimed to systematically characterise recombination variability across multiple sorghum populations and develop a framework that moves beyond traditional consensus mapping approaches to capture population‑specific recombination landscapes.

High‑quality linkage maps were constructed for 18 F₂ populations derived from crosses among 13 racially diverse sorghum parental lines. A scalable, continuously updatable framework was developed to integrate multiple genetic maps. Novel statistical approaches, incorporating splines within mixed models, were applied to quantify regional variation in recombination rates along chromosomes and to characterise recombination landscapes within each population.

Substantial fine‑scale variation in recombination was detected among populations. Certain genomic regions exhibited elevated recombination in specific genetic backgrounds while showing reduced or absent recombination in others, revealing pronounced population‑specific patterns. In contrast, some regions displayed consistently low variability across populations, suggesting conserved recombination landscapes. As additional populations were integrated, the consensus recombination landscape became progressively refined, with total map length decreasing from 1,620.2 cM (three populations) to 1,532.8 cM (fifteen populations), indicating increasing stability and representativeness.

The mixed‑model spline framework developed here offers a scalable and dynamic approach to integrating genetic linkage maps while preserving population‑specific recombination variation. Anchored to physical genome coordinates, it enables seamless updating of consensus recombination landscapes and can be readily adapted to alternative assemblies or pan‑genome references. Taken together, this framework provides a robust resource for informed breeding decisions with direct relevance to sorghum genetics and breeding.

sc.x: Hybrid seed production in sorghum relies on cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS), where maintaining complete male sterility in female parents is crucial for ensuring hybrid seed purity. However, rising temperatures are posing challenges for both sorghum improvement and hybrid seed production. Some sorghum CMS lines harbour genes that confer partial fertility when exposed to high temperatures around the flowering. This partial fertility can lead to self-fertilisation of female lines in hybrid seed production fields, resulting in the presence of selfed, non-hybrid seeds and thereby reducing the overall quality of the final hybrid product. This introduces significant financial risk to the commercial seed industry by limiting the market potential of hybrid varieties. Understanding the developmental stage most susceptible stage to the high temperatures that induce partial fertility in susceptible CMS lines is therefore critical. Such knowledge would enable breeders and seed producers to develop strategies that mitigate the risk of producing seed in environments that induce partial male fertility.

Our findings indicated two critical windows for temperature-induced pollen production in susceptible CMS lines. The first is a two-day window occurring between 8 and 12 days before flowering, depending on the environment, corresponding to −190 ± 10 to −160 ± 10 degree days relative to flowering. The second is a 4-5 day window immediately pre-flowering, corresponding to −90 ± 10 degree days relative to flowering.

We conducted a seven-year study across diverse environments, evaluating 2,847 CMS lines. Mixed model incorporating environmental covariates was used to isolate the effects of temperature at different developmental stages on partial male fertility. In addition we conducted controlled environment experiment to validatete the field experiments reuslts.

The timing of high-temperature susceptibility for sterility breakdown in sorghum CMS lines ptovided a foundation for breeding and seed production strategies that protect hybrid seed quality in a changing climate.

sc.x: Protein language models are currently among the most promising AI models for predicting the effect of protein-coding variants on plant phenotypes. However, few studies have evaluated their accuracy in plants. A critical step for deploying this technology in plant breeding is the calibration of predicted variant effects against observed effects on plant fitness and agronomic traits, such as grain yield and plant height.

In this presentation, I explore the relationship between scores from ESM (a foundational protein language model) and phenotypic effects in grass species. I will discuss three key findings: (1) the association between ESM scores and fitness effects in the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP); (2) the utility of ESM scores for predicting agronomic traits in the SAP; and (3) the direct validation of five candidate variants selected with ESM scores, using targeted mutagenesis of the reference genotype BTx623.

Our results suggest that ESM predicts the fitness effects of missense variants more accurately than standard tools based on multiple sequence alignment (SIFT). Furthermore, we found that ESM scores are well-calibrated to selection coefficients, showing a significant enrichment for beneficial effects among variants with positive ESM scores. We also showed that ESM scores correlate with agronomic traits like plant height in the SAP. Finally, I will present the results of targeted mutagenesis for the direct validation of candidate variants (analyses in progress, results expected in June 2026).

Our findings highlight both the promise and the current limitations of protein language models in plant breeding. Additionally, our work provides new datasets for validating variant effect prediction tools, providing much-needed benchmarking resources for the plant science community.

abstracts.t: Optimising kafirin extraction using Gibbs free energy of cavity creation to rationalise solvent choice

sc.x: Sorghum contains up to 14% proteins. Its main storage proteins, kafirin, are highly hydrophobic and crosslinked, resulting in very low solubility and a propensity to aggregate. As a result, they remain underused and are not developed or produced for food and non-food applications. Our working hypothesis is that protein solubility is key to controlling functional properties, such as structuring and surface abilities. For proteins like kafirin, which readily self-assemble, understanding the relationship between structure and hydration is essential for industrial valorisation.

Results show high positive ΔGC values in water, that decrease by adding alcohol. The experimental design showed that ΔGC and temperature are the main factors influencing in kafirin dispersibility. The solvents’ ranking is ΔGC(tert-butanol)<ΔGC(Isopropanol)<ΔGC(Ethanol)<ΔGC(Water), with values from 0.157 to 0.317 kJ.mol-1.Å-2. Lower ΔGC are correlated with higher dispersibility. In turn, solvents with high cohesive energy and low packing density, like water, require a considerable energy to accommodate large hydrophobic solutes.Optimal extraction was achieved using dehulled grains, 60% tert-butanol–water (v/v) at 60 °C, 1:100 sample-to-solvent ratio, and two 10-minute extraction cycles.

Thermodynamically, protein solubility is dictated by the free energy of solvation (ΔG<sub>solv</sub>), composed of work of cavity creation (ΔG<sub>C</sub>) and interaction energy (ΔG<sub>I</sub>). Due to limited structural data of kafirin, this study focuses on ΔG<sub>C</sub>. Using a hard-sphere exclusion volume, ΔG<sub>C</sub> was determined to quantify the energy needed to disperse kafirin in solvents commonly used for their extraction. An experimental design was used to optimise extraction, with protein quantification by SE-HPLC.

These results highlight kafirins’ hydrophobic nature, as well as, their size being a main obstacle to their solubility. The work of cavity creation may also explain kafirins’ anisotropic shape in solvent, as it lowers ΔG<sub>C</sub> by 5-10% depending on cavity radius.

abstracts.t: Engineering SURON: A Novel Broad-Spectrum ALS-Tolerance Trait in Sorghum via Heuristic Breeding
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: BioHeuris, Rosario, Argentina

sc.x: Weed competition remains one of the most critical challenges for sorghum growers, drastically reducing yields. Developing robust, flexible herbicide-tolerance traits is an established path to provide farmers with sustainable weed management systems. Using Heuristic Breeding, an integrated framework that accelerates trait development, we developed SURON: a novel herbicide-tolerance trait providing broad-spectrum protection against multiple families of ALS-inhibiting herbicides.

Microbial screening identified a diverse set of ALS variants with distinct tolerance profiles, revealing specific mutation-by-herbicide interactions across different ALS-inhibitor families. Following deployment in plants, lead mutations were confirmed via sequencing and, in the case of gene editing, transgene-free segregants were selected. Subsequent field trials in Argentina demonstrated consistent tolerance at commercial label rates and above to pre- and post-emergence applications of multiple ALS herbicides—both as stand-alone treatments and in mixtures—without compromising crop yield or overall agronomic performance.

Optimized genetic variants of the ALS target-site enzyme were identified and characterized through high-throughput in vivo microbial screening to predict in planta herbicide-tolerance levels. Candidate variants were deployed into elite sorghum germplasm using gene editing or chemical mutagenesis. Commercial hybrids were evaluated in greenhouse and field trials to validate functional efficacy, dose-response, and crop safety of each mutation.

By integrating microbial screening, precision mutagenesis, and rapid phenotyping, we seamlessly engineered single traits that stack broad-spectrum cross-tolerance against multiple ALS-inhibitor families. Although these genetic variants created through gene editing and chemical mutagenesis are indistinguishable, in some countries they are currently regulated differently. While global gene-editing frameworks continue to harmonize toward science-based deregulation, our chemical mutagenesis-derived lines are ready to deliver high-value, non-GMO traits to farmers immediately, enhancing sorghum resilience globally. Beyond this trait, this validated platform can now be used to co-develop the next generation of novel agronomic traits.

sc.x: Sorghum is a drought-tolerant alternative to corn silage in regions with limited irrigation capacity. The objectives of this split-split plot experiment were to evaluate the effects of sorghum hybrid (F10 vs. F24, Richardson Seeds), roll gap (0.5 vs. 1.0 mm) of DurraCut™ kernel processor (KP, Scherer Inc.), and ensiling duration (0, 3, 6, and 9 months) on berry processing score (BPS) and in-situ rumen starch disappearance after 7 h of incubation (isSD7).

There were no significant interactions. Hybrid F10 had higher BPS2.36 compared to F24 (P = 0.0002). Reducing the roll gap from 1 mm to 0.5 mm increased BPS2.36 (P = 0.01). Linear increase (P < 0.0001) and a quadratic trend (P = 0.052) in isSD7 were observed with longer ensiling duration.

Sorghum was seeded at 5.6 kg/ha and grown under center-pivot irrigation, applying approximately 400 mm of water. During the growing season, mean air temperature was 25.2 °C (range: 4.4 to 41.1 °C), growing degree day accumulation was 1572 oC d, and cumulative rainfall was 143 mm. Sorghum was harvested at the hard dough stage (35% DM; 31% starch) with a forage harvester with on-board kernel processors. After ensiling, samples were analyzed for nutrient composition and digestibility. Berry processing score was expressed as the percentage of starch passing a 2.36-mm sieve (BPS2.36). Data were analyzed using a mixed model including hybrid, roll gap, ensiling duration, and their interactions as predictor variables linear and quadratic contrasts were tested.
Sorghum hybrid F24, harvested with kernel processing and ensiled for 6 months, significantly improved starch digestibility compared to hybrids F10 and F24 not ensiled.

sc.x: In West African countries especially in the Sahel region (Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Senegal, etc.), millet and sorghum are the basis of population's diet, in the form of thin and thick porridge. Over the past twenty years, however, the processing of millet and sorghum into new products with added value such as dégué, couscous and pastry products has experienced a meteoric boom, mainly due to urbanization and the development of consumption model with instant products. However, the method used to obtain these products is almost artisanal and manual and does not always meet the growing demand. The extrusion technic promoted by the SMIL/USAID transformation project is a new opportunity to produce these products abundantly and quickly in order to fill this gap. It is estimated to save 10 times less time than the artisanal and manual processing method. However, the economic profitability of producing these products by extrusion is not yet known and measured. The objective of this study is to determine the economic profitability of the production of extruded millet and sorghum-based flour used in the production of extruded couscous and thick porridge.

The method used is based on the calculation of the costs and margins of the production of extruded sorghum and millet based flour, in addition to the high time savings of the extrusion technic (10 times more observed, compared to the traditionnal technic).

It shows that in addition to the high time savings of the extrusion technic (10 times more observed, compared to the traditionnal technic), the production of extruded millet and sorghum flour is largely profitable with a gain of 66.42 US$ per 100 kg bag processed, which is economically profitable.
These have a double advantages of business opportunity and satisfaction for the growing demand of sorghum and millet based processed products.

abstracts.t: Efficacy of biological control agents (BCAs) in the suppression of sorghum anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum sublineolum

sc.x: Anthracnose, caused by fungus Colletotrichum sublineolum, Henn. Ex Sacc. & Trotter, is the most devastating disease affecting sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench]. Under severe conditions, yield losses can exceed 80% on susceptible cultivars. Preventing disease infection usually requires a high number of chemical treatments, but international market legislation imposes the minimization of their accumulation in the ecosystem due to threat on humans and fauna.

In our study, BCAs, tested at two agroecologically different locations; Serere (NaSARRI) and Abi (AbiZARDI) in Uganda, showed promising results for control of sorghum anthracnose. SESO1, a highly susceptible sorghum variety, was subjected to a four-time weekly foliar spray of B. safensis, B. velezensis, positive control (Mancozeb), and untreated SESO1. Controlled disease inoculation was done in the field and disease severity was scored using a 1-9 scale.

The results demonstrated significant differences (p ≤ 0.05) among treatments. BCAs and Mancozeb, were associated with low anthracnose severity, compared to untreated SESO1. A percentage disease severity reduction of 50.60% for B. safensis, 40.9% for B. velezensis, and 49% for the positive control, was observed. There was a general yield increase on plots treated with BCAs as supported by a strong significant negative correlation (r = - 0.58, p ≤ 0.001) with disease severity
These biological treatments provide a potential eco-friendly option for an integrated disease management of anthracnose in sorghum.

sc.x: An integrated biorefining approach was implemented to sequentially refine the hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin polymers from sorghum stover, the best-suited crop for semi-arid regions, with the objective of maximizing biopolymer yield while minimizing feedstock waste.

Extractives rich in 3-deoxyanthocyanins, proteins, and monosaccharides were first recovered via solvent extraction using water and ethanol at their respective boiling points. The extractives-free biomass was then subjected to hydrothermal fractionation (170°C, 30 min, 10% w/v loading) to isolate hemicellulosic oligosaccharides. The resulting xylooligosaccharide-enriched liquid fraction was fed to pre-weaned dairy calves (7–21 days old) as a dietary supplement, and exhaustive transcriptomics profiling of the hindgut epithelia was conducted to assess anti-inflammatory mechanisms and gut microbiome shifts. Subsequently, the hydrothermally treated solid residues underwent organosolv fractionation (propionaldehyde, 1,4-dioxane, hydrochloric acid) under three optimized conditions varying in temperature (80 and 100°C), duration (3 and 5 h), and acid loading (1×, 2×, and 4×). The isolated cellulose fractions with varying lignin content were then spun using the viscose process.

Hydrothermal fractionation yielded hemicellulosic oligosaccharides at 18% w/w, with the liquid fraction containing 44% xylooligosaccharides. Organosolv fractionation achieved lignin and cellulose yields of 18% w/w and 80% w/w, respectively. Overall, the sequential fractionation process enabled utilization of ≥90% of sorghum stover into diverse value-added products.

This systems based integrated biorefinery approach demonstrated near-complete utilization of sorghum stover across multiple high-value applications, underscoring its potential for improving both the profitability and sustainability of the biorefining industry.

sc.x: Staple grain crops typically contain some iron (Fe), zinc (Zn) and other important micronutrients for human diets, but typically not high enough to alleviate deficiencies. Sorghum bicolor is a widely consumed cereal crop worldwide, often by populations who suffer from malnutrition who could benefit from biofortified grains. The Sorghum EMS mutant collection can be used to understand mechanisms of accumulation of nutrients in grains and alleles into high yield backgrounds. Our main objective was to quantify micronutrient diversity in EMS mutant collection.

The concentration of Fe and Zn varied from 13 to 48 mg/kg and 12 to 40 mg/kg respectively. Copper (Cu), Fe and Zn were all highly correlated (77-87%), which is expected due to known transport mechanisms of these divalent cations. High and low Fe and Zn accumulating EMS lines were grown in two locations with significantly different soil profiles, and we found that plants grown in North Texas had overall lower micronutrient accumulation in grains compared with South Texas grown plants.

Eleven micronutrients were measured in the grains of 347 EMS mutant lines using ICP-MS from seeds collected in 2025 from Lubbock, TX. A subset of plants with high and low accumulation of Fe and Zn were grown in 2026 in South and North Texas to quantify differences in micronutrient accumulation and soil concentrations. Genes with large effect mutations will be identified in the lines with the highest and lowest accumulation of Fe and Zn, which are expected to consist of membrane transporters, metal ion transporters, oxidative stress related genes, and transcription factors that regulate micronutrient transport.

The micronutrient accumulations will provide valuable phenotypic data to accompany the sequenced EMS mutant collection for further functional genetics or breeding studies to gain increases in the accumulation of essential micronutrients regardless of marginal soil conditions and high temperatures.

abstracts.t: From Field to Food: Scaling Sorghum for Human Nutrition Through Processing Innovation and Market Adoption
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Nu LIfe Market, Scott City, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is gaining renewed attention as a resilient, nutrient-dense grain with strong potential to support sustainable food systems. While extensive research has demonstrated sorghum’s agronomic advantages and nutritional attributes, broader adoption in human food applications remains constrained by a lack of consumer awareness and commercial familiarity, largely due to it’s historical positioning as a feed and ethanol crop. This presentation explores how targeted processing innovation and value chain collaboration can accelerate sorghum’s transition from an underutilized crop to a mainstream food ingredient.

Nu Life Market’s work focuses on developing food-grade sorghum ingredients including whole grain, cut, pearled, flour, and crisps designed to meet functional, sensory, and scalability requirements for modern food manufacturers. Emphasis is placed on aligning grain selection, cleaning, milling, and post processing techniques with end use applications such as baked goods, cereals, snacks, and better for you formulations. Key considerations include granulation control, hydration behavior, texture development, and consistency across production runs. In addition to technical processing considerations, this work highlights market driven factors influencing adoption, including clean label formulation needs, gluten free demand, supply reliability, and sustainability expectations. Sorghum’s low water requirements, adaptability to U.S. growing regions, and compatibility with regenerative agriculture practices position it as a compelling ingredient for manufacturers seeking climate resilient raw materials.

The presentation further discusses the importance of collaboration across growers, researchers, processors, and brand owners to reduce barriers to commercialization. By bridging applied research with commercial execution, sorghum can move beyond niche applications and play a larger role in human nutrition.

These insights support conference themes related to novel human food applications, emerging commercialization pathways, and strengthening sorghum value chains, while offering a practical framework for expanding sorghum’s footprint in global food systems.

abstracts.t: High efficiency Sorghum bicolor transformation through CRISPR-knockout for Maturity (Ma) and Dwarf (Dw) genes.
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Texas A&M University, College Station, Tx, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a climate-resilient cereal crop widely grown in semi-arid regions, where its productivity is often constrained by plant architecture and flowering time. Two major genetic systems controlling these traits are the dwarfing (Dw) loci, which regulate stem elongation, and the maturity (Ma) loci, which control photoperiod sensitivity and flowering time. For example, the Dw2 gene influences internode elongation, while Ma genes such as Ma1 delay flowering under long-day conditions. Together, these loci play a critical role in determining plant height, biomass allocation, and regional adaptability. The objective of this study is to implement a CRISPR-based multiplex knockout (“CRISPR-Combo”) targeting key Dw and Ma genes in sorghum to modulate plant height and flowering time simultaneously.

Phenotypically, knockout of Dw genes (e.g., Dw2) is expected to result in reduced plant height due to decreased internode elongation, producing a more compact architecture. In contrast, disruption of Ma genes is expected to alter photoperiod sensitivity, with many edited lines showing earlier flowering, particularly under long-day conditions.

This project aims to: (1) design and validate multiple sgRNAs targeting conserved regions within selected Dw and Ma loci; (2) construct a multiplex CRISPR-Cas9 vector capable of efficient editing in sorghum; (3) generate and screen edited lines for mutations at target loci; and (4) evaluate resulting phenotypes under controlled conditions. By combining edits in both developmental pathways, this work seeks to create novel sorghum ideotypes with optimized architecture and adaptability. Ultimately, this approach demonstrates the potential of multiplex genome editing to accelerate crop improvement and provide a foundation for next-generation breeding strategies.
Creating a gene-editing pathway for future sorghum projects will allow researchers/breeders to drastically reduce experimental time while enabling precise, simultaneous trait optimization.

sc.x: Enhancing the nutritional value of cereal grains is a global priority for food security, human health, and sustainable agriculture. Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), a climate-resilient staple for over 500 million people, offers untapped potential for nutritional improvement through systematic dissection of its grain metabolome and lipidome. Here, we integrated large-scale metabolomics and lipidomics with genome-wide association analyses to characterize grain biochemical diversity and identify its genetic basis.

Extensive natural variation was observed across the population, particularly in amino acid, polyphenol pathways and Triacylglycerols (PEs) relevant to nutritional quality. This broad biochemical diversity highlights substantial genetic potential for improving grain nutritional traits through targeted breeding. Genome-wide association analysis of the metabolites (mGWAS) identified approximately 4.15 million significant SNP–metabolite associations, enriched in regulatory regions and organized into 38 metabolite-associated genomic clusters. GWAS of 528 lipid species across 266 accessions identified approximately 1.6 million associated variants, demonstrating that variation in grain oil content is primarily driven by differences in triacylglycerol accumulation, with additional contributions from phospholipids. A Polygenic Lipid Score strongly predicted grain oil content and identified elite high-oil accessions. These results establish a population-scale atlas of sorghum grain metabolic diversity and provide a genetic framework for improving nutritional quality and oil yield in climate-resilient crops.

A total of 266 accessions from the Sorghum Association Panel were used in this study to capture broad genetic diversity. Plants were cultivated under standard field conditions, and mature grains were harvested for downstream analyses.
These results establish a population-scale atlas of sorghum grain metabolic diversity and provide a genetic framework for improving nutritional quality and oil yield in climate-resilient crops.

sc.x: Diarrhea, caused by both infectious and non-infectious agents, is a major disorder of the pre-weaned phase of dairy calves, contributing to poor welfare, delayed growth, calf mortality, and significant economic losses to the dairy industry. Therefore, this study evaluated the dietary impact of xylo-oligosaccharides (XOS) extracted from sorghum stover on the gut microbiome and structural integrity of the gut epithelium in pre-weaned dairy calves.

Sorghum was selected as the model crop due to its heat resilience, high biomass yield, and multipurpose utility in semi-arid regions. Stems and leaves from a dryland grain sorghum variety were ground and pre-extracted with ethanol and water to remove monosaccharides, wax, proteins, and anthocyanins. The extractives-free biomass was hydrothermally fractionated at 170°C for 30 min at 10% w/v solid loading in a 2-liter Parr reactor to obtain an XOS-enriched liquid hydrolysate, which was freeze-dried and incorporated into a milk-replacement formula. Pre-weaned dairy calves were divided into a control group fed a commercial crude fiber source and a treatment group fed the sorghum-XOS product from Day 1 to Day 21. Body weight gain, histopathology, and ex vivo inflammatory studies were conducted on jejunum, ileum, and colon tissue samples to assess treatment effects.

The crude XOS extracts from sorghum provided comparable benefits to those of the commercial fiber source (inulin). Specifically, sorghum XOS protected gut integrity and induced a time- and tissue-dependent response consistent with prebiotic-like activity, as evidenced by histopathological and inflammatory assessments across the evaluated intestinal regions.

This study demonstrated the viability of crude XOS extracts from sorghum stover as a health-promoting dietary supplement for pre-weaned dairy calves, offering a sustainable and cost-effective alternative to commercial prebiotic sources for supporting gut health and integrity in early calf development.

sc.x: Mexico is one of the world’s largest pet food producers and a growing market for grain-based pet food products, yet evidence on household pet food demand and willingness to pay for alternative ingredients remains limited. This study examines the market potential for sorghum, including U.S. sorghum, as a pet food ingredient in Mexico.

Using data from a survey of 300 Mexican pet owners, we document household pet food purchasing patterns, estimate demand relationships, analyze consumer awareness of sorghum in pet food, and recover willingness to pay premia using double-bounded contingent valuation.

Results show that dry food dominates feeding practices and that pet food demand is shaped primarily by pet ownership intensity, price, and income. Instrumental-variables estimates indicate that demand is price inelastic in the full sample and among dog-owning households. Awareness that pet food can be made from sorghum is limited, but stated acceptance is not low: many respondents report neutral to favorable purchase intentions. Estimated willingness to pay is positive for both sorghum-containing pet food and pet food made with U.S. sorghum, with mean premia of about 16.5% and 14.7%, respectively.

Prior awareness of sorghum is one of the strongest predictors of willingness to pay, suggesting that consumer information and product positioning may be central to market development in this emerging segment.

sc.x: Challenges exist with current N management approaches that potentially do not allow growers to optimize both agronomic and economic strategies.

Initial evaluations indicated that nitrogen applications could be delayed until 28–35 days after planting without significantly reducing grain yield. However, assessment of physiological responses revealed that delayed nitrogen application reduced tiller development, particularly at lower seeding rates. No single yield component compensated for the reduction in tiller production, suggesting limited physiological plasticity to offset this effect.

Field trials were conducted to evaluate the effects of nitrogen application timing in combination with varying seeding rates. Locations across Oklahoma represented a range of geographic and environmental conditions. Initial evaluations were conducted weekly from planting through 60 days after planting. A secondary evaluation examined nitrogen application strategies, comparing applications made entirely at planting to those split between planting and 30 days after planting. In-season growth parameters were measured throughout the growing season to assess treatment effects on crop development. Greenseeker® readings were collected to monitor nitrogen status and identify potential deficiencies. At maturity, ten sorghum plants per plot were sampled to evaluate yield components, and a small-plot combine was used to estimate grain yield. Statistical analyses were conducted using SAS, with treatment effects evaluated using a linear mixed model. Mean separations were performed using a Tukey-adjusted post hoc test.

The results of this study indicate that growers have flexibility in managing nitrogen applications in sorghum, allowing them to adjust decisions based on market prices, environmental conditions, and crop status. This adaptability may enhance both the effectiveness and efficiency of nitrogen management strategies.

sc.x: Identifying gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that govern plant development and environmental response can be used for characterizing gene function and contribution to valuable traits. In addition to narrowing the gene targets for such applications as CRISPR editing or transgenics, these GRNs also function to classify which gene sets in a given haplotype could be selected for integration into breeding programs. By integrating novel pan-transcriptomic data from specific tissues and multi-omics information from online database SorghumBase, we can build more accurate GRNs, identify candidate genes and loci for functional studies, select germplasm for breeding and trait discovery, and ultimately apply these findings to crop improvement.
RNA-seq. Weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA). DNA-affinity profiling (DAP-seq).

Key developmental gene sets showed distinct expression patterns across early tissue stages. To connect these developmental modules with grain trait outcomes, we paired ionomics data from mature seeds with weighted gene correlation network analysis to identify genetic modules linked to trace element accumulation. Integrating TF-binding data from DAP-seq profiles revealed unique promoter binding patterns in meristematic gene clusters. These refined GRNs yielded subnetworks that highlighted new targets for functional characterization. Utilizing genetic variation and germplasm information hosted on SorghumBase, this functional characterization step was accelerated by selecting germplasm with disruptive variants to improve molecular characterization of candidate genes.

There were several candidate loci and modules identified that are anti-correlated to two different, but important inflorescence traits: panicle size and grain content. These modules can be further dissected through future biochemical and genetic interrogation through EMS mutant lines and possible CRISPR editing. Together, these findings demonstrate how multi-omics approaches can resolve GRNs and gene modules underlying sorghum development and seed traits, providing a framework for discovering regulatory modules and genetic targets with potential value for breeding programs.

abstracts.t: Genes and pathways determining flowering time variation in temperate-adapted sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: University of Nebraska, Lincoln, United States

sc.x: Flowering time is a key adaptive trait controlled by a complex genetic architecture that integrates environmental and endogenous signals. However, substantial divergence in the identity and function of pathway components has been observed across plant species, limiting the ability to translate knowledge from model systems to crops. Here, we aimed to identify the genetic and regulatory determinants of flowering time variation in temperate-adapted sorghum across environments.

While FT-like and SOC1-like gene families retain conserved roles in regulating flowering time in sorghum, the specific genes driving natural variation differ from the primary orthologs characterized in related species. In addition, the ageing pathway plays an important role in regulating non-photoperiod variation in flowering time, with multiple components identified through integrated genome-wide and transcriptome-wide association analyses.

We employed an integrative approach combining genome-wide and transcriptome-wide association studies (GWAS and TWAS) to identify genetic determinants of variation in flowering time across multiple environments in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor). Analyses were conducted using a large panel of primarily photoperiod-insensitive genotypes drawn from the Sorghum Association Panel and Sorghum Diversity Panel. Flowering time phenotypes were collected across field environments in Nebraska and Alabama to capture environmental variation and enable cross-location validation. Transcriptomic data were generated from field-grown plants in Nebraska, encompassing 738 genotypes, and were used in TWAS analyses to link gene expression variation with flowering time.

Our results demonstrate that while the functions of major gene families are conserved, functional information from even closely related species is not a reliable predictor of which specific gene copies drive natural variation in flowering time.

sc.x: Modern sorghum breeding increasingly relies on functional genomics to identify genes underlying important agronomic traits, yet accessing and interpreting gene expression data often requires specialized bioinformatics expertise. SorghumBase addresses this gap by providing breeders with curated, user-friendly gene expression and biological pathway resources that support candidate gene discovery and prioritization for crop improvement.

SorghumBase integrates high-quality RNA-seq datasets focused on key breeding targets including abiotic stress tolerance and plant development. Curated in collaboration with the EMBL-EBI Expression Atlas, these datasets enable users to examine when and where genes are active across tissues, growth stages, and environmental conditions. Visualization tools including heatmaps and the eFP Browser allow rapid identification of tissue-specific and stress-responsive genes without requiring computational expertise. The platform also supports comparison of expression patterns among gene family members (paralogs), helping users assess functional redundancy and prioritize the most relevant targets. In addition, SorghumBase links genes to biological pathways through the Plant Reactome, providing views of gene function within networks controlling metabolism, hormone signaling, and developmental processes.

For breeders, the combination of expression profiles and pathway context offers practical advantages over single-gene approaches. Expression data supports the selection of candidate loci for marker development or genomic selection by revealing which genes respond to drought, heat, or other target stresses. Pathway views provide systems-level understanding that is valuable for identifying key regulators and anticipating potential trade-offs between traits such as stress tolerance and yield. By integrating gene expression and pathway resources in an accessible platform, SorghumBase enables biology-driven selection strategies that accelerate the identification of functional markers and support the development of improved sorghum varieties adapted to diverse and changing environments.

sc.x: Semi-dwarf phenotypes are highly desirable traits in modern crop breeding, particularly following the widespread adoption of fertilizers during the Green Revolution. Although several dwarfing genes have been identified in sorghum, additional loci contributing to reduced plant height remain to be characterized. In this study, we aimed to characterize a semi-dwarf mutant carrying a stop-gained mutation in a C2H2 transcription factor with an INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD), referred to as IDD-A, and to elucidate its role in regulating plant height.

To investigate the molecular basis of the dwarf phenotype, we performed transcriptome profiling of wild-type and IDD-A mutant plants. Given the central role of gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis and signaling in plant height regulation, we selected a set of transcription factors, including IDD-A and GA-associated genes, to construct a gene regulatory network. Yeast one-hybrid and yeast two-hybrid assays were conducted to identify protein–DNA and protein–protein interactions.

We found that IDD-A interacts with a GRAS family transcription factor, GRAS-B, and directly binds to its promoter. Furthermore, IDD-A and GRAS-B co-bind to the promoters of key genes involved in the GA signaling pathway.
These findings support a role for IDD-A as a previously uncharacterized regulator of plant height, acting through GA-associated gene regulatory networks in sorghum.

sc.x: Efficient haploid induction is essential to implementing doubled haploid–based breeding in sorghum. In this study, we present a haploid induction system designed to increase the recovery of haploid progeny from breeding crosses.

The system is based on allelic variation of processes that promote haploid formation, enabling reproducible induction across diverse genetic backgrounds. Testcrosses of inducers were made to test haploid induction frequency. Progeny were grown to identify hybrid induction frequency. To further improve haploid induction frequency, next-generation inducer lines are being developed.
Across multiple hybrid combinations evaluated in both greenhouse and field environments, the system generated consistent haploid induction frequencies ranging from 5–20%.

These observed induction rates represent a substantial improvement in haploid recovery and overcome a limitation in sorghum doubled haploid development. Collectively, these results establish genetic resources sufficient to enable the implementation of doubled haploid breeding in sorghum improvement programs. When integrated with genomic prediction, this system will accelerate breeding cycles and increase overall genetic gain.

abstracts.t: Decortication-gelatinization coupling in Sorghum processing: a decade of industrial evidence for superior food quality, shelf-life extension, and nickel reduction
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Framens, Rome, Italy

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) holds exceptional promise as a gluten-free, climate-resilient grain for next-generation human food systems. Yet its large-scale commercial adoption remains constrained by pericarp-associated challenges: elevated tannin and phenolic load, lipid oxidation susceptibility, high nickel bioavailability, and post-harvest instability. This work presents findings from over 10 years of industrial-scale trials, evaluating the impact of decortication combined with gelatinization and twin-screw extrusion across multiple food matrices — dry pasta, extruded snacks, and infant food formulations.

Decortication reduced nickel content from 50–90 µg/100g in whole-grain sorghum to an average of 1.7 µg/100g in decorticated flour — a reduction exceeding 95% — rendering the product safe for nickel-sensitive individuals and fully compatible with pediatric nutritional standards. Decorticated sorghum dry pasta achieved firmness, elasticity, and cooking loss profiles indistinguishable from conventional wheat-based pasta, with markedly superior surface smoothness and color uniformity. Starch digestibility and protein bioavailability improved significantly, consistent with reduced tannin-mediated inhibition of digestive enzymes.

The decortication-gelatinization combination proved effective in inactivating endogenous lipases, extending shelf-life from approximately 6 to 18 months without modified atmosphere packaging (nitrogen or CO₂ flushing) — eliminating a major logistical and economic barrier for global distribution. These outcomes, validated across a decade of industrial-scale production, confirm that decortication is not merely a quality-enhancing step but a structural solution to sorghum's most critical commercialization bottlenecks.

Decortication-gelatinization coupling represents a scalable, investment-ready processing platform capable of repositioning sorghum as a mainstream ingredient in gluten-free, functional, and infant food markets — with immediate industrial applicability and measurable impact on food security and consumer health.
