Although cover crops reduced yield in the short term, they remain important for long-term system sustainability.

Field experiments were conducted using a randomized complete block design with four replications. Two cropping systems were evaluated: a grain sorghum (GS)–cotton system with 4 rotations treatments (GS-fallow-Cotton, GS-cover crop-Cotton, Cotton-Fallow-GS, Cotton-cover crop-GS). and a forage sorghum (FS)–corn system with 4 rotations treatments (FS-fallow-Corn, FS-cover crop-Corn, Corn-Fallow-FS, Corn-cover crop-FS). Cover crop mixture consisted of Austrian winter pea and oat (70:30 ratio). Organic amendments were made through poultry litter applied based on crop yield goals. Data were collected on crop growth parameters, biomass production, grain yield, forage yield, and weed biomass.
Continued research is needed to optimize management in organic sorghum-based systems.

abstracts.t: A Review of Sorghum Fungal Diseases in Kenya: Status, Distribution, Management and Implications for Yield Gaps and Crop Resilience
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Kenya Agricultural Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), AMRI-Katumani, Machakos, Kenya

sc.x: Fungal diseases are among the most significant biotic constraints to sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.) production in Kenya, causing substantial yield losses in grain quantity, quality, and herbage. Major pathogens include anthracnose (Colletotrichum sublineola), leaf blights (Exserohilum turcicum, Curvularia spp., Bipolaris spp.), rust (Puccinia purpurea), gray leaf spot, and smuts (Sporisorium spp.), which are widespread across diverse agro-ecologies. Under conducive conditions, yield losses can exceed 70%, highlighting the contribution of diseases to existing yield gaps.

Findings indicate that disease prevalence and severity vary widely across agro-ecological zones, influenced by genotype susceptibility, pathogen virulence diversity, crop management practices and use of informal seed systems. While some diseases are widespread but relatively mild, anthracnose and certain smuts have been reported to cause severe yield losses in susceptible varieties, often associated with highly virulent strains and favourable environmental conditions. Emerging challenges, including climate variability and change, are increasingly creating conditions favourable for fungal pathogens, with studies reporting yield losses of up to 67% in susceptible varieties. Molecular evidence indicates high pathotype diversity, complicating the development of durable resistance.

This review synthesizes current knowledge on the prevalence, epidemiology, and host-pathogen-environment interactions of sorghum fungal diseases in Kenya, integrating both qualitative prioritization and quantitative assessments such as incidence, severity scoring, and modelling of disease distribution patterns.

Effective management requires integrated strategies combining host resistance, gene pyramiding, climate-informed surveillance, and use of strengthened breeding programs. Enhancing seed systems and promoting farmer adoption of improved climate-smart technologies are critical to improving productivity and resilience under changing environmental conditions. By integrating insights from epidemiology, breeding, and agronomy, this review proposes a framework for future research to support sustainable sorghum production, enhance smallholder livelihoods, and strengthen regional food security in Kenya

sc.x: Post-emergence (POST) grass weed control is limited in grain sorghum due to the sensitivity of the crop to grass-selective herbicides. Tembotrione, a 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD)-inhibiting herbicide, is effective for broad-spectrum weed control but is not registered for use in grain sorghum due to crop injury concerns. Greenhouse and field experiments were conducted to evaluate the response of tembotrione-resistant genotypes (G-200 and G-350), their F<sub>1</sub> hybrids with 4 US lines, along with a few susceptible inbreds and commercial hybrids.

The results from the greenhouse and field studies revealed considerable genotypic variation to tembotrione. The most susceptible genotype, S-1, showed a GR<sub>50</sub> of 49 g ai ha<sup>-1</sup>, while the resistant parental lines G-200 and G-350 and the F<sub>1</sub> hybrid (G-10 x G-200) showed much higher resistance with GR<sub>50</sub> = 186, 140, and 174 g ai ha<sup>-1</sup>, respectively, in controlled conditions. In the field experiments, G-200 and its derived F<sub>1</sub> hybrids showed the least visual injury, high chlorophyll retention, and comparatively higher biomass than other genotypes, even at a 368 g ai ha<sup>-1 </sup>of tembotrione. Enhanced tolerance in the F<sub>1</sub> hybrids compared with their susceptible parents demonstrates the utility of resistance in US germplasm, though genetic background has an impact on herbicide tolerance level.

In greenhouse, 22 genotypes were evaluated for tembotrione in a dose-response [0, 23, 46, 92 (label recommended dose), 184, and 368 g ai ha<sup>-1</sup>] assay. Similarly, tembotrione-resistant parents and their crosses were evaluated in the field for visual injury, chlorophyll retention, and biomass at 0, 184, and 368 g ai ha⁻¹.

These results indicate that G-200 and G-350 are valuable sources of tembotrione resistance for introgression into breeding lines to develop agronomically desirable sorghum hybrids with postemergence tembotrione tolerance.

abstracts.t: Early Season Chilling Tolerant Forage Sorghum to Extend Planting Window and Enhance Productivity in Texas High Plains
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: Texas Tech University, Plant and Soil Science, Texas Coalition for Sustainable Integrated Systems TecSIS, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a C4 tropical crop typically planted later than maize, exposing it to intense summer heat and drought that reduce forage productivity and quality. Identifying forage sorghum hybrids tolerant to early-season chilling stress could extend the planting window and improve yield potential under Texas High Plains conditions.

Cultivar and planting date were the primary drivers of biomass production (both p < 0.0001), while seeding density had no significant effect (p = 0.46). A significant cultivar × planting date interaction (p = 0.0003) indicated hybrid performance varied across environments. Chilling stress reduced mean biomass by 17.5% relative to the optimal planting date (4,949 vs. 5,996 kg ha⁻¹). Despite this, WarnerP4205, AltaF8322, and RichardsonF27 ranked among the top performers across all environments.

Eleven forage sorghum hybrids and one maize hybrid were evaluated across three planting dates (April 1, April 15, May 1) and three seeding densities (65,000; 78,000; 91,000 seeds/acre) in 2025. A three-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD comparisons, and ANCOVA adjusting for stand establishment were used to assess treatment effects. Top-performing hybrids are being validated in 2026.

Several forage sorghum hybrids demonstrated resilience to early-season chilling stress and maintained competitive biomass yields relative to the optimal planting date. These findings support the feasibility of earlier planting to extend the forage production window in the Texas High Plains, with 2026 validation trials ongoing.

abstracts.t: Germplasm evaluation and multi-omics approaches for strategic improvement of plant defense and sustainable sorghum production
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: USDA Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS), Stillwater, United States

sc.x: Achieving stable, high-yield crop production requires a shift from reactive protection to proactive, genetics-based improvement. Our research integrates large-scale germplasm evaluation with multi-omics approaches to identify and deploy insect resistance and yield potential in sorghum.

These traits have been incorporated into breeding lines across grain, forage, and biomass sorghum. In parallel, multi-omics approaches have been employed to decode and deploy these superior traits, including resilience and high yield potential. Genomics has enabled the identification of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and the development of marker-assisted selection (MAS) strategies, allowing for efficient selection of resistance genes without relying solely on time-consuming field trials. Transcriptomics has provided insights into gene expression changes in response to insect infestation, revealing key regulatory networks and candidate genes underlying resistance. More recently, proteomics and metabolomics analyses have identified the proteins and metabolites that execute defense responses, thereby confirming the downstream effects of genetic variation.

We screened a large and diverse germplasm collection, including over 43,000 accessions from the National Plant Germplasm System, along with several hundred exotic lines, and identified over 120 germplasm lines exhibiting strong resistance to insects and desirable agronomic traits.

While germplasm screening identifies what is resilient, multi-omics approaches explain why it is resilient and provide the tools needed to efficiently transfer these traits into elite cultivars. This work demonstrates the power of integrating these approaches through a systems biology framework. By combining genomics (to identify resistance genes), transcriptomics (to confirm their activation), and metabolomics (to validate the production of defensive compounds), we achieve a comprehensive understanding of resistance mechanisms in sorghum and accelerate the development of improved crop varieties.

sc.x: Nitrogen (N) fertilizers are critical for maintaining crop productivity; however, excessive N inputs contribute to air and water quality degradation. Naturally occurring N transformations, including nitrification and denitrification, produce nitrous oxide (N<sub>2</sub>O), a potent greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting substance. In addition, N is lost from agricultural systems through nitrate (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) leaching, which contaminates groundwater and surface waters. Biological nitrification inhibition (BNI) is a plant-mediated process in which root exudates suppress soil nitrifying microorganisms, maintaining N in the ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) form and reducing N losses.

A greenhouse study was conducted at Texas A&M University (College Station, TX, USA) to evaluate the effect of BNI on NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> leaching using a 3 × 2 factorial design with three replications. Two sorghum genotypes with contrasting BNI capacity were grown under urea fertilization with or without a synthetic nitrification inhibitor (SNI; nitrapyrin). Plants were grown in soil columns (76 cm × 10 cm) to allow root development and leachate collection. Water samples were collected throughout the growing period. Rhizosphere soils were analyzed for NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA), and nitrification rates.

High-BNI (HBNI) reduced cumulative NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> leaching by 45% compared to low-BNI (LBNI) under urea without SNI. LBNI soils contained 2.4 times more NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>, whereas HBNI maintained 3.9 times greater NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (p < 0.05). These shifts were supported by lower AOB and AOA abundance in HBNI soils, reduced by 60% and 50%, respectively. Net and potential nitrification rates were also suppressed in HBNI by 68% and 59%, respectively (p < 0.05).

Overall, reduced NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> leaching losses, microbial abundance, and nitrification rates indicate a strong link between BNI activity and improved N retention, highlighting its potential to mitigate N losses under field conditions.

abstracts.t: Bridging value chain gaps through stakeholder insights, consumer research and applied food science for premium sorghum foods
abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

a: The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia
The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

sc.x: Sorghum has strong agronomic and sustainability advantages, yet its uptake as a human food remains limited in many developed markets. This study aimed to identify barriers and opportunities for advancing food‑grade sorghum by integrating value‑chain stakeholder perspectives, consumer research and applied food engineering approaches. The objective was to link social and market insights with ingredient and product properties to inform more coordinated pathways for premium sorghum foods.

Consumer focus groups were conducted to explore awareness, perceptions and willingness to trial sorghum-based foods. In parallel, semi‑structured interviews were undertaken with stakeholders across the sorghum value chain—including growers, processors, food manufacturers and industry organisations. Guided by these insights, selected sorghum varieties were evaluated, with sensory, functional and physical properties measured to explore their relevance to stakeholder needs and consumer expectations.

Consumers demonstrated low familiarity with sorghum as a food ingredient and limited understanding of its culinary uses, relying heavily on taste, price and familiar product formats to guide adoption. Stakeholders highlighted misalignment across the value chain, including limited information flow between production and food manufacturing, lack of demand for sorghum as a food ingredient and challenges related to consistency and functionality. Ingredient and product evaluations illustrated how specific varieties with certain functional and sensory properties could be aligned with identified market and processing requirements.

The findings indicate that advancing sorghum for human consumption requires coordinated value‑chain action supported by consumer insight and applied engineering and food science, rather than isolated product innovation. Integrating stakeholder perspectives, consumer research and ingredient functionality provides practical pathways to strengthen market readiness and support more resilient premium sorghum food systems.

abstracts.t: Comparing Water Use Efficiency, Evapotranspiration, and Greenhouse Gas Footprints of Forage Sorghum and Forage Corn in the Semi-arid Texas High Plains.

sc.x: The Texas high plains is one of the agricultural regions that supports the US dairy industry and forage production. Producers in this region rely on corn for silage as a primary forage crop for the dairy industry, but its cultivation is highly water intensive and associated with a substantial greenhouse gas (GHG) footprint. In contrast, sorghum offers a more sustainable option, being both drought-tolerant and water-efficient with lower GHG footprint. This study was conducted on a producer’s field in Plainview, Texas, to find an alternate drought tolerant forage crop that can conserve water with less GHG footprint that will provide similar nutrient requirement as corn for dairy animals.
An eddy covariance system equipped with LI-COR trace gas analyzers and long-term chambers was deployed to monitor environmental variables and quantify GHG fluxes.

Preliminary results showed that forage sorghum used less water than forage corn during the growing season. Seasonal evapotranspiration for forage sorghum was 491 mm, compared with 847 mm for forage corn. The seasonal average water use efficiency was higher in forage corn, 3.5 g C mm⁻¹ of water, than in forage sorghum, 3.0 g C mm⁻¹ of water. However, forage sorghum exhibited a lower greenhouse gas footprint.
These findings suggest that forage sorghum exhibits potential as a more sustainable forage crop under water‑limited conditions.

sc.x: Brazil is a global leader in cereal production, but the presence of Sorghum halepense (Johnsongrass) poses a significant economic threat as it is classified as a quarantine pest for importers of Brazilian grains. Visual differentiation between S. halepense and other disseminated species, such as S. arundinaceum and S. verticilliflorum, is extremely difficult, necessitating the development of rapid, reliable diagnostic tools to ensure grain quality and maintain international market access. The objective of this study is to demonstrate that Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy applied to fresh sorghum leaves provides a significantly more effective identification system.

The superiority of leaf data stems from its ability to capture active metabolic information and moisture levels, which produce distinct spectral signals. The optimized identification model used Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification with a linear kernel. Data preprocessing included Standard Normal Variate (SNV) to normalize variations in leaf thickness and the 1st Derivative of Savitzky-Golay (11-point window, 2nd order polynomial) to highlight chemical peaks. Analysis of Variable Importance in Projection (VIP > 1.2) identified critical spectral fingerprints. These regions reflect unique anatomical and biochemical traits, such as mesophyll structure and specific wax compositions.

The NIR-SVM model achieved high performance in cross-validation, yielding an F1 Score of 0.93 and a recall of 99.0%, ensuring that nearly all S. halepense plants are identified. It also reached a balanced accuracy of 88.3% and a precision of 88.0%.

In conclusion, the NIR-SVM method using fresh leaves is highly recommended for field and greenhouse monitoring. Its exceptional sensitivity and robust diagnostic capabilities offer an innovative solution for the rapid detection of S. halepense, facilitating more assertive management strategies and safeguarding the integrity of Brazilian agricultural exports. abstracts.t: Sorghum Wild Relatives: Pipeline Between Ecology and Pre-Breeding
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

sc.x: Climate change is intensifying abiotic stress pressures on global cropping systems, with rising temperatures and aridity threatening yield stability. Improving resilience in Poaceae crops, the dominant global calorie source, is therefore critical. Currently, adaptive capacity is constrained by genetic erosion and strong GxExM interactions. Crop Wild Relatives (CWRs) offer underutilized reservoirs for potential adaptive variation, particularly in Sorghum. To support pre-breeding and conservation, SDMs and subsequent phenotypic variation were used to identify and prioritize Sorghum wild relatives for crop improvement.

Saccharinae CWR richness was highest in Southeast Asia and Oceania, particularly in Northern Australia; however, conservation levels were limited, with only seven of forty-two taxa showing over thirty percent range as protected. Several under-protected species of Sorghum and its closely related genera, with promise for adaptation to extreme environments, also occur in unprotected regions undergoing significant human modification. These results informed prioritization for ongoing experimental evaluation.

42 Saccharinae wild relatives, including 21 Sorghum species, were modelled to assess their global distributions and derived niche occupancy, which showed their exposure to temperature and moisture extremes. Conservation gaps in the current protected area network were also identified. Candidate taxa representing putative heat and drought tolerance amongst Australian Sorghums were collected and subsequently experimentally validated. Controlled-environment phenotyping experiments on these candidates were conducted to quantify responses to short-duration, high-temperature stress during critical reproductive phases to understand effects on seed set, plant architecture, and other traits.

This study applies the SDM prioritisation framework, with experimental validation, to Sorghum and its allies, supporting the integration of CWR into pre-breeding. Ongoing phenotyping will test whether ecogeographic signals translate directly into functional heat-tolerance variance or reflect additional constraints. Together, these approaches address a critical bottleneck in bridging the gap between CWR ecology and pre-breeding.

abstracts.t: Landscape impacts of sorghum, alfalfa and cotton on biological control of insect pests
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, United States
New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, United States

sc.x: Alfalfa can act as an insectary providing predators for nearby cotton and sorghum fields. while increasing biological control of insect pests. A field trial was conducted in 2026 in Artesia, NM to evaluate predation of sentinel eggs in sorghum and cotton surrounded by alfalfa. Prior trials at the same location were conducted to examine the impact of nearby alfalfa hay on biological control in cotton and found a dramatic increase in egg predation. Some trials were also conducted to evaluate biological control in sorghum. Cotton near hay in commerical fields had over 90% predation of sentinel eggs up to 1000 feet from uncut alfalfa. Predation in sorghum ranged fom 56-71%.
2026 field trial results will be analyzed and discussed.

Sentinel eggs from a laboratory colony were attached to foliage of cotton, hay and sorghum. Eggs were in groups of 30-60 eggs per 'mass" using 24 hour old eggs. Eggs were collected back from the field after 48 hours and placed under a dissecting microscope to examine eggs remains and to classify them by damage from specific mouthparts. Predators were also collected to compare the number of predators of various species to the percent predation by classes of predators with different mouthparts.

Prior trials indicated that biological control can be enhanced with proximity to alfalfa. Some work with sorghum at this location suggest that it is a better enviroment for predators than cotton but that it may also benefit from close proximity to alfalfa hay.

sc.x: Australian sorghum production is highly exposed to rainfall variability, heat stress, shifting sowing opportunities, and market uncertainty. Although regional crop models support in-season yield estimation, objective production forecasts with useful lead time before harvest, and ideally before sowing, remain limited. This study aimed to develop an operational framework to extend lead time for sorghum production forecasting from field to regional scales in Australia.

The framework integrates seasonal climate forecasts from general circulation models, Earth Observation (EO), and biophysical crop models to generate spatially explicit sorghum production forecasts. ECMWF seasonal forecasts were downscaled to station scale and disaggregated to daily weather inputs for crop simulation. EO data were used to update crop condition, growth dynamics, and seasonal development through the season. EO-AI derived soil moisture estimates from Sentinel data were also used to characterise starting soil water prior to sowing, reducing uncertainty around initial conditions and helping inform management choices under variable seasonal conditions. Field-scale summer cropping area was mapped from EO to define the extent of sorghum production and support aggregation from paddock to regional scales.

The framework was applied across major sorghum-growing regions of north-eastern Australia and extended into routine monthly forecasting from August to March. This shifted forecasting from mainly in-season assessment to a pre-sowing and early-season outlook, providing several additional months of lead time. Forecasts resolved seasonal and regional differences across Australia, Queensland, and New South Wales, with uncertainty narrowing as the season progressed and EO information accumulated.
Integrating climate forecasts, EO, and crop models can significantly improve sorghum production foresight in Australia and support more climate-resilient decision-making across sorghum systems.

sc.x: The parasitic weed Striga hermonthica remains a major constraint to sorghum production in sub-Saharan Africa. Host plant resistance is the most eco-friendly means of controlling Striga. Resistance conferred by loss-of-function of the LOW GERMINATION STIMULANT 1 (LGS1) gene changes host-derived strigolactones profile to suppress striga germination. Like any other biotic stress, the spatial variability in Striga incidence complicates phenotypic evaluation for identifying resistant sorghum genotypes. Breeder-friendly genetic tools that facilitate efficient selection of resistant lines and introgression of resistant alleles into locally adapted sorghum varieties are imperative for developing striga-resistant varieties. The study focused on identifying genomic variants associated with the loss-of-function lgs1 alleles (lgs1-1, lgs1-2, and lgs1-3) and the development and validation of Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP) markers for efficient tracking across diverse sorghum breeding programs.

KASP assays reliably differentiated LGS1 and lgs1 alleles across diverse genetic backgrounds, demonstrating robustness despite underlying allelic diversity at the locus. Marker calls were consistent with expected resistance phenotypes, supporting their predictive accuracy for identifying loss-of-function alleles.

We leveraged a pangenome resource of 1676 sorghum lines that capture global diversity to identify genomic variants linked and in linkage disequilibrium with the loss-of-function alleles of the LGS1 locus, and translated these to KASP markers. The performance of the KASP markers was evaluated in the Sorghum Genetics and Molecular Breeding Lab at Kansas State University, and 17 National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS) sorghum breeding programs from Africa.
These KASP markers provide robust, high-throughput tools for marker-assisted selection of lgs1 alleles, enabling efficient deployment of Striga resistance in African sorghum breeding programs.

abstracts.t: Rain matters: Dryland sorghum yield in the Texas High Plains
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

sc.x: Agriculture in the Texas High Plains (THP) is transitioning from irrigated systems to dryland production due to declining groundwater availability from the Ogallala aquifer. Grain sorghum, a drought-tolerant crop, is central to this shift. This study examines long-term patterns of non-irrigated grain sorghum yield in relation to rainfall and temperature across the THP.

County-level dryland (non-irrigated) grain sorghum yield data (1985–2018) were obtained from the USDA-NASS database. Climate data, including daily rainfall and maximum and minimum temperature, were sourced from the NASA POWER database.Climate variables were aggregated to the growing season for each county in the Texas High Plains. A yield-to-rainfall ratio was calculated to estimate crop water productivity (CWP). Spatial and temporal variability in yield, rainfall, and temperature were analyzed across counties and years.

Dryland sorghum yield exhibited strong spatial and temporal variability, ranging from approximately 0.9 to 4.4 t ha⁻¹ across counties and years. Rainfall showed a strong positive relationship with yield, indicating that precipitation was the primary driver of productivity in dryland systems. Crop water productivity (CWP) varied widely among counties, reflecting differences in rainfall distribution, soil properties, and management practices. Temperature effects were also evident, with higher temperatures during critical growth stages, associated with reduced yields. Northern counties demonstrated relatively stable yields, while southern counties showed greater variability due to higher temperatures and sandier soils.

Rainfall is the dominant factor controlling dryland sorghum yield variability in the Texas High Plains. While sorghum is drought-tolerant, its productivity remains highly dependent on seasonal precipitation patterns. Spatial differences in soil and climate contribute to variability in water use efficiency across the region. As groundwater resources from the Ogallala Aquifer continue to decline, improving water productivity and adapting management practices to variable rainfall conditions will be essential for sustaining dryland sorghum production.

sc.x: Soil compaction is a major physical constraint on crop productivity worldwide, restricting root growth, water uptake, and nutrient acquisition. In sorghum, improving root system performance in mechanically resistant soils represents a promising strategy to enhance yield stability and resilience to abiotic stress. However, the genetic basis of root penetrability remains poorly understood, largely due to the lack of scalable and quantitative phenotyping approaches. This study aims to establish a high-throughput phenotyping platform to characterize root penetrability across a diverse panel of sorghum accessions and link phenotypic variation with genomic analyses.

We present a high-throughput phenotyping framework to quantify root penetrability using a two-layer Phytagel-based cylinder system integrated with 3D imaging (RADICYL) and a computer vision pipeline (RootXplorer). This platform enables the evaluation of large sorghum diversity panels under controlled mechanical impedance, generating robust quantitative proxies of root penetration, including Root Count Ratio (RCR) and Root Area Ratio (RAR). Using this system, we are screening a diverse panel of sorghum accessions to characterize natural variation in root penetrability and its association with performance under compacted soil conditions.

Preliminary results obtained under controlled mechanical impedance conditions reveal substantial phenotypic diversity among sorghum accessions. A critical range of mechanical resistance enables clear discrimination between high- and low-penetrating genotypes. These findings demonstrate the platform's capacity to capture biologically meaningful variation in root penetration under compacted conditions. The resulting phenotypic data will be integrated with genomic information to conduct genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to identify loci and candidate genes underlying root penetration capacity.

This work establishes root penetrability as a scalable and quantifiable phenomic trait and provides a framework to bridge phenomics and genomics for gene discovery. This approach ultimately supports breeding strategies to improve sorghum productivity under soil compaction, contributing to climate-resilient agriculture.

abstracts.t: Constraints and Opportunities in the Sorghum Value Chain: Implications for Enterprise Development in Lesotho
abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

a: National University of Lesotho, Maseru, Lesotho

sc.x: Sorghum is a climate-resilient cereal with strong potential to enhance food security and rural livelihoods in Lesotho. However, its commercial development remains constrained by limited processing infrastructure, inconsistent product quality, and weak market linkages. This study examined the sorghum value chain to identify key constraints and opportunities for enterprise development and value addition.

A participatory research approach was employed, involving semi-structured interviews with 30 small holder farmers across five councils ( Makhoarane, Likila, Menkhoaneng, Tenesolo and Tebe-tebe). Additional insights were obtained from agro-entrepreneurs, including a startup incubated at the National University of Lesotho Innovation Hub and local sorghum beverage producers. Data collection was completed by a training intervention to enhance participant's understanding of sorghum value chain dynamics and postharvest practices. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, with coding of key themes related to production, processing, postharvest losses, and market opportunities.

Low sorghum productivity was primarily attributed to erratic rainfall, limited access to inputs, and inadequate agronomic practices. Significant losses were identified during handling, storage, and processing stages. Limited access to appropriate processing facilities further reduced product quality and market competitiveness. Despite these constraints, emerging agro-entrepreneurs demonstrated strong potential for innovation through value-added sorghum products.

The findings revealed critical gaps across the sorghum value chain in Lesotho, particularly in processing capacity, quality control and market integration. The study underscored that strengthening the sorghum value chain sector requires a focus on four key pillars: understanding consumer preferences, reducing postharvest losses, meeting quality standards and building strategic partnerships. Areas identified for further research include targeted capacity building, improved access to processing technologies and strenghethened market linkages which are essential to unlock the sorghum's potential, promote sustainable agro-enterprises and enhance food and nutrition security in Lesotho.

Key words: Enterprise Development, Farmers, Lesotho, Sorghum, Value Addition, Value Chain

abstracts.t: Comparative Analysis of Testcross Strategies: Can Experimental Crosses Substitute Traditional Testers in Sorghum Breeding?
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: Texas A&M University, College Station, United States
Texas A&M University, College Station, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is valued for its drought tolerance, adaptability, and versatile uses across grain, forage and bioenergy industries. Due to the crop’s economic and agricultural importance, sorghum breeding programs aim to develop high-yielding hybrids that align with growers’ needs and interests. However, these systems are often time-consuming and costly. In a world that is constantly changing, adaptations must be made to shorten the timeframe and produce quality lines to the market that are still of interest. Recent advances such as biotechnology, machine learning, and genomic prediction have improved breeding efficiency, though bottlenecks still remain. A primary obstacle is the necessity of test crosses, which – despite beneficial assessment of combining ability – require significant time and resources while introducing bias. This project focuses on improving breeding pipeline efficiency by analyzing test crosses within a population, with the objective of evaluating “experimental by tester” and “experimental by experimental” crossing strategies.

This trial consists of 210 hybrids, representing a subsample of an elite population of 1,045 lines. Selection was based on at least three test crosses being made the previous year. During the 2025 growing season, hybrids were evaluated across three locations using a randomized complete block design (RCBD). To account for spatial variation and accuracy, two commercial checks were included within each block of the trial.

By incorporating statistical analyses between the two groups, preliminary results show similar trends between non tester and test crosses, therefore providing a path to reduce the use of test crosses within a program. Future experiments including a familial structured population containing both crossing types will be conducted to provide a distinct conclusion.

By exploring this process, more efficient crossing and selection strategies may be identified which can enhance the sorghum industry’s productivity and serve as a model for other crop improvement efforts.

abstracts.t: The Influence of Environment and Genetics on Sorghum Grain Weight and Size
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Department of Soil and Crop Sciences,Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, United States
Department of Soil and Crop Sciences,Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, United States

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) is a resilient cereal crop grown worldwide and, in the United States, primarily used for animal feed and ethanol production, with increasing interest in food applications. In primary industries, they seek uniform grain kernel size to improve milling efficiency. However, variation in grain weight and size can be attributed to spatial, environmental, and genetic factors. The goals of this study are to quantify the variance attributable to the factors mentioned and to evaluate differences in individual grain kernel size parameters.

Two populations were examined: a commercial hybrid population (CHP) used to characterize spatial, environmental, and genetic variance, and an experimental hybrid population (EHP) with defined population structure to evaluate additive and dominance genetic variance. Both populations were used to assess the uniformity of individual grain kernel size parameters. The CHP was grown across multiple environments of Kansas and Texas, while the EHP was grown in three different locations in Texas. A 250-kernel grain sample was weighed, then a picture of the sample was captured. Images were used to obtain size parameters: area size (AS), perimeter length (PL), length (L), width (W), and circularity (CS).

For grain weight, CHP exhibited moderate environmental variance and low genetic variance. Spatial variation within environments had the lowest variance of all factors. The EHP exhibited low genetic variation, with most of the variation attributable to the pollinator parents. The grain size parameters showed a trend like that of grain weight. These results indicate that variation in sorghum grain weight and size is primarily attributable to environmental factors, with negligible spatial variation and little genetic contribution.
For milling purposes, the most uniform grain kernel will come from the same production site or region, while the least uniform will come from across production sites and regions.

abstracts.t: Grain Quality and Potential of Large Seeded Sorghums
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Department of Agronomy, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, United States
Department of Agronomy Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, United States
USDA-ARS Grain Quality and Structure Research Unit, Manhattan, Kansas, United States
USDA-ARS Plant Stress and Germplasm Development Research Unit, Lubbock, Texas, United States
Agricultural Research Center, Kansas State University, Hays, Kansas, United States

sc.x: Large seeded sorghum has the potential to improve grain quality and processing efficiency for both human food and animal feed markets. While conventional grain sorghum typically averages 3g/100 seeds, this study identified populations reaching up to 8g/100 seeds. The central hypothesis is that these larger seeds possess distinct quality attributes such as increased starch and protein content

We selected the top 0.1% of kernel weight lines from the GRIN database, and new populations were developed through crossing two photoperiod-insensitive lines (KS115 and Ajabsido), followed by selection in four selfed generations based on size and shape. Seed quality was evaluated using a Single Kernel Characterization System (SKCS 4100) and Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy to measure hardness, protein, lysine, and starch. Additionally, microscopic image analysis was used to estimate the percentages of germ and vitreous endosperm.

The large seeded selected lines demonstrated enhanced nutritional profile that includes crude protein, averaging 14% compared to the conventional 10.5%, along with slightly higher lysine levels. The larger endosperm while maintaining kernel hardness improved processing in the selected lines suggesting better flour yields, finer textures, and improved popping abilities. The feed efficiency for steam flaking, essential for cattle feed digestibility, takes nearly twice as long for sorghum as it does for corn. In addition, the large seeded lines may offer faster water absorption, potentially reducing processing time and costs for large feed yards.

We identified that the large seeded sorghums have improved grain chracteristics and quality, which can help increase sorghum’s market share relative to corn. Significant "roadblocks" still remain, as much of the screened large-seeded accessions are photoperiod sensitive and needs continuous conversion introgression breeding efforts; we are currently introducing dwarfing genes and converting these accessions to be photoperiod insensitive.

Extension Arable Crops, Agroscope, Zurich, Switzerland
Agridea, Cadenazzo, Switzerland
Neobiota, Agroscope, Cadenazzo, Switzerland
Neobiota, Agroscope, Cadenazzo, Switzerland

sc.x: Sorghum is a minor crop in Switzerland but offers potential for climate-resilient cropping systems and gluten-free food applications. The RiSorgo project, is a 3-year Swiss research project in partnership with, Agridea, Agroscope, UCA, Monia Caramma, Sorghum ID and INRAE, and aims to develop a protocol to assess grain sorghum varieties for agronomic performance, suitability for pasta production for human consumption, and economic potential under Swiss conditions.

Fifteen varieties from four breeding programs were evaluated in Switzerland and subjected to advanced laboratory analyses, including physical and biochemical characterization (grain size, hardness, ash and protein content, starch gelatinization temperatures, and protein digestibility). Four varieties were selected for large-scale field cultivation, and food-processing trials targeting gluten-free dry pasta production were conducted using decorticated and pre-gelatinized flour.

Preliminary results show that the varieties present low variabilities among breeding programs with some exceptions. For instance, analyses using Differential Scanning Calorimetry have shown that in 2024 there weren’t significant differences between European varieties in terms of gelatinisation temperature, indicating substantial genetic uniformity. The results from the production of single-variety dry pasta show that, in order to obtain a product that is palatable, retains its texture during cooking and has a shelf life of three years, the sorghum must be hulled and gelatinised. The particle size of the flour is a key factor.

The results from the 2024 and 2025 trials show that, depending on the variety, the hulling and gelatinisation processes can be adapted in order to standardise and industrialise the pasta extrusion and drying parameters. The continuation of field trials will provide a more robust basis for evaluating agronomic and grain quality traits of sorghum varieties. In vitro digestibility tests should make it possible to evaluate the nutritional quality of pasta over the agronomic trials opening new opportunities to use sorghum as sustainbale food.

abstracts.t: Screening for Novel Sorghum Mutants with Increased Protein Digestibility using Near Infrared Spectroscopy
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Purdue University, West Lafayette, United States
Purdue University, West Lafayette, United States

sc.x: Sorghum protein digestibility (PD) is a quantitative trait that is lower compared to other cereals such as corn, wheat, and rice. Previous efforts helped create or identify sorghum lines with highly digestible protein (HDP) phenotypes that are more comparable to these cereals using mutagenesis. Phenotyping for this trait is highly time consuming using wet-chemistry techniques and has slowed forward breeding progress.

A subset of M1s from the Purdue Sorghum EMS mutant population were screened with near infrared spectrosopy (NIRS) to predict cooked PD. This screen was used to non-destructively detect potential novel HDP mutant lines. An in vitro assay was employed to verify screened mutant material and compare to existing HDP mutants.

Three putative positive mutants were identified using an in vitro phenotyping assay and found to be segregating for PD. Kernels from these mutants displayed variation in endosperm texture and grain hardness as well as PD that was comprable to previously identified HDP mutants.

Increased ability to identify and characterize phenotypic extremes for this trait via NIRS allows for more effective trait utilization, specialized downstream applications, and identification of causative alleles for novel gene discovery. The putative positive mutants detected via NIRS will be advanced to homozygosity for characterization of either existing or novel genes.

abstracts.t: Integrating Root Traits, Microbiome Dynamics, and Hormone-Regulated Metabolism toIntegrating Root Traits, Microbiome Dynamics, and Hormone-Regulated Metabolism toEnhance Drought Resilience in Sorghum-Legume Systems
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Rhine-Waal University of Applied Science, Kleve, Germany

sc.x: Drought limits sorghum productivity in dryland systems. While above-ground traits are well studied, below-ground processes-including root architecture, rhizosphere microbiome dynamics, and metabolic regulation-remain poorly understood. In sorghum–legume intercropping, these interactions are shaped by nitrogen transfer and microbial activity. Brassinosteroid signalling regulates phenylpropanoid metabolism, influencing lignin and flavonoid accumulation. This study investigates flavonoids as key drivers of root structure, barrier formation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress responses.

Stable isotope (¹³C and ¹⁵N) labelling is used to trace carbon and nitrogen fluxes between Vigna unguiculata and Sorghum bicolor intercop or sole crops under drought stress in pot experiments. Nutrient dynamics are analysed using ICP-based methods, and root–rhizosphere samples are subjected to microbiome and multi-omics analyses. In parallel, S. bicolor wild type and brassinosteroid receptor mutants are tested under PEG-induced drought, with or without methyl jasmonate. Root tissues are examined for lignin and suberin deposition, alongside gene expression and omics analyses to link hormonal regulation with rhizosphere processes

Experimental systems have been established under both field and controlled conditions. Preliminary results show genotype-dependent variation in root architecture, water uptake, and metabolic profiles. Ongoing analyses are expected to reveal coordinated shifts in rhizosphere microbiomes, carbon and nitrogen allocation, and phenylpropanoid metabolism, influencing root barrier formation and microbial recruitment under drought stress. Complementary field trials by EIAR and UQ assess diverse sorghum intercropping systems, capturing genotype × environment × management interactions, with root traits and soil water dynamics analysed using electromagnetic induction (EMI)-based phenotyping.

This study provides a systems-level understanding of drought resilience by linking root traits, microbiome dynamics, nutrient fluxes, and hormone-regulated metabolism. Integrating field and mechanistic insights of below-ground traits and molecular pathways to improve sorghum performance and adaptive responses. These findings will support breeding strategies and development of resilient sorghum legume systems under changing climate stress conditions.

abstracts.t: Genomic Predicition of Anthracnose Resistance in Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Texas A&M University, Texas, United States
Texas A&M University, Texas, United States

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) production is significantly constrained by biotic stresses, among which anthracnose—caused by the fungal pathogen Colletotrichum sublineola—is one of the most destructive. Yield losses can reach up to 80% in susceptible cultivars, highlighting the importance of developing resistant varieties. Although resistance loci have been identified, their effectiveness in breeding programs is often limited by variation in population structure and the high genetic diversity of pathogen races. These challenges reduce the reliability of marker-assisted selection across environments and germplasm. To accelerate genetic gain for anthracnose resistance, genomic prediction with genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP), offer a promising alternative by capturing small effect loci. Integrating it with genome-wide association study (GWAS) signals could enhance predictive ability by capturing the full spectrum of geneic effects.

Under the CV1 cross-validation scheme, genomic prediction models incorporating GWAS information outperformed the additive-only model. The additive model achieved a predictive ability of approximately 0.62, whereas GWAS-assisted genomic prediction reached accuracies of up to 0.83.

A total of 680 inbred lines and 313 experimental hybrids from the Texas A&M sorghum breeding program were screened for anthracnose resistance in College Station over three years. Genome-wide association analysis was conducted using GAPIT with the BLINK model on 2458 SNPs with AUDPX as the phenotype. A multi environment genomic prediction was also implemented in BGLR where two models were evaluated: (1) model including an additive Genomic Relationship Matrix (GRM) model for all SNPs and (2) a partitioned model with separate GRMs for GWAS identified QTLs and non-significant SNPs

These results demonstrate that genomic prediction models incorporating GWAS-identified markers improve predictive accuracy compared to standard approaches. Integrating GWAS-assisted genomic prediction into breeding pipelines can reduce reliance on extensive field phenotyping and accelerate the identification of anthracnose-resistant material during early selection stages.

abstracts.t: Enhancing Sorghum Yield Potential through Integration of Twin-Seed and Large Seed Traits in Elite Germplasm
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Iowa State University, Ames, IA, United States
Iowa State University, Ames, IA, United States

sc.x: U.S. sorghum acreage has declined in recent years as yield improvement has lagged behind other major crops. The recent identification of DG1, the gene underlying the dominant twin-seed phenotype, provides a potential avenue to increase seed number per panicle, historically a primary driver of yield gain in sorghum. However, a strong negative correlation between seed number and seed size has been consistently observed across single-, twin-, and tri-seeded genotypes, highlighting the need to better understand the genetic relationship between these yield components. The objective of this research is to develop and evaluate germplasm combining the twin-seed trait with favorable alleles for seed size and to characterize the genetic basis and interaction of these yield components.

Population development is ongoing across multiple elite genetic backgrounds. Resulting materials are expected to enable evaluation of both seed number and seed size as well as their interaction in twin-seeded and non-twin-seeded individuals.

Populations are currently being developed by introgressing DG1 from SAP-420 and large-seed alleles from KS115 (SAP-074) into elite inbred lines from the Sorghum Association Panel. Segregating populations of twin-seeded and non-twin-seeded individuals will be evaluated for seed number and seed size. Genotypic and phenotypic data will be used to identify genomic regions associated with variation in these traits and to assess their interaction across genetic backgrounds.

This work will generate a novel germplasm resource to investigate the relationship between seed number and seed size in sorghum. Integration of the twin-seed trait with large-seed alleles is expected to provide insight into yield component relationships and inform breeding strategies to enhance sorghum yield potential.

abstracts.t: Genomic evidence for decoupling perenniality and yield in diploid perennial sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: The Land Institute, Salina, United States
University of Georgia, Athens, United States
University of Georgia, Athens, United States
University of Georgia, Athens, United States
The Land Institute, Salina, United States

sc.x: Perennial sorghum, derived from interspecific hybridization between Sorghum bicolor and S. halepense, represents a promising pathway toward resilient grain production systems. However, perenniality has long been assumed to impose a yield penalty due to linkage with wild growth traits. This study aimed to characterize the genetic architecture underlying perenniality and yield in diploid perennial sorghum and to determine whether these traits are genetically constrained or can be decoupled.

Genome-wide association analyses revealed that grain yield is controlled by a highly polygenic architecture distributed across all chromosomes, whereas perenniality-related traits, including rhizome-associated regrowth, were associated with more discrete genomic regions. Local ancestry analysis showed that S. halepense-derived haplotypes were retained in specific genomic segments linked to perenniality, while yield-associated regions were largely independent of these segments. Dosage–response analyses further demonstrated locus-specific effects, with some genomic regions exhibiting compatibility (positive effects on both yield and regrowth) and others showing trade-offs.

A set of F₄ lines derived from interspecific hybridization between Sorghum bicolor and S. halepense was evaluated in a field trial in Tifton, GA, for grain yield and spring regrowth capacity. Genotyping data were used to perform genome-wide association analyses for both traits. Local ancestry inference was conducted to distinguish genomic regions of S. bicolor and S. halepense origin, and dosage–response relationships were assessed to quantify locus-specific effects.

Perenniality and yield can be partially decoupled in diploid sorghum, providing a genomic foundation for breeding perennial grain sorghum with improved agronomic performance. These findings indicate that the relationship between these traits is governed by locus-specific genetic architecture rather than a fixed biological constraint, supporting the use of genomics-enabled strategies to integrate perenniality into high-yielding sorghum germplasm.

abstracts.t: Assessment of Factors Influencing Performance of New Improved Bird Tolerant Sorghum Varieties among Smallholder Farmers in Makueni County, Kenya
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Machakos, Kenya
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Machakos, Kenya
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Machakos, Kenya
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, Machakos, Kenya

sc.x: Bird pests are a major challenge in sorghum production among smallholder farmers especially ASAL regions of Kenya. To mitigate against this challenge, the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), recently released five bird resistant and drought tolerant sorghum varieties (Smart sorghum, Jaziri, Ndume, Pato1 and Hummer). Therefore,this study was undertaken to promote the new sorghum varieties, assess the farmer typologies, and performance determinants of new improved sorghum varieties among smallholders in Makueni County, Kenya.

Systematic Random sampling technique was applied to select 134 farmers for the study. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests of association, principal component analysis (PCA), K-means clustering, was used to provide a comprehensive evaluation of farmer typologies and factors influencing performance.

Descriptive statistics reveal that the sampled farmers are predominantly female (73.1%), with high levels of farmer group membership (82.8%) and widespread use of certified seed (69.4%). Notably, uptake of the bird tolerant varieties is universal (100%), indicating successful promotion of improved technologies. Chi-square analysis identifies a strong and statistically significant association between farmer group membership and certified seed use (χ² = 13.765, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.321), confirming the central role of farmer groups as dissemination pathways. To examine farmer heterogeneity, PCA reduces multiple correlated socioeconomic and agronomic variables into five principal components explaining 72.3% of total variance. K-means clustering based on these components identifies seven distinct farmer typologies, reflecting substantial diversity in resource endowment, labour use, and input adoption. Cluster profiling and ANOVA results confirm statistically significant differences across typologies (p < 0.05 for most variables). Yield differences across farmer typologies are also statistically significant (p < 0.001), reinforcing the importance of farmer heterogeneity in determining productivity outcomes.
The findings highlight the need to move beyond input dissemination towards targeted, typology specific agronomic support to enhance productivity for improved food security.

sc.x: The U.S. sorghum production under organic systems is extremely limited, despite being the largest producer in the world. This represents a missed opportunity for greater economic profitability, alongside promoting resilience and sustainability via organic cropping systems. The study investigates an agronomic potential for organic sorghum production in the Texas High Plains (THP).

Two three-year field experiments: (1) Grain sorghum (GS) – Cotton (CT) and (2) Forage sorghum (FS) – Corn (CN) rotation systems under limited irrigation supply with dryland cover crop (CC) and no cover crop (NCC) were established at Bushland, TX. Treatments were GS – CT; GS – CT + CC; CT – GS; CT – GS + CC for the GS–CT system and FS – CN; FS – CN + CC; CN – FS; Corn – FS + CC for the FS – CN system.

In both years, weed was a critical issue during early vegetative period, prior to crop canopy suppression later in the season. In 2024, poor plant stand issues resulted in low plant density, particularly for CT and CN, while GS and FS were resilient and maintained sufficient stands. Yields for GS were 5.7 and 7.69 Mg ha<sup style="box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0px; padding: 0px; text-size-adjust: none; border: 0px; font-size: 12px; line-height: 0; position: relative; color: #000000; font-family: 'Open Sans', Arial, 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, sans-serif; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: #ffffff; text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial;">-1</sup> and dry biomass for FS averaged 14.6 and 16 Mg ha<sup style="box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0px; padding: 0px; text-size-adjust: none; border: 0px; font-size: 12px; line-height: 0; position: relative; color: #000000; font-family: 'Open Sans', Arial, 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, sans-serif; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: #ffffff; text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial;">-1</sup> in 2024 and 2025, respectively. In 2025, high yields corresponded to greater plant density and lower weed pressure in relatively cool and wet growing conditions. abstracts.t: Self-scaling millet- and sorghum-based food processing system improves nutrition indicators in rural communities of Sahelian West Africa
abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

IDEMS, London, United Kingdom

University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, United States

sc.x: Malnutrition impacts greater than 250 million people in Africa, particularly in rural regions. Amelioration strategies for improved nutrition have relied extensively on donor-supported fortification and supplementation programs, which inherently lack sustainability. Novel and local-based approaches are needed to drive sustainable nutrition solutions, particularly in rural areas.
In Niger, a technology-based Hub-and-Spoke food processing innovation system was developed with rural women's associations based on local knowledge generation.

Over a 10-year period, they co-created sustainable markets for high quality food-to-food fortified millet- and sorghum-based food products designed for local preferences. Notably, the empowered women’s groups self-initiated sharing of knowledge with women in nearby communities to process nutritionally-fortified products, thus creating self-scaling of processing and markets. In years 2020-2024, in addition to other products, ~30 MT of fortified products were profitably sold at the five primary rural sites. In 2023, a nutrition impact study (3600 participants) showed significant improvements in nutritional indicators (FAO Food Consumption Scores, modified to focus on children) that was independent of household food expenditure.

Notably, nutritional improvement occurred up to 30 km spatially out from one of the primary sites making this an effective sustainable model for rural market-led nutrition in Sahelian West Africa, and perhaps other regions. Supported by SMIL-USAID and McKnight Foundation programs.

abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

Purdue University, West Lafayette, United States
Purdue University, West Lafayette, United States

Kansas State University, Colby, United States

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) is an important forage crop that is gaining value in northern regions of the United States. As sorghum production expands into cooler environments, proper management to avoid hydrogen cyanide (HCN) toxicity becomes increasingly important, particularly following frost events. In southern regions, growth can resume after light frost events. Previous research has produced conflicting results regarding whether frost increases dhurrin or HCN potential; additionally, the magnitude and persistence of the response create uncertainty for management decisions.

In Stage 1, dhurrin concentration increased following frost at select locations. Dhurrin concentrations increased by 64% at Colby, KS (2020), and by 94% at West Lafayette, IN (2020), three days after frost. At Garden City, KS (2020), dhurrin concentrations increased by 92% seven days following frost. Post-frost weather conditions influenced dhurrin persistence: dhurrin concentrations declined within seven days at West Lafayette following a return to warmer temperatures, but remained elevated at Colby, where colder conditions and successive frost events occurred. No differences in dhurrin content were observed at Ames, IA (2024); Hays, KS (2020); or West Lafayette, IN (2024). The dhurrin-free hybrid produced no detectable dhurrin throughout the trial. Stage 2 analyses are ongoing and will evaluate the contribution of tissue viability to whole plant dhurrin accumulation following frost.

This study was conducted in two stages to evaluate frost effects on dhurrin concentration in sorghum. Stage 1 evaluated dhurrin response in the top collared leaf (green tissue) before and after frost events across six site-years using eight hybrids, including a dhurrin-free hybrid. Stage 2 examined differences in dhurrin content between living and frost killed tissue above and below the top collared leaf across two site-years using two hybrids per location.
Collectively, results from this study will improve our understanding of post-frost dhurrin dynamics and will help refine management recommendations.

abstracts.t: Sorghum varietal selection for tolerance to Striga hermonthica in Niger
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: INRAN-Maradi, MARADI, Niger

sc.x: Striga hermonthica is a major parasitic weed of sorghum in sub-Saharan Africa, causing severe yield losses in Niger, especially in Tahoua, Maradi, and Dosso. Its impact is worsened by poor soil fertility, erratic rainfall, and limited access to inputs. Sorghum varietal selection offers a sustainable and accessible solution for managing Striga. This study aimed to evaluate sorghum lines under severe infestation and identify tolerant genotypes.

Significant variability was observed among varieties. Best (tolerant): MDK, SRN39, L153-5, AG-8XN13 BC3F5, TXN13 BC3F5-41
Delayed Striga emergence, low infestation, good vigor, high yield Moderate: Mota Maradi Susceptible: El Tsedaoua (high infestation, low yield)

Fifteen sorghum varieties (10 introduced lines, 3 INRAN lines: MDK, L153-5, SRN39, 1 improved variety, and 1 local check) were evaluated at Konni using a randomized complete block design with five replications under infested and non-infested conditions. Striga was artificially applied at 1 g per hill. Parameters included Striga emergence (45, 60, 90 DAS), plant vigor, flowering, height, and grain yield.

Varietal selection effectively identified Striga-tolerant sorghum lines. The best varieties (MDK, SRN39, L153-5, AG-8XN13 BC3F5, TXN13 BC3F5-41) are promising for improving sorghum productivity in Striga-infested areas.

abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Canyon, United States
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, Canyon, United States

Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, Canyon, United States
Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Canyon, United States

sc.x: In 2025, the re-emergence of Sorghum ergot was documented in the Texas High Plains. Examination of infected fields revealed honeydew and sphacelia structures present in infected glumes, and microscopy revealed conidia consistent with Claviceps sp. While symptomology is easily recognizable, questions remain about the disease’s true impact on forage quality and potential for alkaloid production in effected fields that would adversely affect animals that consume said forage. To address these questions, forage quality and toxin analysis was performed.

Samples from multiple locations were collected. At the Dumas, TX location samples were selected based on appearance of symptoms and pooled by asymptomatic and symptomatic. At the Bushland, TX location, using samples collected from the annual Texas A&M AgriLife forage sorghum silage trial, ergot ratings were taken bi-weekly starting at the first appearance of symptoms and continuing until forage harvest. Severity in sorghum plots with half bloom dates after September 8<sup>th</sup> averaged twice the severity of sorghum plots with half bloom dates prior to September 8<sup>th</sup>. No ergot symptoms were observed in plots with half bloom dates prior to August 25<sup>th</sup>. Symptom development coincided with a cool and wet weather pattern. Select samples were collected from both locations and tested for feed quality and ergot alkaloid presence. Samples were processed with a forage harvester and either dried immediately for feed quality analysis or placed into vacuum sealed bags for a 90 day ensile to be used for toxin analysis.

Feed quality analysis revealed an approximate 14% decrease in forage nutritive value between asymptomatic and symptomatic plants. Following the 90-day ensiling process, alkaloid levels in tested asymptomatic samples ranged from 2.5 to 104.1 ppb and from not detected to 1.3 in asymptomatic samples.
Based on previous literature, ergot alkaloid levels detected in this study represent a low risk for feeding.

abstracts.t: From Tradition to Technology: Unlocking the commercial potential of sorghum-based functional foods in South Africa
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Tshwane Universitu of Technology, Pretoria, South Africa

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is a nutrient‑dense, climate‑resilient cereal with functional properties such as prebiotic activity, improved glycaemic control, and anti‑inflammatory effects. Despite these benefits, its consumption in South Africa remains low. National production averages 95,000–155,000 tons annually, contributing only ~0.4% to the gross value of field crops, compared to maize production exceeding 15 million tons per year. This disparity highlights the underutilisation of sorghum and its untapped potential for integration into modern food systems. Traditional foods such as bogobe (stiff porridge), Ting (fermented porridge) and mageu (fermented beverage), offer culturally relevant platforms for innovation but face barriers including weak value chains and limited diversification. The objective of this study is to explore how traditional sorghum‑based foods can be modernised through emerging technologies and community‑driven strategies to create a scalable model for sorghum commercialisation in South Africa.

Results showed that dietary fibre ranged from 6.8–8.1 g/100 g in ting and 8.5–10.2 g/100 g in bogobe. Fermentation increased iron bioavailability by 35% and zinc absorption by 22%. Functional mageu contained 1.8 × 10^8 CFU/mL probiotic bacteria. Extrusion trials produced ready‑to‑eat sorghum snacks with 78% higher consumer acceptability than bogobe. Surveys revealed 72% willingness to purchase fortified sorghum products, with 71% of younger consumers open to modernised sorghum snacks. Economic modelling projected R2.5 million annual turnover per cooperative and 900 jobs created.

Methods included nutritional profiling of sorghum products, assessment of emerging technologies such as extrusion and fortification, consumer surveys (n=500), and economic modelling of sorghum enterprises.

Sorghum holds significant promise as a functional food ingredient, but its commercialisation requires technological innovation, decentralised enterprise models, and consumer education. This integrated approach strengthens food security and offers transferable lessons for sorghum commercialisation.

abstracts.t: Multi-Year Evaluation of Commercial Sorghum Hybrid Responses to Contrasting Management Practices

a: Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St Louis, United States

sc.x: Improving sorghum performance under changing field conditions requires studies that evaluate both genetic variation and management-driven responses over time. This multi-year field trial was designed to assess commercial sorghum hybrids under contrasting management practices. The study integrates measurements spanning agronomic performance, root and soil phenotypes, seed composition, and environmental context, creating an opportunity to examine how hybrid × management interactions shape yield, resilience, and end-use traits under realistic field conditions.

A distinguishing feature of the study is its combination of above- and below-ground phenotyping. Across field seasons, the trial has incorporated conventional agronomic measurements together with soil coring, seed analyses, and minirhizotron imaging to characterize plant responses under different management treatments. These data support evaluation not only of yield-related outcomes, but also of rooting behavior and other traits likely to contribute to performance stability under variable conditions. The study also integrates field sensing and environmental monitoring to improve interpretation of treatment effects across sites and seasons.

Initial analyses show that commercial hybrids differ in their responses across management treatments, with treatment effects evident in agronomic performance, root-associated traits, and seed composition. These results indicate that hybrid performance is not uniform across management conditions and suggest that specific trait profiles may be associated with more favorable responses under particular practices. By combining longitudinal field evaluation with multi-scale phenotyping, this work is beginning to resolve how above- and below-ground traits contribute to sorghum performance under contrasting management conditions.

This work establishes a framework for linking management, phenotype, and performance in sorghum and for identifying trait combinations associated with improved resilience under contrasting field management practices.

sc.x: Iron and zinc are micronutrients essential for proper growth, maintenance, and immune function. Supplementation programs and fortification strategies have been implemented in many countries to combat micronutrient deficiencies, however in rural regions or places of government and economic instability, these options may not be accessible. Micronutrient biofortification is underway in most staple crops and has been tested and employed in several countries. Biofortification of sorghum grain iron and zinc can be accelerated in breeding programs with the deployment of marker assisted selection (MAS), however identification of quantitative trait loci (QTL) and casual genes is needed in order to develop effective markers to use for selection.
These markers have potential to assist breeders in MAS of lines to accelerate the nutritional improvement of sorghum.

Through a reverse genetics pipeline, we have identified several putative causative variants in candidate genes derived from literature. These variants have been turned into genetic markers and are in the process of validation and testing.

Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Cold Spring Harbor, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a climate-resilient crop of growing global importance for food, feed, and bioenergy, yet its improvement is limited by genotyping tools that do not fully capture genomic and functional diversity across breeding germplasm. To address this, we are developing a high-density ~100K sorghum genotyping array using a community-driven, pangenome-informed design framework. This effort integrates curated trait-associated markers contributed by researchers from USDA, universities, international breeding programs, and global collaborators. Marker sources include loci linked to biotic resistance, abiotic stress tolerance, and grain, biomass, and quality traits, including GWAS SNPs, functional markers, cloned genes, QTL-linked variants, and pangenome-derived candidates. Additional marker discovery is supported by large-scale genomic resources, including resequenced sorghum diversity panels and comparative variant datasets spanning cultivated, wild, and weedy accessions. To maximize biological relevance and utility across diverse populations, marker prioritization considers allele frequency, haplotype diversity, gene context, and regulatory annotation, including overlap with open chromatin and intergenic functional regions. The design also leverages sorghum pangenome resources containing tens of thousands of pan-genes across multiple assemblies, enabling inclusion of presence–absence variation, lineage-specific genes, and non-reference loci often missed in single-reference arrays. This is especially valuable for rapidly evolving regions such as disease resistance intervals, including F-box candidate regions and NB-LRR/NLR-enriched loci linked to anthracnose and related resistance traits. Probe development is being conducted with Twist Bioscience, with attention to assay constraints such as GC content, repetitive sequence, multi-mapping risk, and local variant density. The resulting array will support genomic selection, association mapping, diversity analysis, trait dissection, and molecular breeding, providing a scalable platform to accelerate sorghum discovery, breeding, and global collaboration.

abstracts.t: Lodging Gated Fusion Network (LGF-Net): A Spatial Attention-Based Multimodal Network for Lodging Type and Severity Prediction
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States

sc.x: Lodging is a major constraint on sorghum productivity because it reduces yield, complicates harvest, and can be difficult to assess consistently at field scale. Image-based methods alone often do not fully capture the structural and environmental factors associated with lodging expression. To address this, we developed the Lodging Gated Fusion Network (LGF-Net), a multimodal deep learning framework for prediction of lodging type and severity in sorghum.

Across multi-environment datasets, LGF-Net consistently outperformed baseline CNN and CNN-MLP models. For lodging type classification, distinguishing shoot versus root lodging, performance improved by up to 21% relative to CNN and 11% relative to CNN-MLP. For lodging severity prediction, improvements reached up to 42% over CNN and 4% over CNN-MLP. These gains were observed across individual years as well as combined datasets, supporting the robustness of the approach under variable field conditions.

LGF-Net integrates multispectral imagery with agronomic features using a spatial attention-based fusion architecture. The model combines a convolutional neural network image encoder with a multilayer perceptron tabular encoder. A spatial attention module is used to highlight informative lodging patterns in imagery, while a gated fusion mechanism adaptively weights contributions from image-derived and tabular features prior to prediction. The model was trained end-to-end and evaluated using cross-year and cross-site validation across sorghum datasets collected in Missouri and South Carolina.

These results show that multimodal learning can improve high-throughput lodging assessment by capturing both visual and contextual signals associated with lodging outcomes. LGF-Net provides a scalable framework for sorghum lodging phenotyping and has potential to support breeding, field evaluation, and more precise characterization of lodging responses across environments.
