sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is naturally rich in phytochemicals, antioxidants, and essential nutrients, with medicinal properties that vary by grain color and processing methods. It is also gluten-free and non-GMO crop. This study investigated metabolite variation across sorghum genotypes and their potential health effects, particularly in regulating inflammation in adipocytes, a key feature of obesity and related metabolic diseases.

Six diverse genotypes from the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP)-white, yellow, dark red (Sumac), light violet, dark orange, and dark brown-were analyzed. Phytochemical profiles were characterized using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS). For in vitro assays, 3T3-L1 preadipocytes and adipocytes were treated with varying concentrations of sorghum extracts. Cell viability was assessed using MTT assay, and lipid accumulation was measured via Oil Red O staining. Inflammation was induced with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and the effects of extracts on inflammatory markers were evaluated at the protein (ELISA) and gene (qRT-PCR) levels. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism10.2.1.

Metabolomic profiling revealed substantial variation in phytochemical composition, including vitamins, polyphenols, and flavonoids, across sorghum varieties. Random Forest analysis showed enrichment of non-polar metabolites (e.g., fatty acyls, steroids, terpenoids, flavonoids) in darker-colored genotypes. Correlation analysis identified significant associations between metabolite classes and IL-6 secretion. All extracts were non-cytotoxic to 3T3-L1 preadipocytes. Several polar and non-polar extracts significantly reduced LPS-induced IL-6 secretion in both 3T3-L1 preadipocytes and adipocytes (p ≤ 0.01), consistent with reduced interleukin 6 (IL-6), mRNA levels for toll like receptor 2 (TLR2), inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), and macrophage inflammatory protein 2 (MIP-2) were also downregulated. No significant effects on lipid accumulation were observed.

Phytochemical-rich sorghum varieties exhibit potent anti-inflammatory effects. These findings support further investigation into animal models and human studies to evaluate how sorghum impacts systemic inflammation, metabolic and gut health.

Federal University of São João del-Rei, Sete Lagoas, Brazil

Federal University of Lavras, Lavras, Brazil

sc.x: Phenolic compounds and anthocyanins may contribute to plant resilience, but their relationships with aphid fecundity remain poorly understood. This study investigated correlations between different classes of compounds and the fecundity of the aphid Melanaphis sorghi in sorghum.

Pearson correlation analyses showed that ferulic acid exhibited a significant negative correlation with nymph fecundity (r = -0.78; p = 0.037). The other compounds analyzed (luteolinidin, apigeninidin, 5-methoxy luteolinidin, 7-methoxy apigeninidin, total anthocyanins, caffeic acid, p-coumaric acid, sinapic acid, and total phenolic acids) showed no significant correlations (p > 0.05).

Trials were conducted in a climate-controlled chamber (24±2°C, 60±10% RH, 12h photoperiod). The M. sorghi colony was established from field-collected individuals. Leaf discs (3.8 cm diameter) from seven sorghum hybrids at the nine-leaf stage were placed on agar (20 g L⁻¹). One adult female was transferred to each disc. After 24 hours, the female and offspring were removed, leaving one nymph per replicate (completely randomized design, 20 replicates). Fecundity was assessed daily by quantifying offspring. Flavonoids and 3-deoxyanthocyanidins were determined by High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) after acidified methanol extraction and centrifugation (wavelength 480 nm). Phenolic acids were obtained after alkaline hydrolysis, ethyl acetate extraction, and HPLC analysis (320 nm). Quantification was performed using calibration curves, with results expressed as µg/g dry sample.

The negative correlation between ferulic acid and nymph fecundity suggests that this compound may be associated with sorghum resistance to M. sorghi. Additional studies are needed to validate these findings under field conditions and to investigate the underlying mechanisms.

abstracts.t: From Fermentation to Fortification: Unlocking Sorghum's Nutritional Promise using Innovative Processes and Formulations
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, Advanced Agriculture and Food Cluster, Nutrition and Food Safety, Pretoria, South Africa

sc.x: Advances in sorghum processing highlight its potential as a functional food ingredient, bridging traditional practices with modern health-focused innovations. Sorghum, a drought-tolerant crop, is adaptable to climate change and grows in conditions where other cereal crops like maize, wheat and rice will not thrive. Certain sorghum varieties have been shown to possess valuable nutritional qualities, including higher mineral content compared to other cereals. They also contain unique bioactive compounds such as diverse phenolic compounds and enzyme-resistant starch, which contribute to potential health benefits.

Incorporated baobab fruit helps boost micronutrient content, including zinc, potassium, magnesium, iron, calcium, and protein, which may reduce nutritional deficiencies. Other ingredients for innovative sorghum products involve incorporation of legume powders to boost protein content as well as other starch sources to improve beverage consistency.

For many centuries, traditional sorghum processors have prepared fermented non-alcoholic sorghum products to be used for making beverages and porridges. In recent times, traditional sorghum processors have begun experimenting/innovating with other natural ingredients available, such as some indigenous African fruits like baobab (Adansonia digitata L.) and Marula (Sclerocarya birrea), these fruits that are naturally high in vitamin C. In addition, baobab fruit is also an important source micronutrient, including zinc, potassium, magnesium, iron, calcium, and protein, which may reduce nutritional deficiencies. Other ingredients for innovative sorghum products involve incorporation of legume powders to boost protein content as well as other starch sources to improve beverage consistency.

The study shows that innovative ingredients and convenient processes can be adopted for the traditional processing of fermented non-alcoholic sorghum beverages, as well as in the production of dried non-fermented instant sorghum beverage mixes, for improved nutritional intake. Addition of ingredients such as Moringa, baobab powder and hemp seed powder improves nutritional content and may lead to development of sorghum-based ready-to-eat nutritious food supplements.

abstracts.t: Advancing Sorghum as a Value‑Added Crop Through Characterization of Polyphenols and Their Bioactive Properties
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: USDA-ARS- Center for Grain and Animal Health Research, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Sorghum contains a diverse set of bioactive polyphenols with emerging potential for use in health, food, and industrial applications. This presentation will highlight work from the USDA‑ARS Manhattan research program, which aims to characterize these compounds, evaluate their biological activity, and identify sorghum lines with traits that can support development of high‑value specialty markets, ultimately enhancing profitability and opportunity for American farmers. Across cell‑based and animal models, extracts from high‑phenolic sorghum lines consistently demonstrate anticancer and anti‑inflammatory activity, including suppression of colon cancer cell growth and reduction of oxidative and inflammatory signaling in immune cells. Parallel studies reveal promising antimicrobial properties, with ongoing research evaluating the use of sorghum polyphenols to extend shelf life in aquaculture products such as tilapia. Because sorghum‑derived polyphenols are more economical than many alternative sources, their commercial adoption would directly benefit U.S. producers. Compositional profiling is being conducted across diverse sorghum varieties to measure phenolic content, mineral levels, and other nutritional attributes. These comparisons help identify red and black sorghums with consistently elevated polyphenol concentrations and improved nutrient profiles, providing breeders, growers, and industry partners with the information needed to prioritize lines suitable for value‑added applications. Processing studies aim to determine how different cooking and manufacturing methods influence polyphenol retention. These topics, including bioactivity, antimicrobial potential, varietal comparisons, and processing considerations will be discussed to illustrate how coordinated research can advance sorghum from a commodity grain to a value‑added crop with strong market differentiation.

sc.x: Iron deficiency chlorosis (IDC) limits sorghum productivity in high pH soils by reducing chlorophyll, vigor, and yield, with sorghum often more susceptible than crops like maize. Genetic improvement is challenging due to strong interactions between soil variability and environmental conditions. This study aimed to identify genomic regions associated with IDC tolerance using an integrated approach combining a biparental population, control-adjusted micro-plot phenotyping, precision soil sensing, and genetic analysis to link soil variability with phenotypic responses.

A biparental RIL population (SC399 × RTx2737) was evaluated under field conditions with natural IDC stress. Phenotypic data were filtered using replicated tolerant and susceptible controls to retain informative environments and improve genetic resolution. Spatial soil variability was mapped using Veris MSP3 (pH, EC, OM). SNP genotyping was used to construct a quality-controlled linkage map. Genome-wide association analysis was followed by QTL detection using interval mapping (IM) and composite interval mapping (CIM).

Significant quantitative variation for IDC tolerance was observed across the RIL population. Variation in IDC severity was strongly influenced by soil heterogeneity, particularly soil pH. Soil mapping identified high IDC risk zones, highlighting the role of micro-environmental variability in IDC expression. A stableQTL on chromosome 5 was identified, with the favorable allele contributed by SC399, explaining ~7–10% of phenotypic variance. Additional loci on chromosomes 1, 2, 8, and 9 indicated a polygenic architecture underlying IDC tolerance.

IDC tolerance in sorghum is controlled by multiple loci, while its phenotypic expression is strongly shaped by soil-driven environmental variability. An integrated framework combining a biparental population, control-adjusted micro-plot phenotyping, and genomic analysis improves QTL detection and supports marker-assisted and genomic selection. Precision soil sensing further enables effective characterization of soil heterogeneity and its linkage to phenotypic variation, highlighting the role if micro-environmental factors in IDC expression under field conditions.

sc.x: There is a growing demand and market of feed products to support the poultry meat and egg production in Madagascar. Development of sorghum based poultry feed is a key priority of Livestock Feed Ltd. (LFL) where sorghum producers can gain access sustainable private sector led markets.

LFL direct purchases sorghum grain, at equal to maize pricing for small holders in Madagascar with an annual demand of 50,000 MT. This has resulted in better environmental and land management, providing small holders an alternative to 'cut and burn' maize production in fragile 'dry forests'.

The Global Collaboration on Sorghum and Millet (GCSM@K-State) in partnership with Livestock Feed Ltd. (LFL) of Madagascar, provided poultry feed study support, improved sorghum seed varieties, production training and small holder market access to strengthen the overall sorghum value chain.

LFL's annual demand for 50,000 MT is equivalent to a 30 million USD economic benefit. Market development and integration of small holder sorghum producers is a socio-economic benefit a country with 3 - 5 USD average daily income.

sc.x: Grain sorghum is an important agronomic crop in the Texas Plains and Oklahoma. Palmer amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri S. Watson) is the most common weed in sorghum in this region. Compared to other crops there are limited PRE and POST herbicide options. Effective season-long Palmer amaranth control can be achieved with a program of PRE and POST herbicides. PRE combinations were more effective than single herbicide treatments.
Rinskor controlled Palmer amaranth as effectively as dicamba and more effectively than 2, 4-D with less crop injury. Rinskor was also effective on larger weeds (12” tall) without crop injury.

In 2024 and 2025, Rinskor (florpyrouxifen-benzyl) was compared POST to 2, 4-D, dicamba, Huskie + atrazine, and atrazine + dicamba. Rinskor was applied alone or in combination with atrazine to weeds 3” tall or later POST when Palmer amaranth was 12” tall.
Rinskor provides a potential effective herbicide option for Palmer amaranth control in grain sorghum.

sc.x: Root traits are central to sorghum performance under drought, nutrient limitation, and management conditions that influence soil function, but they remain difficult to measure at field scale. We propose SubterraAI, which couples minirhizotron imaging with adaptive AI analysis to improve speed, consistency, and genetic relevance of field-based root phenotyping in sorghum.

The core aim of SubterraAI is to build an analysis framework that converts minirhizotron images into quantitative root phenotypes for biological interpretation and genotype association. A central challenge in root image analysis is that image characteristics vary across experiments, making static pipelines difficult to generalize. To address this, SubterraAI uses a human-in-the-loop strategy with iterative annotation and model updating so workflows can be refined as image conditions and root patterns change. This versioned model adaptation is intended to improve reproducibility and support broader use of AI for belowground phenotyping.

Subterra demonstrated end-to-end, closed-loop phenotyping performance under field-like domain variability. In analyzed runs, phenotyping throughput averaged 4.55 s/image on Apple M1 (MPS) and 4.07 s/image on NVIDIA CUDA. Transfer learning from a PRMI-pretrained U-Net substantially improved generalization, with Dice increasing from 0.79 to 0.94 in sorghum and 0.78 to 0.89 in maize; augmentation ablations further improved robustness (approximately 0.78 to 0.92 Dice from no augmentation to full augmentation policy). In an online adaptation setting (n=100 corrected images across five annotation batches), versioned updates improved agreement and stabilized trait estimates over time. Subterra outputs were also directly usable for downstream genetics, including a depth-1 root-area GWAS case study over 2,956,926 markers.

By increasing the scalability and interpretability of root image analysis, SubterraAI aims to make belowground phenotyping more useful for sorghum genetics, physiology, and field research. More broadly, it provides a framework for adaptive AI-enabled analysis of root images that can support future datasets and emerging phenotyping platforms.

sc.x: With the U.S. cattle feed market exceeding $16 billion and projected to surpass $22 billion by 2033, reliance on water-intensive forages such as corn silage threatens stable production with depletion of the Ogallala Aquifer, particularly in the Southern Great Plains of the United States. Kansas, a rapidly expanding dairy state, recorded a 17% increase in milk production in 2025, with semi-arid western regions contributing over 90% of total output. This highlights the need for water-efficient, high-quality forage systems. In this context, drought-tolerant, high-biomass forage sorghum offers a promising alternative, and this project aims to concurrently evaluate on-market sorghum silages, while developing a roadmap for trait-based sorghum forage breeding.

We found significant variability among lines for agronomic and quality traits, indicating strong potential for selection and genetic improvement. Notably, bmr line exhibited high biomass and increased gas production, suggesting that yield and digestibility can be improved simultaneously without major trade-offs. Dhurrin content did not affect agronomic performance but influenced gas production.

Field experiments were conducted evaluating 16 forage sorghum lines during the summers of 2024 and 2025 in a randomized complete block design. Evaluated lines represented diverse traits paired with an isogeneic or similar background without trait expression to evaluate efficacy of hypothesized feed traits of bmr, dhurrin content, high protein digestibility, and waxy grain. Key agronomic traits, grain quality, and forage quality parameters including in vitro dry matter disappearance were measured, some of which were recently summarized (Vignati, et al., 2026. J. Dairy Sci. 109, Suppl. 1; accepted). Data were analyzed with linear mixed models in R, with genotype as a fixed effect and block(year) as random effect.
These findings suggest that forage sorghum can serve as a viable option for dairy cattle feed enabling reduced irrigation water use while maintaining forage yield and quality.

Department of Agronomy, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Stay-green, a post-anthesis drought-tolerance trait in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), is characterized by the plant's ability to sustain leaf greenness and photosynthetic activity under severe drought for a longer duration during the grain-filling stage, which significantly improves grain yield stability under moisture-limited conditions. Despite the extensive characterization of major QTLs like Stg1–Stg4, targeting the Stg5 locus remains an essential strategy for improving drought resilience and grain yield. Previous research identified significant co-localization between leaf dhurrin levels and the Dhu1 QTL on chromosome 1, involving a biosynthetic gene cluster containing CYP79A1, CYP71E1, and UGT85B1.

Genotypic analysis showed that the KASP marker in CYP79A1 accounted for 19% of the total variation in dhurrin in the SAP. The flanking markers for Stg5 were only linked to the drought-tolerant donor BTx642 for breeding purposes. Near-isogenic lines (NILs) were developed using KASP markers to introgress the Stg5 locus into four different US sorghum inbreds. Field evaluation of Stg5⁺ and Stg5⁻ NILs showed a 2x to 4x increase in dhurrin concentration and a significant increase in the post-flowering stay-green trait.

In this study, we developed and validated a high-throughput Stg5 molecular marker targeting the CYP79A1 gene, a gene in the dhurrin biosynthesis pathway. Seven flanking SNPs in a ~153 kb window on Chromosome 1 were developed into KASP molecular markers to introgress the Stg5 locus from the BTx642 stay-green inbred. A validation panel of 380 sorghum genotypes from the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP) was screened for dhurrin with eight KASP markers.

The development of these validated markers provides a robust tool for introgressing the Stg5 trait into elite breeding lines, facilitating the improvement of sorghum productivity in water-limited environments.

abstracts.t: Sorghum as a Healthy Option for U.S. Consumers: Perceptions, Attitudes, and Behaviors Explained by the Theory of Planned Behavior
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Texas Tech University, Lubbock, United States
Texas Tech University, Lubbock, United States
Texas Tech University, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: Sorghum has potential health benefits: nutrient-dense, anti-diabetes, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant activity, and cancer prevention. Texas is the second largest sorghum producer in the U.S., yet most of the sorghum is used for biofuel and animal feed in the country. Despite the benefits and high production, awareness of sorghum as human food is extremely low, and little research about sorghum as a whole grain option for U.S. consumers has been conducted. This study explored perceptions, attitudes, and intentions to eat sorghum among the U.S. consumers and identified influencing factors of sorghum intake using Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB).

Grain consumers with no dietary restrictions were recruited using local advertisements. Seven focus groups (with 5-8 participants/session) with forty-one participants (21-74 years old) were held. Structured interview questions were used for each session led by a professional moderator. Focus groups were audio recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. The authors reviewed transcriptions to generate codes and discussed until agreement on emerged themes. Based on TPB, a conceptual model was developed to explore factors that affect sorghum-related behavior.

Majority were female (75%), White (44%), and single (59%). Eight themes were identified: health consciousness, agricultural concerns, sensory properties, product characteristics, awareness/knowledge, attitudes/beliefs, grain eating habits, and behavioral intentions. Belief about sorghum benefits, locally grown food support, and expectations from families to eat healthy were positive factors to promote attitudes, subjective norms, and intention to eat sorghum. However, perceived high price for healthy options, sensory preferences, and lack of market awareness were barriers.

Most participants were open to trying sorghum because of health benefits, more options for whole grain and gluten-free products, and support for U.S. or local businesses. However, public education and collaborations with government food programs to build sorghum awareness were suggested to improve sorghum consumption and health.

abstracts.t: NIR calibration models developed to predict protein content in single sorghum kernel (SSK) and protein distrubution profiles
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Retired USDA-ARS CGAHR, Manhattan, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States
Retired USDA-ARS CGAHR, Manhattan, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: This study aimed to develop a near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy model for predicting protein content in single sorghum kernel (SSK) using partial least squares (PLS) regression.

Sorghum kernels from representative samples harvested in different sorghum growing areas and crop seasons in the United States were selected for this study. NIR spectra were collected on a custom-built single kernel NIR device. A total of 800 models were evaluated with various preprocessing methods and latent variables (LVs), to identify the most suitable model for SSK protein prediction. The performance of the models were evaluated by their R<sup>2</sup>, RMSEC (root mean square error of calibration), RMSECV (root mean square error of cross validation), and RMSEP (root mean square error of prediction) values.

The results show that PLS models from spectra preprocessed with normalization, standard normal variate (SNV), and the 1st derivative showed excellent performance in predicting protein contents in single sorghum kernels. The model performance is notably influenced by the number of LVs (1-10), but overfitting is not observed in most models, as indicated by RMSECV/RMSEC and RMSEP/RMSEC values ranging from 1.0 to 1.2. The best prediction model is obtained with 10 LVs using 1st derivative. Specifically, the results show the protein calibration model with 10 PLS LVs in 390 sorghum grain spectra has R<sup>2</sup>cal of 0.946, R<sup>2</sup>cv of 0.923, RMSEC of 0.783%, and RMSECV of 0.931%. When applied to an independent validation set of 190 sorghum grain spectra, a R<sup>2</sup>pred of 0.931 and RMSEP of 0.892% were achieved.

Overall, this study for the first time established a reliable NIR model to predict protein content in single sorghum grains, which can be a valuable tool for sorghum breeding programs, quick method for evaluating grain quality (both protein conents and distribution profiles), and application research.

abstracts.t: A Long-Term Sorghum Diversity Trial Enables GWAS of Above- and Below-Ground Traits Across Contrasting Field Environments
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, Creve Coeur, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, Creve Coeur, United States

Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, Creve Coeur, United States
Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, Creve Coeur, United States

sc.x: Identifying sorghum alleles that contribute to adaptation and resilience requires field datasets that extend beyond a single season, a single environment, or a single trait class. To address this, we established a long-term sorghum diversity trial in which 344 diverse lines have been repeatedly evaluated in the same field locations across multiple years in Missouri and South Carolina. These sites provide contrasting field environments, enabling analysis of trait stability, environmental sensitivity, and genotype-by-environment effects over time.

This trial combines longitudinal above- and below-ground phenotyping with genomic analysis. Above-ground datasets include plant height, tiller number, tiller height, stem diameter, biomass, lodging, and photosynthesis-related traits, complemented by UAV-based phenotyping to capture field-scale variation in canopy and plant performance. Below-ground datasets include soil coring and root phenotyping measurements that support evaluation of rooting depth, root distribution, and related root system traits. Genotype data for the diversity panel are being integrated with these phenotypes to perform genome-wide association analyses across both above- and below-ground trait classes.

Genome-wide association analyses have identified significant marker-trait associations across multiple above- and below-ground phenotypes, including traits related to plant architecture, biomass allocation, lodging, and root system characteristics. Several loci show evidence of persistence across years and/or locations, while others appear to be environment-specific, highlighting both stable and context-dependent components of trait architecture. Because the same panel has been followed longitudinally, this system provides unusual power to evaluate the consistency of genetic signals through time and across contrasting field environments. Together, these data create a rare whole-plant field phenotyping resource spanning organs, seasons, and environments.

This long-term diversity trial establishes a framework for linking sorghum genetics to whole-plant field performance and for identifying loci relevant to adaptation, resilience, and crop improvement under contrasting field conditions.

sc.x: Fura is a popular pearl millet-based thin porridge beverage consumed in Sahelian West Africa. The traditional fura process is laborious and time-consuming, and consumers often purchase pre-made from neighborhood women.

A modification of a low-cost single-screw extrusion process for thick porridge flour was used to make instant fura. Physicochemical characteristics, consumer acceptability, and sales potential in Niamey, Niger were assessed.

Fully gelatinized millet extrudate rods (~14 m.c.) were produced, dried < 10% m.c., and ground to a fine flour. Instant millet fura porridge had higher elasticity and lower shear thinning property, and better textural attributes (creamy, elastic, gelling), and lighter color than the traditional porridge. Overall consumer acceptability of instant fura was good and comparable to traditional fura. A market test in Niamey for 10 weeks showed repeat purchases with good frequency of sale. Instant fura flour sold second best compared to 34 other traditional cereal foods.

A high-quality, instant and convenient version of a popular traditional millet product, fura, was produced using a low-cost, single-screw extruder. A market study in Niamey, capital city of Niger, showed very good acceptability and demand. The comparably high throughput of the process suggests a good business opportunity for local food processing entrepreneurs and a way of increasing urban markets for millet producers. Supported by SMIL-USAID and McKnight Foundation programs.

abstracts.t: Evaluation of locally fortified 'food-to-food' sorghum-based flours (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) without premix
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

sc.x: In the Sahelian context, where malnutrition remains widespread particularly among children under five and women of reproductive age, this study aimed to develop innovative locally fortified flour formulations using a "food-to-food" approach without industrial premixes. The main objective was to enhance the nutritional quality and acceptability of traditional porridges using locally available resources.

Physicochemical analysis results revealed, moisture content ranging from 4.06±0.05% to 4.87±0.04%, ash content between 3.21±0.00% and 3.36±0.01%, protein level from 13.18±0.04% to 14.11±0.01%, lipid content ranging from 11.15±0.05% to 11.90±0.04%, and energy density fluctuating between 423.39±0.94 and 429.94±0.26 Kcal. These nutritional values compared well, and in cases exceeded, to those found in premix-based fortified flours for children, generally distributed to mothers in community health centers. Results of a sensory acceptability test revealed a higher preference by mothers for porridges fortified with carrot, followed by those fortified with moringa.
Eight (8) sorghum-based fortified flour formulations were developed by incorporating cowpea, groundnut, moringa, African locust bean (‘’néré’’), and carrot in nutritionally optimized proportions.

These findings highlight the strong potential of locally available ingredients rich in macro- and micronutrients for developing culturally appropriate, nutritionally adequate fortified flours, and support their performance and integration into community-based programs contributing to the attenuation of malnutrition in Niger and West Africa. Supported by SMIL-USAID and McKnight Foundation programs.

abstracts.t: REVISITING SEASONAL SORGHUM SUDAN SEEDING RATES: EFFECTS ON MORPHOLOGY, BIOMASS PRODUCTION, AND NUTRITIVE VALUE
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: University of Florida, Gainesville, United States
Universidad de la Republica, Paysandu, Uruguay
University of Florida, Gainesville, United States
United Sorghum Check-Off Program, Lubbock, United States
University of Florida, Gainesville, United States

sc.x: Sorghums are high-yielding, versatile forage crops used for silage, hay, or grazing and are well adapted to challenging growing conditions. However, optimal seeding rate remains understudied across planting seasons, particularly in subtropical climates. This study evaluated seeding rate responses of sorghum × Sudan (Sorghum bicolor L. × Sorghum sudanense) across spring and summer plantings in a subtropical climate.

Realized seedling density exhibited season × year-dependent responses to seeding rate. In spring, maximum densities were similar between years (~65 plants/m<sup>2</sup>) but were reached at 85 seeds/m<sup>2</sup> in 2024 and 75 seeds/m<sup>2</sup> in 2025. In summer 2024, density increased linearly across the full seeding-rate range, reaching ~70 plants/m<sup>2</sup>, whereas in summer 2025 it plateaued at 75 seeds/m<sup>2</sup>. Tiller number increased linearly with seedling density across seasons and harvests, reflecting more plants per unit area rather than greater tillering per plant. Stalk diameter decreased with density and was 43% smaller at the second harvest. Biomass yield increased with plant density, reaching 6,950 and 7,960 kg DM/ha at 47 and 74 plants/m<sup>2</sup> in spring and summer 2024, respectively, whereas responses in 2025 were weaker. Nutritive value was unaffected by seeding rate.

The experiment was conducted in Citra, Florida, during the spring and summer of 2024 and 2025. Sorghum x Sudan hybrid ‘Advanta AS6501’ was planted in April and July at 25, 37, 49, 62, 74 and 99 seeds/m<sup>2</sup> in a randomized complete block design (n=4). Plots were harvested at least twice per season to a 10-cm stubble height once plants reached approximately 114 cm. Measured responses included seedling density, tiller number, stalk diameter, biomass yield, and nutritive value.
Optimal seeding rate was season-dependent. Higher seeding rates in summer may help improve productivity through greater tiller production without compromising forage nutritive value.

sc.x: Sorghum is a naturally drought tolerant crop predominantly cultivated in arid and semi-arid regions, particularly western Kansas, a state in the Southern Great Plains, where frequent drought persists with high vapour pressure deficit (VPD) days (>2.5 KPa). DropXL was initiated to understand the genetics of limited transpiration, and develop water use efficient sorghum. Genotypes with limited transpiration (LT) traits restrict the transpirational water loss at high VPD conditions and conserve the soil moisture for later growth stages, as compared to non-limited transpirers (Non-LT). The objectives of the study were to develop DropXL inbreds and hybrids which have LT traits, analyse LT traits using stomatal conductance and canopy temperature (CT) as proxies, and assess yield across contrasting water-stress environments.

A population with LT and non-LT parents was advanced to the F8 generation. The DropXL and non-DropXL inbreds were hybridized with a US elite line with good general combining ability. These lines were evaluated for stomatal conductance using a handheld porometer, CT using UAV imagery, and yield via combine. The experiment was conducted at Manhattan (67 days VPD>2.5) and Hays (109 days VPD>2.5), Kansas, with three replications in an RCBD design. Stomatal conductance and CT were evaluated on high VPD days during canopy closure to panicle emergence stage; yield was collected post freeze in November.

The stomatal conductance of the DropXL lines was significantly lower than the non-DropXL lines in Manhattan. DropXL lines exhibited higher yield than non-DropXL lines across both locations. The results indicate reduced transpirational water loss with DropXL hybrids overperforming the non-DropXL hybrids.

These findings provide preliminary evidence for the value of DropXL sorghums which introgress LT traits to develop yield-stability and opportunity under water-limitation. Further validation under effective water stressed treatments and water limited locations is needed to confirm agronomic performance.

sc.x: Biogas produced through anaerobic digestion is a renewable energy source, and sorghum has emerged as a promising feedstock due to its high biomass productivity, adaptability to low-fertility soils, and tolerance to water and climatic stress. This study evaluated the biochemical biogas potential (BBP) and biochemical methane potential (BMP) of biomass and sweet sorghum hybrids harvested at 120 and 150 days after sowing (DAS).

Twelve biomass and sweet sorghum hybrids were cultivated and harvested at 120 and 150 DAS. Samples consisting of six plants per hybrid were ensiled in laboratory silos for 40 days. Silages were then evaluated in Continuous Stirred Tank Reactors (CSTR) operated under mono-digestion conditions at 37°C with continuous stirring (60 rpm). All reactors were operated at the same organic loading rate (0.5 kg VS m⁻³ d⁻¹). BBP and BMP were determined for all hybrids and harvest stages.

Significant differences were observed among hybrids and harvest stages. At 120 DAS, hybrid CMSXS5035 showed the highest BBP (762 LN biogas kgVS⁻¹) and BMP (450 LN CH₄ kgVS⁻¹). At 150 DAS, hybrids CMSXS5041 and CMSXS5043 achieved the greatest fresh matter biogas productivity, reaching 168 and 184 m³ biogas tonFM⁻¹, respectively. Methane concentration ranged from 44 to 59%, demonstrating substantial bioenergy potential. Overall, both genotype and harvest stage significantly influenced biogas and methane production..

Biomass and sweet sorghum hybrids showed high potential for biogas and biomethane production. Harvest stage and genetic background strongly affected bioenergy performance, highlighting the importance of hybrid selection and harvest management to maximize renewable energy generation from sorghum silage.

Acknowledgments: CNPq, Latina Seeds, Toyota Tsusho, and BNDES.

abstracts.t: Genomic analysis reveals the genetic structure underlying US commercial sorghum breeding programs
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Colorado State University, Fort Collins, United States

sc.x: Knowledge of the genetic structure underlying public- and private-sector breeding populations is essential for increasing adoption of grower-preferred traits from public-sector to commercial breeding programs. Previous studies have assessed genetic diversity and relatedness in sorghum using pedigree information and low- density molecular markers, but these approaches provided incomplete genome coverage and limited representation of breeding germplasm.

Population genomic analysis revealed that the commercial programs capture a substantial proportion of the genetic variation present in public germplasm. This indicates extensive historical exchange, and it is further structured by the widespread use of the cytoplasmic male sterility system. This structure is characterized, across all programs, by the tight clustering of male-sterile (A) and maintainer (B) lines, with a clear divergence from restorer (R) lines. When compared with the sorghum association panel, the B and R lines predominantly clustered with kafir and caudatum bio-types, respectively, reflecting historical selection decisions for the sorghum hybrid seed system. Fixation (FST) and diversity analysis (π) revealed that the divergence between the heterotic groups might be driven by specific genomic regions, with FST outliers and reduced diversity that colocalized with restorer fertility (Rf) loci. Using KASP markers, we are also characterizing allelic variations underlying major agronomic traits in commercial sorghum, such as height, maturity, and tannins, to identify cis-elite lines.

Here, we leverage high-density SNP genotyping (DArT-Seq) to accurately characterize 40 elite inbred lines sourced from one public and four commercial breeding programs. To facilitate rapid and efficient trait transfer across programs, our goal is to identify patterns of relatedness that define cis-elite lines that share similarity at major fixed genes

Together, these insights demonstrate that the underlying genetic structure of sorghum commercial programs is shaped by shared ancestry and targeted selection. Identifying cis-elite relationships provides a framework for accelerating trait transfer and crop improvement in sorghum breeding

sc.x: Sorghum is widely used for silage production due to its adaptability, drought tolerance and high biomass yield. This study evaluated agronomic performance, nutritional quality, fermentation characteristics, fiber digestibility and animal production potential of grain, forage and biomass sorghum hybrids grown under tropical conditions.

Significant differences were observed among hybrids for all evaluated traits. Grain sorghum hybrids BRS 373 and BRS 3002 showed the highest crude protein, starch, TDN, RFV, RFQ and milk production per ton of dry matter. Biomass hybrids BRS 662, BRS 665 and BRS 716 produced the greatest fresh and dry matter yields. BRS 716 achieved the highest biomass productivity (156.0 t ha⁻¹ fresh matter and 45.55 t ha⁻¹ dry matter), whereas BRS 665 presented the highest fiber digestibility (73.23% dNDF240), associated with the brown midrib (bmr6) gene. All silages showed adequate fermentation quality, with low pH and low butyric acid concentrations.

Six sorghum hybrids were evaluated during the 2025/2026 growing season in Sete Lagoas, Brazil: BRS 373, BRS 3002, BRS 658, BRS 662, BRS 665 and BRS 716. The experiment was conducted in a randomized complete block design with two replications. Agronomic traits, chemical composition, fermentation profile, fiber digestibility, Relative Feed Value (RFV), Relative Forage Quality (RFQ), Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) and estimated milk production were determined in silages analyzed by NIRS.

Grain sorghum hybrids provided superior nutritional quality, while biomass hybrids maximized forage production per hectare. BRS 665 combined high biomass yield and fiber digestibility, whereas BRS 716 showed outstanding biomass productivity. Hybrid selection should balance forage quality and yield according to livestock production goals.

sc.x: The study aimed to evaluate the seed quality of F1-producing crosses, using sorghum lines with masculine sterility induced by TFMSA as female parental lines. Ten fertile sorghum lines were employed, representing grain sorghum, forage, sugar, and biomass types.

Significant differences among the F1 seeds were observed for all evaluated traits, likely driven by genotype rather than the chemical treatment. Importantly, high-quality hybrid seeds with normal germination and seedling development were obtained, supporting the viability and potential of TFMSA to broaden genetic variability in sorghum breeding programs. Key findings suggest TFMSA-enabled cross strategies can expand the genetic base without compromising early seedling vigor. The results underscore the feasibility of using chemically induced male sterility to generate diverse, robust F1 hybrids, contributing to accelerated genetic gains and diversified germplasm in sorghum improvement initiatives.

Among these, two were maintainer lines (B) and eight were fertility-restorer lines (R) developed by Embrapa’s sorghum breeding program, displaying differences in use, stature, and cycle. The lines were divided into two groups: Group I consisted of lines treated with TFMSA solution, whose plants served as female parents in crosses to obtain F1 seeds; Group II comprised the same lines but without TFMSA treatment, used as pollen donors to evaluate hybrid seed production. n total, 28 distinct F1 combinations were generated, and seedling emergence and early growth were assessed, focusing on shoot length and root length.

F1 hybrid seeds produced showed comparable performance with no significant transgenerational effects. Trifluoromethanesulfonamide is a new and valuable tool for sorghum breeders that can be used to generate new crosses and enable a higher number of crosses while ensuring that the produced seed is an F1 hybrid.
Further work should explore longer-term field performance, heterosis stability across environments, and molecular mechanisms underlying TFMSA-induced sterility to optimize application protocols.

abstracts.t: From Trait to Trade: Farmer Perceptions of Risk, Value Chains, and Possibilities of Gene-Edited Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, United States

sc.x: As sorghum gains renewed attention as a sustainable and climate-resilient crop, emerging bioengineering tools such as gene editing are creating new opportunities for carbon sequestration, value-added traits, and market expansion. However, the potential of innovations in sorghum depends on whether they align with farmer decision-making and the existing value-chain. Farmer perceptions of gene-edited sorghum are shaped less by the technology itself than by broader questions of market access, risk management, and long-term farm viability. Sorghum is a critical case because of its existing soil-building and drought-tolerant properties, which researchers are now seeking to enhance through gene editing for carbon sequestration and other commercially valuable traits. However, this is not a simple question of attitudes toward biotechnology; rather farmer perceptions are situated within commodity markets, supply chains, and existing farm management practices.

Findings show that farmer perceptions of new technologies and practices are driven by concerns over market stability, input costs, insurance access, and the long-term profitability of climate-resilient production systems.

This presentation reflects on a survey of 200 sorghum farmers and 200 additional row-crop farmers (corn, cotton, and soy) to compare how producers make crop and soil management decisions and what challenges might be particular to sorghum farmers. In addition to the survey, I conducted nine months of fieldwork across Northern Colorado and the Texas High Plains, including interviews with farmers, extension personnel, breeders, farm advisors, and supply-chain stakeholders, alongside participant observation at field days and producer conferences.
For sorghum improvement efforts, climate-resilient traits must be designed to work within farmers’ existing economic and ecological constraints while also translating into clear on-farm benefits.

abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States
University of Nebraska-Lincoln, North Platte, United States

Purdue University, West Lafayette, United States

sc.x: Sorghum phenology is determined by the interaction between genotype cycle length and sowing date, yet information on this interaction for modern genotypes remains limited.
To assess these effects, early, medium, and full season sorghum genotypes were evaluated across fifteen experiments conducted in the Great Plains, U.S., during 2024 and 2025.

Thermal time to anthesis was not affected by sowing date (p = 0.23), whereas early season genotypes required 191°Cd less to reach anthesis than full season genotypes (p < 0.001) and 125°Cd less than medium season genotypes (p < 0.001). Full season genotypes required 66°Cd more to reach anthesis than medium season genotypes (p < 0.05).
The maximum number of expanded leaves was affected by genotype cycle length (p < 0.001) but not by sowing date (p = 0.91). Early season genotypes exhibited on average 2.8 fewer leaves than full season genotypes (p < 0.001) and 2 fewer leaves than medium season genotypes, while full season genotypes exhibited 0.7 more leaves than medium season genotypes (p < 0.05). On average, the maximum number of expanded leaves was 12.8, 14.9, and 15.7 for early, medium, and full season genotypes.
The rate of leaf expansion was affected by both genotype cycle length and sowing date (p < 0.001). While no differences in leaf expansion rate were observed among cycle length groups in the late sowing date, early season genotypes exhibited a lower rate of leaf expansion than full and medium season genotypes in the early sowing date (p < 0.001; 0.0117 vs. 0.0157 and 0.0155 leaves GDD-1, respectively).
These results suggest that genotype cycle length is the driver of sorghum phenological variation across environments, with sowing date playing a secondary role mainly in leaf expansion dynamics.

abstracts.t: Potential of Deep Learning Models for Real-Time Detection of Palmer Amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri) in No-Till Dryland Grain Sorghum of Western Kansas
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Kansas State University, Agricultural Research Center, Hays, United States
Kansas State University, Agricultural Research Center, Hays, United States

sc.x: Palmer amaranth is one of the most problematic weeds in dryland production systems of western Kansas. The objectives of this study were to (1) develop an annotated image database of Palmer amaranth in no-till dryland grain sorghum systems in western Kansas, (2) train five variants of the “You Only Look Once” (YOLO) object detection model (YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLOv8m, YOLOv8l, and YOLOv8x) to locate and identify Palmer amaranth in field images, and (3) compare the effectiveness of the YOLOv8 model variants for Palmer amaranth detection.

Images of natural populations of Palmer amaranth were collected early in the season, aerially and at ground level, during summer 2025 in grain sorghum fields established in no-till production systems in Hays, KS. The images were annotated using the CVAT AI tool. Each model variant was trained in Google Colab for 120 epochs, using the default training hyperparameters.

A dataset comprising 582 annotated images was combined with 1,622 publicly available annotated Palmer amaranth images to train the YOLOv8 model variants. The performance of the models was evaluated using mean average precision metrics (mAP50 and mAP50-95). All YOLOv8 variants demonstrated robust Palmer amaranth detection capabilities, achieving precision of at least 90% and recall of at least 82%. The mAP50 values for Palmer amaranth localization and identification were 90.5%, 96.3%, 97.5%, 97.8%, and 98.0% for YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLOv8m, YOLOv8l, and YOLOv8x, respectively. Corresponding mAP50-95 values were 61.0%, 72.1%, 76.1%, 78.4%, and 80.0% for the same model variants.

The findings indicate that, under dryland no-till conditions with residue cover, YOLOv8 demonstrates significant potential for real-time Palmer amaranth detection when adequate data are available. Integrating deep learning models with drone-based remote sensing and computer vision could facilitate the effective implementation of site-specific weed management strategies in western Kansas, thereby reducing herbicide usage and associated costs.

abstracts.t: TraitAI: Multi-Trait Modeling of Sorghum Yield, Grain Quality, and Nutritional Composition
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

sc.x: Improving sorghum value requires better prediction of both agronomic performance and grain characteristics relevant to downstream use. TraitAI is being developed as a multi-trait modeling framework to predict sorghum yield, grain quality, and nutritional composition from integrated field, environmental, and compositional datasets. Rather than evaluating yield or quality traits in isolation, this approach is designed to capture relationships among agronomic performance, grain properties, and nutritional composition across production conditions.

The framework is centered on prediction of yield, grain moisture, and test weight, with extension to near-infrared spectroscopy-based compositional traits including protein, starch, fiber, and oil. Machine learning and deep learning models are being developed using integrated field, environmental, and grain composition data to capture relationships across these trait classes. By combining agronomic, physical, and compositional traits within a single analytical framework, the approach is designed to connect field performance with grain quality outcomes relevant to food, feed, and ingredient applications. The broader effort also supports benchmarking across environments, seasons, and management conditions.

Initial machine learning and deep learning models are performing well across multiple trait classes, supporting prediction of agronomic and grain quality outcomes from integrated datasets. Early results indicate that these models can capture relationships among productivity, grain physical traits, and nutritional composition under variable production settings. Ongoing analyses are comparing model behavior across environments, identifying trait combinations associated with favorable performance profiles, and extending prediction toward scenario-based analyses under alternative management conditions.

TraitAI provides a data-driven framework for integrated sorghum trait prediction that links agronomic performance with grain quality and composition. This approach has potential to improve sorghum evaluation for breeding, production, and end-use alignment by enabling more holistic assessment of trait combinations that contribute to crop value.

abstracts.t: Towards Building a Global Food Systems Datahub: Lessons from Wheat Knowledge Graphs for Sorghum Systems
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

sc.x: Modern agriculture produces large volumes of heterogeneous and structurally fragmented data from field trials, sensors, drones, satellites, laboratory analyses, and management records. Although these data contain critical information for understanding crop performance and sustainability, their lack of interoperability limits integration, interpretation, and reuse across studies, crops, and decision-support settings. In this work, we present our completed knowledge graph and ontology development effort for sustainable wheat production as a proof-of-concept for a broader, transferable infrastructure approach toward a global food systems datahub.

Using the Knowledge Acquisition and Representation Methodology (KNARM), we developed a modular, semantically enriched knowledge graph framework that formalizes key concepts relevant to wheat production, including sustainability factors, management practices, environmental conditions, and stakeholder-informed variables. The framework integrates information from public data sources, experimental results collected at Kansas State University, and input gathered through a sustainability workshop involving stakeholders across the wheat value chain. The resulting ontologies and knowledge graphs provide a structured, machine-readable representation of wheat production knowledge using formal logic and reusable vocabularies.

Our preliminary results show that this approach can harmonize diverse agricultural datasets into a coherent semantic framework that supports interoperability, complex querying, and downstream AI/ML applications. More importantly, the wheat effort reveals a set of transferable design principles for other crops. Because the schema is modular, core components related to climate, soil, management, stressors, and sustainability can be reused and localized for sorghum with comparatively limited structural modification.

This work showcases wheat as a successful testbed for reusable agricultural knowledge graph infrastructure and demonstrates how such infrastructure can support sorghum researchers seeking semantically integrated, AI-ready data resources. By building from wheat lessons, we move closer to a scalable global food systems datahub capable of supporting resilient and sustainable crop production across domains.

abstracts.t: Evaluating Florpyrauxifen-Benzyl for Palmer Amaranth Control in Grain Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Kansas State University, Agricultural Research Center, Hays, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Field experiments were conducted in 2024 and 2025 at the Kansas State Agricultural Research Center in Hays, as well as in 2025 at the Ashland Bottoms Research Farm, to evaluate crop injury and weed control associated with florpyrauxifen-benzyl (Loyant) in comparison to commonly used postemergence herbicides in grain sorghum.

A randomized complete block design was implemented in both years with 3 or 4 replications to test differnt herbicide programs including an early POST (EPOST) application of 2,4-D Amine, 2,4-D Amine + COC, Ally + 2,4-D + Amine +Atrazine + NIS, Atrazine + Clarity + Moxy + NIS, Clarity, Clarity + COC, Huskie FX + Atrazine + AMS + NIS, Loyant + MSO (0.5 + 0.5 pt/a), Loyant + MSO (1 + 0.5 pt/a), and Loyant + Atrazine + COC) and a late POST (LPOST) application of Loyant + MSO (1 + 0.5 pt/a) and 2,4-D Amine + COC.

Results indicated that application of 2,4-D Amine, whether EPOST or LPOST, was ineffective at controlling Palmer amaranth at 3 and 4 weeks after treatment (WAT). In contrast, Loyant, combined MSO, applied either EPOST or LPOST, achieved improved control (93%) compared to 2,4-D amine and dicamba. Furthermore, tank-mixing Loyant with atrazine resulted in enhanced Palmer amaranth control at 2, 3, and 4 WAT (97%). Overall, Loyant + MSO at both 0.5 + 0.5 pt/a and 1 + 0.5 pt/a rates applied EPOST caused lower crop injury than 2,4-D amine and dicamba at 1, 2, 3, and 4 WAT.

These results suggest that florpyrauxifen-benzyl could be safely applied to grain sorghum for weed control under favorable environmental conditions. More experiments are needed across years and locations to evaluate the impact of environmental conditions on crop injury and weed control.

sc.x: Genetic gain in sorghum is constrained by low hybridization efficiency due to labor-intensive emasculation methods, which limit recombination and breeding throughput. Trifluoromethanesulfonamide (TFMSA) induces male sterility in sorghum, but its effectiveness was evaluated in only a limited number of elite genotypes, doses, and application timings. This study was conducted to evaluate genetic variability to TFMSA, optimize application strategies, and assess effects on other agronomic traits.

Field experiments using 35 diverse sorghum germplasms evaluated at five rates (0, 15, 30, 45 & 75 mg plant⁻¹), and single- and split-applications in Manhattan, KS, for two seasons. Data on seed set (sterility), flowering time, plant height, and seed germination were recorded.

Sterility responses varied among genotypes in both years. The variation was strongly influenced by application rates, frequency, and timing. At 45 & 75 mg, most genotypes were fully sterile except for a few. Dose–response modeling revealed a wide range (7–170 mg plant⁻¹) was required to achieve 99% sterility, demonstrating substantial genetic variation in TFMSA response across germplasm. Early-maturing, taller genotypes and dw3 revertants were relatively more tolerant to the TFMSA sterilizing effect than shorter, medium- to late-maturing genotypes and dw3 dwarf mutants, suggesting that developmental timing and plant architecture influence TFMSA's effectiveness. TFMSA also delayed flowering, reduced plant height, and germination, with effects generally increasing with dose. This variability indicates that TFMSA response is genetically controlled and warrants future studies to understand the underlying genetic and physiological mechanisms.

For TFMSA, as an effective gametocide, genotype-specific dosing and application timing should be considered to achieve reliable sterility while minimizing undesirable effects on plant performance and seed viability. The findings provide a foundation for integrating TFMSA as a scalable hybridization platform into breeding programs with the potential to increase recombination frequency, accelerate breeding cycles and genetic gain in sorghum.

abstracts.t: Effects of Plant Density and Row Spacing on Sorghum Stalk Rot and Grain Yield: A Zero-Inflated Modeling Analysis Under Environmental Stress
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Sorghum stalk rot is a worldwide threat to sorghum production and can severely compromise stalk integrity, leading to lodging and yield losses. Unfortunately, there are currently no in-season management options for stalk rots, and management recommendations are limited to pre-planting strategies. This study evaluated how row spacing (15 and 30 inches) and plant density (target populations ranging from 25,000 to 80,000 plants/acre) influence sorghum grain yield, while simultaneously modeling stalk rot severity and lodging probability under abiotic stress using a zero-inflated beta distribution.

Split-plot experiments were conducted across three Kansas locations during 2024 and 2025 seasons.Water stress was quantified by a cumulative water balance evaluated during flowering and the grain-filling period. Yield was analyzed via GLMMs; stalk rot and lodging were modeled using zero-inflated beta (BEZI) generalized additive models.

Across all locations, sorghum grain yield was consistently higher with wider row spacing and showed a positive linear relationship with final plant stand. Lower drought stress during the flowering period and higher plant densities significantly increased the probability of observing no stalk rot, while reduced drought stress during grain-fill and increased plant density significantly reduced stalk rot severity when symptoms were present. Stalk rot severity and late-season wind speed were the primary drivers increasing the probability of lodging occurrence. When lodging did occur, higher plant densities and wider row spacing significantly reduced lodging severity. Although it has been reported that increased canopy shading under high plant densities can increase stalk rot severity and lodging risk, the final stands observed in these experimental conditions did not reach population levels sufficient to induce the negative effects of extreme shading and competition.
Ultimately, by predicting both the expected severity and its uncertainty, we can anticipate lodging risk during the season, allowing growers to make informed decisions and minimize yield losses.

abstracts.t: Machine learning and pan-genomic analysis reveal climate-adaptive alleles in global sorghum germplasm
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Institute of Genomics for Crop Abiotic Stress Tolerance (IGCAST), Texas Tech University, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: With concerns of climate variability growing, achieving stable yields in diverse environments has marked a major challenge in crop improvement. The resilience of Sorghum bicolor affords a unique opportunity to investigate the genetic basis of environmental plasticity. However, allelic determinants responsible for stable performance under concurrent drought and heat stress are still incompletely characterized. The objective of this study is to utilize publicly available GWAS datasets augmented with past climatic variables (period between 1990 and 2025) to elucidate allelic variants associated with stability in climate-adaptive yield.

Integrative analysis in silico identified putative loci linked to pathways responsive to stress, such as ABA signaling and root system architecture. Many SNPs showed strong genotype-by-environment interactions, especially in accessions from semiarid environments. Remarkably, a cohort of these variants appears to be underrepresented in modern breeding lines, highlighting untapped genetic potential for climate adaptation.

Additional shared genomic datasets from the genome-wide association study (GWAS) from sorghum were pooled into a meta-analysis with geo-spatial climate data. Stable yield performance across environments, measured by type 4 biplot analysis using genotype × environment interaction (GxExM) data of the corresponding SNPs, was identified using machine learning, such as Random Forest modeling. The biological significance of the identified variants was assessed via functional annotation and pathway enrichment analyses.

These results suggest a possible lag between natural adaptation and modern breeding objectives. These allelic variants can be used for genomic selection or gene editing to improve climate resilience without sacrificing yield potential.

abstracts.t: A Web-Based AI Platform for Automated Sorghum Panicle Quantification via Segmentation-Based Vision Models
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: University of Houston – Clear Lake, Houston, United States
University of Houston – Clear Lake, Houston, United States

Smart Agriculture Research Center, Arlington, United States
Agriculture Research Station, Fort Valley State University, Fort Valley, United States

sc.x: Accurate measurement of sorghum panicle traits such as length and width is essential for understanding yield variability and supporting breeding programs. However, conventional phenotyping approaches rely on manual measurements that are labor-intensive, subjective, and difficult to scale across large field trials. This work aims to develop a scalable, AI-driven solution for automated panicle quantification and to enable accessible deployment through a web-based platform for high-throughput phenotyping.

Segmentation-based approaches demonstrated superior performance compared to detection-based models in dense field conditions, achieving high accuracy in panicle delineation (e.g., DeepLabV3 ~97.9% segmentation accuracy in prior evaluations). The proposed system enables consistent estimation of panicle length and width across varying imaging conditions. Preliminary observations suggest that increased panicle length is associated with higher grain count due to greater spikelet-bearing capacity, while panicle width provides complementary information related to grain density and structural compactness. The web-based deployment facilitates efficient data processing and reduces manual annotation effort.

We propose a web-based AI platform that allows users to upload sorghum images and videos for automated analysis. The system leverages segmentation-based vision models, including promptable foundation models (e.g., SAM2), to isolate panicle regions from RGB imagery captured under field conditions. A segmentation-first approach is adopted to improve robustness in dense planting scenarios with overlapping panicles and occlusions. Geometric features are extracted from segmented masks to estimate panicle length and width. The platform is designed for near real-time inference and supports scalable usage by breeders and researchers without requiring specialized computational expertise.

This work presents a scalable and accessible framework for AI-driven sorghum phenotyping that integrates segmentation-based vision models with a user-friendly web interface. By enabling automated extraction of panicle morphological traits, the platform supports high-throughput, objective phenotyping and provides a pathway for linking image-based traits with yield potential.

abstracts.t: Hybrid Vision–Language AI for Annotation-Free Sorghum Panicle Quantification and Interpretation
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, United States
Center for Robotics and Intelligent Systems, The University of Texas at Tyler, Tyler, United States
The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, United States
Smart Agriculture Research Center, Arlington, United States
Agriculture Research Station, Fort Valley State University, Fort Valley, United States

sc.x: High-throughput phenotyping of sorghum panicle traits is essential for understanding yield variability and accelerating breeding programs. However, existing approaches rely heavily on annotated datasets and task-specific supervised models, which are costly, time-consuming, and difficult to generalize across field conditions. This work aims to develop an annotation-free AI framework that combines visual perception and language-based reasoning to enable automated quantification and interpretation of sorghum panicle traits directly from field imagery.

We propose a hybrid Vision–Language AI framework that integrates segmentation-driven visual analysis with multimodal reasoning models. Panicle regions are first isolated using annotation-free or prompt-based segmentation techniques under varying field conditions. Geometric descriptors are extracted to estimate panicle traits such as length and width. These visual features are then integrated with a vision–language model (VLM), enabling semantic interpretation of panicle structure, trait variability, and potential yield implications. The framework is implemented using a modular pipeline combining classical image processing (e.g., OpenCV-based preprocessing) and modern multimodal models for image-to-text reasoning and structured output generation.

The proposed annotation-free framework demonstrates robust performance in complex field environments, effectively handling occlusions, varying illumination, and dense canopy conditions without requiring labeled training data. The system produces consistent estimates of panicle length and width and generates interpretable descriptions of panicle characteristics. Preliminary observations indicate that the integration of vision-based measurements with language-driven reasoning enables richer phenotypic insights, including qualitative assessment of grain distribution patterns and potential yield-related traits. The approach reduces reliance on manual annotation while maintaining practical utility for field-scale phenotyping.

This work presents a novel hybrid Vision–Language AI framework for annotation-free sorghum panicle quantification and interpretation. By combining geometric trait extraction with semantic reasoning, the system moves beyond traditional measurement pipelines toward intelligent phenotyping. The proposed approach enables scalable, interpretable, and annotation-efficient analysis of sorghum panicles.

abstracts.t: Closing Yield Gaps or Shifting Environments? Rethinking Resilience in Sorghum Systems
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: Center for Sorghum Improvement, Kansas State University, MANHATTAN, United States
Kansas State University, MANHATTAN, United States

sc.x: Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) is a foundational crop for water-limited production systems across the U.S. Great Plains, where approximately 2.5 million hectares are cultivated and Kansas accounts for 50% of planted area. While sorghum yields increased at a rate of 0.07 Mg ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ from 1957 to 1990, progress has slowed in recent decades, with evidence of yield stagnation across Kansas and the broader U.S.

This study quantified yield gaps and evaluated the drivers of stagnation in rainfed sorghum systems. Current yield (Y<sub>c</sub>) was defined as the mean of the most recent 10 years, while maximum attainable yield (Y<sub>a</sub>) and water-limited potential yield (Y<sub>w</sub>) were estimated using frontier yield functions derived from 2,997 site-years, including performance trials, yield contest data, and county-level observations.

Statewide average yields (4.7 Mg ha⁻¹) represent 77% of Y<sub>a</sub> but only 49% of Y<sub>w</sub>, indicating a substantial water-limited yield gap. Regional trends diverge with western and central Kansas show increasing yield potential alongside widening gaps, whereas eastern Kansas exhibits stagnation with limited exploitable yield gaps. These findings suggest that yield stagnation is not primarily driven by genetic limitations or management inefficiencies, but rather by a structural shift in production toward environments with greater water deficit.

Advancing sorghum productivity in water-limited systems will require prioritizing water-use efficiency, drought resilience, and environment-specific management. These results underscore the importance of aligning crop improvement and cropping system design with dynamic water availability across semi-arid regions globally. This abstract is based on previously published work (Sexton‐Bowser, S., & Patrignani, A. (2024). Yield gap analysis for rainfed grain sorghum in Kansas. Agronomy Journal, 116(6), 2901-2911) with interpretation adapted for a global conference audience.

abstracts.t: Effects of sorghum cultivars on physicochemical properties and functionality of sorghum milk and yogurt
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: kansas state university, Manhattan, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a good source of bioactive compounds associated with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory functionality for designing functional foods. Use of sorghum as human food limited due to limited nutritional characteristics and sensory attributes. Sorghum milk can be fermented with homofermentative cultures to produce yogurt-like with desirable sensory properties and probiotic benefits. This work aims to produce sorghum milks with different cultivars (white, red, black and waxy) using various steeping methods (water, NaOH, lactic acid/sodium metabisulfite); and their fermentation to produce yogurt.

Steeped sorghum grains with water were circulated in colloid mill for 3 min. The resultant slurry was collected and passed through a sieve to remove the insoluble fiber, resulting sorghum milk. The sorghum milk was gelatinized in boiling water with constant shaking. The sample was then placed in 37 °C oven, adding Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus acidophilus

The sorghum milk from selected cultivars were evaluated for their physicochemical properties. The milk derived hot-water-steeping method exhibited desirable protein/oil contents and were selected for yogurt production. The pH of sorghum milk decreased from ~ 6.5 to 4.0 after fermentation for 24 hours. The major acid was lactic acid ranging from 0.26% (waxy) to 0.33% (red). The total phenolic content (TPC) of red sorghum milk was highest (1.09 mg GAE/g), and decreased to 0.7 mg GAE/g after fermentation. The viabilities of LAB in the yogurts derived from black, red and white were similar, ranging at ~ 6.34−6.55 log CFU/mL, being significantly higher than the waxy (~ 5.5 CFU/mL).

LAB fermentation reduces TPC and tannins in sorghum milk while maintaining probiotic viability, with white sorghum showing the best balance and greatest potential for producing a palatable probiotic yogurt.

abstracts.t: Evaluating the Effect of Seed Size on Seedling-Stage Drought Tolerance in Sorghum Near-Isogenic Lines (NILs)
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Department of Agronomy, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA, Manhattan, United States
Department of Agronomy, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Seedling-stage drought tolerance is a challenge in sorghum production; early-season vigor and successful establishment are critical determinants of yield potential, particularly in water-limited regions where erratic rainfall leads to poor crop establishment. This study investigates the impact of seed size on seedling drought tolerance by evaluating different early-stage near-isogenic line (NIL) pairs derived from the Macia background ("Large" versus "Normal" seed size).

Phenotypic evaluations were conducted across two environments, a field and rainout shelters. A randomized complete block design with six replications across varying moisture regimes was used to determine how seed size affects crop establishment under both optimal and water-limited conditions. Key developmental traits, including the emergence count (5 and 7 DAP) and the seedling vigor (15 and 21 DAP), were measured.

Preliminary data analysis using the mixed linear model in the R statistical package reveals that water stress significantly reduced emergence counts across genotypes. Large-seeded NILs (4.5 to 5.3 g/100 seeds) showed better early-stage seedling growth and vigor than normal-seeded NILs (3 to 3.4 g/100 seeds) under both field conditions and controlled rainout conditions. The genotypes evaluated in this study were at the BC1F3 stage of development, representing a foundational stage in the introgression of the 'Large Seed' trait. In this generation, the populations are undergoing genetic stabilization while maintaining a high degree of recovery of the Macia recurrent parent genome, allowing for a precise evaluation of the target phenotype's impact on seedling development.

These findings will support ongoing breeding efforts aimed at improving sorghum adaptation and productivity in drought-prone regions. By identifying the interaction between seed morphology and environmental stress, this research provides a foundation for selecting germplasm with enhanced early-season resilience, ultimately supporting the development of more robust sorghum varieties for diverse agricultural landscapes.

abstracts.t: Identifying the Genetic Basis of Sorghum Chinch Bug Resistance Using the GRF4-GIF1 CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing Pipeline
