sc.x: Grain sorghum is an important crop for both human consumption and livestock feed, with Texas ranking among the leading producers in the United States. However, the evolution and rapid spread of herbicide-resistant weeds, particularly Palmer amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri), pose a significant challenge to sustainable grain sorghum productivity.

This study investigated the evolution of multiple herbicide resistance in Palmer amaranth populations collected across Texas High Plains. Three putative resistant populations (TXR1, TXR2, TXR3) from Castro, Dallam, and Moore counties were screened under greenhouse conditions at 2x field-recommended rates of mesotrione (1x=105 g ai ha<sup>-1</sup>), atrazine (1x=2240 g ai ha<sup>-1</sup>), dicamba (1x=560 g ae ha<sup>-1</sup>), and glyphosate (1x=864 g ae ha<sup>-1</sup>), along with a known susceptible (MSS) population.

The MSS population exhibited 0% survival to the herbicides tested. TXR1 showed high survival to mesotrione (87.5%) and glyphosate (87.5%), moderate survival to dicamba (50%), and low survival to atrazine (37.5%), indicating broad-spectrum, four-way resistance. TXR2 exhibited high survival to mesotrione (87.5%) but low survival to atrazine (25%), dicamba (8.3%), and glyphosate (12.5%). Whereas TXR3 had moderate survival to mesotrione (62.5%) and glyphosate (50%), it had low survival to atrazine (12.5%) and dicamba (8.3%).

These findings confirm the presence of multiple resistance in Texas Palmer amaranth populations, with TXR1 representing a particularly concerning case. Research is in progress to estimate the level of resistance and the mechanism(s) of resistance to multiple herbicides to develop viable weed management strategies to control Palmer amaranth in grain sorghum production systems.

sc.x: For over a decade several research and development initiatives ranging from technologies to delivery and service systems have been carried out to grow the sorghum value chains in ESA. National and regional interventions including input subsidies flour blending, and seed policies have also been enacted and actualized. The One-CG has taken lead in bringing together the sorghum regional stakeholders to develop breeding pipelines responsive to market/end user demands. The objective of this study was to determine the statuses of sorghum value chains in ESA in the last decade.

This was a desktop study done through a review of national and international agricultural research institutions reports and publications, and direct discussions with private sector stakeholders and farmers.

Sorghum in ESA is still a subsistence crop with low yields largely attributed to poor agronomic practices and low grain demand. Despite several research and development initiatives carried out, most countries have recorded a decline or modest growth in acreage over the last decade with the highest growth reported in Rwanda (19%) and Malawi (21%). Sudan still leads in crop acreage (about 7.0 million Ha) with low productivity (0.6 t ha<sup>-1</sup>) whereas South Africa has the highest yields at 3.0 t/ha. Striga still remains a menace in several countries causing 30- 100% yield loss. Except for the clear beer value chain the sorghum markets lack backward linkages to incentivise production.

In order to spur growth of sorghum value chains in ESA, attention should be directed towards expanding demand for grain and increasing productivity to build enough grain volumes for consistent supply. This requires increased diversification of commercial end uses for grain, building smallholder farmers capacity in good agronomic practices and provision of appropriate and affordable production machinery.

abstracts.t: Over 100 years of Sorghum Research at K-State Tribune. Moivng forward with sorghum as a key component of dynamic water-limited cropping systems.
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: K-State Western Kansas Research-Extension Centers, Tribune, United States

sc.x: The Tribune Experiment Station was established in 1911. Sorghum rapidly became a cornerstone in the research efforts of the station. Many long-term datasets have been, and continue to be collected at Tribune with respect to water and nutrient use efficiencies in sorghum production.

These long-term datasets have provided better understandings of water and nutrient dynamics and how to best employ sorghum management techniques. This presentation will synthesize the output from these studies and suggest opportunities for future exploration.

Multiple long-term trials have evaluated management interactions on sorghum productivity in a highly variable environment. These have included long-term rotation trials (est. 1993, 1996), tillage trials (est. 1991), and fertility trials (est. 1961). In addition, numerous on-farm experiments have been conducted across the central High Plains to evaluate a wide range of management techniques.
Sorghum can play a critical role in the development of dynamic cropping systems in the central High Plains that maximize water and nutrient use efficiencies, and minimize farm production risk.

sc.x: Sweet sorghum is a promising bioenergy crop because of its high biomass production and accumulation of readily fermentable sugars in the stem, providing valuable feedstock for biofuel production. Increasing soluble sugar accumulation is therefore an important target for improving the value and utilization of sweet sorghum. However, the mechanisms underlying massive sugar accumulation in sorghum stems remain incompletely understood.

SbbHLH093 expression was negatively correlated with stem sugar levels across genotypes, source–sink treatments, and developmental stages. Loss of AtbHLH093/NFL (NO FLOWERING IN SHORT DAY), the Arabidopsis homolog of SbbHLH093, also resulted in increased sugar accumulation, supporting a link between reproductive development and stem sugar accumulation. Consistent with these findings, field experiments showed that genetically reducing phloem unloading into the reproductive tassel enhanced sugar accumulation in sweet sorghum stems.
To investigate these mechanisms, we performed source–sink manipulations using near-isogenic lines (NILs), dd and DD, which differ in stem sugar accumulation, followed by transcriptomic analysis.

Although the underlying mechanism remains under investigation, our results support a model in which manipulation of reproductive sink strength alters source–sink partitioning and promotes sugar retention in the stem. Together, our work provides new insights into the regulation of sugar partitioning in sweet sorghum and highlights reproductive sink manipulation as a potential strategy for increasing fermentable sugar accumulation and improving the value of sorghum biomass as a biofuel feedstock.

abstracts.t: Genotype-by-environment interactions shape arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal communities in sorghum

sc.x: Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi form symbiotic relationships with over 80% of land plants, including major crops, enhancing nutrient and water uptake in exchange for plant-derived carbon. Plant genotypic traits governing resource exchange and symbiosis regulation are important determinants of mycorrhizal interactions under local environmental conditions<sup>1</sup>. Previous studies in grain crops, including maize<sup>2</sup>, wheat<sup>3</sup>, barley<sup>4</sup>, and sorghum<sup>5</sup>, have shown that different cultivars influence the extent of AM fungal colonization but there is limited information on the differences in community composition between cultivars<sup>6</sup>. Similarly, it is known that the individuals of the same plant species growing in different environments will host different communities of AM fungi<sup>7</sup> but in these studies environmental and host genetic factors are confounded.

To disentangle host and environmental effects, we grew 25 sorghum landraces representing all racial groups across three different environments and characterised root-colonising AM fungal communities using DNA metabarcoding. Fungal taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity were quantified and community composition using abundance and presence/absence metrics were assessed.

Genotype, environment and genotype-by-environment (GxE) effects all significantly influenced AM fungal community composition, indicating that restructuring of fungal communities is occurring. Notably, the GxE interaction (R<sup>2</sup> = 20-22%) explained more variation than either genotype (R<sup>2</sup> = 12-14%) or environment (R<sup>2</sup> = 18%) alone, demonstrating that different genotypes respond differently to different environments. Tests of multivariate homogeneity of dispersion indicated that genotype and GxE effects reflect genuine differences in community composition, demonstrating environmentally contingent host effects.

These findings highlight the importance of considering both host genetics and environmental context when characterizing mycorrhizal communities, with implications for crop improvement strategies that aim to harness AM fungal symbioses for more sustainable and resilient agricultural systems.

sc.x: Ideotyping for Climate Change is designing crop types (ideotypes) with specific traits tailored to perform optimally under future climate scenarios. Advanta is looking at forward-looking breeding strategy that integrates physiology, genetics, and climate projections. An effective sorghum ideotype must address the multiple, interacting constraints across diverse production ecologies, including terminal and early season drought, heat stress, low soil fertility, and increasing climate variability, addressing smallholder farming systems. Key adaptive traits include the stay green phenotype, deep and plastic root systems, rapid seedling vigor, efficient nitrogen and phosphorus uptake, phenological plasticity, and stable yield under low input conditions. Optimizing canopy architecture is central to improving radiation use efficiency while minimizing transpirational water loss, by having erect to semi erect leaves, moderate leaf area index, productive tillering, and a waxy leaf surface. Complementary root traits like deep axial roots, high root length density, steep root angles, and adaptive root plasticity enhance access to soil moisture and nutrients under progressive drying. Stay green expression during grain filling sustains photosynthesis, improves nitrogen remobilization, reduces lodging and charcoal rot incidence by stabilizing grain filling under terminal drought. With increasing climatic uncertainty, stress escape and tolerance mechanisms are essential. Short to medium duration maturity combined with flexible flowering ensures synchrony of parental lines. Heat tolerant pollen viability, a shortened anthesis silking interval, and the ability to maintain grain set under stress are critical for minimizing yield losses during the flowering stage. To meet food, fodder, and bioenergy demands, the ideotype must have lodging resistance, improved stover digestibility (including low lignin or brown midrib variants), and a balanced grain–stover ratio to enhance whole farm sustainability. This paper discusses ideotype design through a system-based breeding approach integrating trait based and genomic selection, crop growth modeling, participatory breeding, and high throughput phenotyping to enhance climate resilience.

sc.x: Early loss of grain dormancy increases pre‑harvest sprouting (PHS) susceptibility, reducing marketable yield and compromising seed quality, two major constraints for resilient sorghum production systems. Using mapping populations derived from contrasting parental lines (Redlan: low dormancy; IS9530: high dormancy), we previously identified a major dormancy QTL, qDOR‑9, located at the distal end of chromosome 9 (Rodríguez et al., 2025; https://doi.org/10.1111/pbi.70007). To refine this region, a panel of Near Isogenic Lines (NILs) was developed. Phenotyping across two locations during the 2024/2025 season confirmed the effect of qDOR‑9 on whole‑grain germination index and embryo sensitivity to abscisic acid (ABA), strengthening evidence for ABA‑related causal genes. Phenotypic and NGS data for NILs also narrowed the qDOR-9 interval from 2.2 Mb to 1.6 Mb. To identify dormancy-related candidate genes, sorghum sequences were compared with ABA‑pathway genes and with dormancy/PHS QTLs from other species through synteny analysis. Whole‑genome resequencing of IS9530 and Redlan enabled detection of high‑confidence SNPs in annotated genes followed by functional prediction using SNPeffect. Candidate genes prioritized for expression analysis included PP2C‑53 (ABI1/ABI2‑like), HISTONE DEACETYLASE‑2 (HD2C‑like), and MAPK9 (ortholog of rice qSD5.2). ABI5, a positive regulator of ABA signaling and dormancy in sorghum, was also evaluated despite lying outside qDOR‑9. Expression analyses (RT‑qPCR) were performed with RNA extracted from embryos dissected from developing grains (20, 25, 30, 36, and 40 dpa) and from 36 dpa imbibed grains (22 h at 25°C). Possible expression and structural variants are discussed. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking embryo physiology, ABA responsiveness, and genetic variation underlying dormancy, while delivering refined genomic coordinates for breeding.

sc.x: The western corn rootworm (Diabrotica virgifera virgifera LeConte) is a major pest of maize in the United States and Europe, causing significant yield losses and exceeding $2 billion annually in damage and control costs. Resistance to key management strategies—including crop rotation and Bt maize expressing Cry3 proteins—has intensified in regions with continuous corn production. This study evaluates the potential of forage sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) as a non-host crop to suppress rootworm populations while maintaining high silage productivity. A two-year field trial (2023–2024) was conducted in Champaign County, Illinois, comparing Bt corn (ADV 1090 D2), non-Bt corn (Phoenix 5892 GT), and forage sorghum (ADVF8322) under high rootworm pressure. Adult emergence was quantified using emergence cages, sticky traps, and whole-plant counts. Root injury was assessed using the 0–3 node-injury scale, and fresh biomass yields were recorded. Rootworm development was minimal in sorghum plots, with fewer than 10 beetles emerging annually, compared to over 100 in corn treatments. Adult beetle activity was consistently lower in sorghum, as confirmed by both trap and plant-based assessments. Root injury was absent in sorghum in 2023 and negligible in 2024, while corn treatments showed substantial root damage. Bt corn did not consistently outperform non-Bt corn, suggesting reduced efficacy of Cry3 proteins under local resistance conditions. Forage sorghum also demonstrated superior biomass production, yielding 62,150 kg ha⁻¹ in 2023 and 137,900 kg ha⁻¹ in 2024, exceeding both corn treatments. These results indicate that forage sorghum can effectively disrupt rootworm life cycles while providing high silage yields. This study supports the inclusion of forage sorghum in crop rotations as a sustainable strategy for managing corn rootworm. Its non-host status and high productivity make it a valuable tool for integrated pest management systems.

sc.x: The “Santa Fé System,” widely adopted in Brazil’s cerrado region, integrates two crops per season to maximize biomass production and soil health. By intercropping grain sorghum with Brachiaria ruziziensis, farmers gain a “third crop” for forage or soil cover without altering equipment or schedules. Benefits include improved soil structure, nutrient cycling, erosion control, and weed suppression. The igrowth® technology enhances this system by enabling sorghum tolerance to imidazolinone herbicides, allowing selective control of brachiaria and minimizing competition. This study evaluated the impact of different doses and timings of Zelone® herbicide (UPL; 75% imazethapyr + 25% imazapic) on brachiaria growth and sorghum yield. The trial was conducted in Rio Verde, Goiás, in 2024, using ADV1151IG sorghum (200,000 plants/ha) intercropped with brachiaria (400 seed quality points/ha). Treatments included Zelone applications at four phenological stages: (A) pre-emergence, (B) post-emergence without tillers, (C) 1–2 tillers, and (D) 3–4 tillers. Atrazine (3.0 L.p.c/ha) was optionally included. Plots were 6 rows × 6 m, sprayed with a CO₂ sprayer. Results showed that brachiaria grown without sorghum reached 108.75 cm and 13,062 kg/ha dry matter at 60 DAP, demonstrating its competitive potential. Late herbicide application (stage D) effectively reduced brachiaria height (86.25 cm) and biomass (4,310 kg/ha), while sorghum yields remained high and stable across all treatments (80.68–92 sc/ha), including manual and chemical controls. The best sorghum yield was achieved with 1.2 L.p.c/ha Zelone applied when brachiaria had 2–3 tillers. The igrowth® system enables precise weed management in sorghum–brachiaria intercropping, supporting full sorghum development while establishing post-harvest pasture and soil cover. This approach enhances sustainability, operational efficiency, and resilience in tropical farming systems.

sc.x: Sorghum has evolved from a secondary crop to a strategic commodity in Brazil, reaching a record cultivated area of 2.1 million hectares in 2025. In this context, improved crop protection practices have become critical to maximize yield and profitability, particularly under “safrinha” (off-season) production systems. This study evaluated the agronomic, phytosanitary, and economic impact of different fungicide management strategies on the grain sorghum hybrid ADV1151 IG. A field trial was conducted at the Advanta Seeds research station in Indianópolis, Minas Gerais, Brazil, using a randomized design with six treatments, including an untreated control. Treatments varied by active ingredients, chemical groups (triazoles, strobilurins, and carboxamides), and application timing (V4–V5, booting, and post-flowering stages). Standardized agronomic practices were applied across all plots except for fungicide programs. Key performance indicators included grain yield (bags ha⁻¹), net profit (US$ ha⁻¹), and return on investment (ROI). Results demonstrated a strong positive relationship between fungicide use and both agronomic and economic performance. The highest yield (152 bags ha⁻¹) and net profit (US$867 ha⁻¹) were achieved with a carboxamide-based early application program (Treatment 3), indicating its suitability for high-investment systems targeting maximum productivity. In contrast, Treatment 4 delivered the highest ROI (2340%), combining high yield (142 bags ha⁻¹) with efficient input use, making it the most attractive option for growers prioritizing cost-benefit optimization. Overall, the findings highlight the essential role of fungicide management—particularly early applications with carboxamide-containing products—in enhancing sorghum yield potential and economic returns under Brazilian safrinha conditions.

sc.x: Currently in the United States, the beef cattle inventory is at an historically low level and consequently cattle prices have reached record high levels. Ongoing drought conditions in the Great Plains have contributed to the cattle shortage as forage supplies have been negatively affected. Summer annual forages such as sorghum-sudangrass hybrids are becoming more popular as “emergency” forages in areas where permanent pastures and other crops have failed due to the lack of moisture. Hybrids with the brown midrib (BMR) trait have reduced levels of lignin, which leads to increased fiber digestibility, higher feed intake, and therefore improved average daily gain. In a 2-yr study at the University of Georgia, steers grazing BMR sorghum-sudangrass exhibited increased average daily gain (ADG) versus steers grazing a conventional sorghum-sudangrass hybrid over a 70-d grazing period (0.90 vs 0.68 kg/day, P<.05). At the current price of US $7.25 per kg for 450 kg steers, this additional gain is worth $1.60 per day, or $112 per animal for the entire 70-d grazing period. Similar studies have shown that steers grazing BMR sorghum-sudangrass exhibit higher rates of gain than steers grazing conventional hybrids. Even with a higher seed cost for BMR versus conventional sorghum-sudangrass hybrids, there is still a distinct economic advantage for the BMR hybrids, especially with the high cattle prices currently in place.

abstracts.t: Eco-physiological mechanisms driving differential adaptation of sorghum and corn across sowing dates under water and heat stress
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

sc.x:
Crop adaptation to water- and heat-limited environments is strongly determined by the interaction between phenological development and resource availability during critical growth periods. In many production systems, corn has expanded into marginal environments despite its sensitivity to abiotic stress, highlighting the need to better understand the physiological basis of crop resilience in comparison to sorghum. This study investigated the eco-physiological drivers of grain yield formation in sorghum and corn under contrasting sowing dates in a temperate environment in Argentina. Field experiments were conducted during the 2024/2025 growing season under rainfed conditions. One corn hybrid and sorghum hybrids representing short-, intermediate-, and long-cycle maturity groups were evaluated across four sowing dates designed to modify the temporal overlap between crop phenology and stress occurrence. Measurements included phenological development, soil water dynamics (0–2 m), biomass accumulation, grain yield, and harvest index.
Results revealed that yield differences among crops and maturity groups were primarily explained by shifts in the timing of the critical period relative to water availability and thermal stress. Short- and intermediate-cycle sorghum hybrids exhibited higher yield stability due to a phenological delay associated with growth latency, which decoupled flowering from peak drought and heat events. This resulted in improved water availability during the critical period and enhanced grain set. In contrast, corn displayed limited phenological plasticity, with flowering frequently coinciding with periods of soil water depletion and high temperatures (>35°C), leading to reductions in grain number and overall yield under early sowing conditions. Under late sowing scenarios, where stress constraints were minimized, corn achieved the highest yield levels. Long-cycle sorghum hybrids showed reduced harvest index and lower productivity, reflecting a mismatch between growth duration and environmental conditions.

abstracts.t: Inclusion of low-tannin sorghum in finishing pig diets: effects on growth performance and carcass traits
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Advanta Semillas SAIC, Santa Fe, Argentina

sc.x: Corn has traditionally been the primary energy source in pig diets across Argentina and other South American production systems. However, increasing pressure to improve cost efficiency and diversify feed ingredients has renewed interest in sorghum, particularly low-tannin hybrids, as a viable alternative. Modern low-tannin sorghum reduces the anti-nutritional effects historically associated with this crop while maintaining competitive nutritional value. This study evaluated the impact of replacing corn with low-tannin sorghum on growth performance and carcass characteristics in finishing pigs under commercial conditions in Argentina. A total of 288 pigs were assigned to a randomized complete block design with four dietary treatments including increasing sorghum inclusion levels (0%, 25%, 50%, and 75%). Diets were formulated to be isoenergetic and nutritionally balanced. Growth performance was monitored over a 94-day period, including average daily gain, feed intake, and feed conversion ratio, while carcass traits were assessed at slaughter. Results showed that high inclusion of low-tannin sorghum (75%) maintained or improved growth performance relative to corn-based diets, achieving the highest final body weight and average daily gain. Increased sorghum inclusion was associated with greater feed intake and a moderate reduction in feed conversion efficiency. Intermediate inclusion levels (25% and 50%) resulted in performance comparable to the control diet. Importantly, carcass quality parameters, including lean percentage, backfat thickness, and muscle depth, were not negatively affected by sorghum inclusion, while carcass weight increased with higher sorghum levels. These findings demonstrate that low-tannin sorghum is a suitable alternative to corn in finishing pig diets, particularly when used at high inclusion levels. The results support its potential to enhance flexibility in feed formulation and contribute to more resilient and cost-effective livestock production systems in sorghum-producing regions.

sc.x: Expanding cropping systems into increasingly variable and water-limited environments requires a better understanding of crop adaptation and stability. In Argentina, corn has historically dominated high-productivity systems, while sorghum remains an alternative for more restrictive conditions. However, comparative data across diverse agroecological environments and management strategies remain limited. This study evaluated the performance of sorghum and corn across a wide range of environmental conditions, integrating seven locations representative of Argentina’s main production regions and multiple sowing dates. The experimental network generated 26 distinct environments, capturing variability in temperature, water availability, and yield potential. Sorghum hybrids representing short, intermediate, and long maturity cycles were compared against a commercial corn hybrid under consistent management practices. Grain yield, environmental characterization, and crop responses were analyzed to assess relative performance and stability. Results showed a strong dependency of crop performance on environmental productivity. In low-yielding environments (<4000 kg ha⁻¹ baseline for corn), sorghum—particularly short and intermediate maturity types—consistently outperformed corn, with yield advantages exceeding 2,500 kg ha⁻¹ and high win rates. In intermediate environments, both crops showed similar performance with variable outcomes depending on sowing date and stress patterns. In high-yielding environments (>8000 kg ha⁻¹), corn clearly outperformed sorghum, reflecting its greater yield potential under favorable conditions. Differences in performance were driven by contrasting responses to water and heat stress, as well as phenological adaptation. Sorghum exhibited greater stability and lower sensitivity to stress, while corn achieved superior yields when environmental constraints were minimal. These findings highlight the importance of aligning crop choice, hybrid maturity, and sowing date with specific environmental conditions. Integrating sorghum into cropping systems can reduce risk and improve resilience in marginal environments, while corn remains the most competitive option in high-productivity scenarios.

sc.x: Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) acreage in the United States has declined over the past three decades, in part because of limited postemergence grass control options. Broadleaf weed management in sorghum typically requires both preemergence and postemergence herbicide applications. The igrowth weed management system (Advanta Seeds) may improve weed control and productivity; however, greater initial input costs may limit producer adoption. This study evaluated the economic return on investment (ROI) of the igrowth system relative to a conventional weed management program. Field experiments were conducted by Kansas State University near Garden City, KS, in 2021 and 2022 to compare conventional and igrowth weed management systems. A regionally adapted igrowth hybrid was used in both years. The conventional system included preplant applications of S-metolachlor and atrazine, followed by postemergence applications of pyrasulfotole + bromoxynil octanoate + bromoxynil Heptanoate in 2021, and dicamba in 2022. The igrowth system included preplant applications of S-metolachlor and mesotrione, followed by postemergence applications of imazamox + atrazine both years. Reported weed control and grain yield data were used to compare system economics based on 2026 seed and herbicide prices. All other production costs were assumed equal between systems and were excluded from the analysis. Grain sorghum price was fixed at $150 Mg-1. Across years, mean grain yield was 3,755 kg ha-1 for the conventional system and 5,999 kg ha-1 for the igrowth system. The igrowth system produced $596.82 ha-1 greater revenue than the conventional system and resulted in an ROI of 147%. These results indicate that, despite greater upfront costs, the igrowth system can provide a substantial economic advantage through improved weed management and increased grain yield.

sc.x: Fungal contamination causes significant global agricultural losses, ranging from 10–23% in the field and 10–20% post-harvest. Ergosterol, a fungal cell membrane sterol, serves as a bioindicator for monitoring fungal contamination in food matrices. Ergosterol quantification techniques frequently rely on gas chromatography (GC), which require highly toxic reagents, or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) methods optimized for yeast and mushrooms rather than grain matrices. This study aimed to optimize a reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography with diode array detection (RP-HPLC-DAD) method to improve the precision, resolution, and recovery of ergosterol quantification in sorghum grains.

Comparative analysis determined that ground grain samples had a significantly lower standard deviation, resulting in higher analytical precision than intact grains. The optimized HPLC conditions yielded superior peak resolution. The linear calibration curve (r² > 0.990) was from 0.89 to 125 μg/mL of ergosterol in methanol. The limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantitation (LOQ) were established at 0.88 μg/mL and 2.66 μg/mL, respectively. Notably, the new method enhanced extraction efficiency, detecting ergosterol concentrations ranging from 65.5 to 753.9 μg/g in naturally contaminated samples representing an increase of over 30-fold compared to the initial method (<1.6 to 21.8 μg/g).

Five sorghum samples (AB003, AB038, AB128, AB137, and AB185), exhibiting a spectrum of microbial contamination levels from sound to moldy, were evaluated. Analytical optimization focused on grain preparation (intact versus ground), column temperature, flow rate, and mobile phase gradient utilizing a Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 column.

The improved RP-HPLC-DAD method offers a highly accurate, precise, and accessible alternative for evaluating fungal contamination in sorghum. This protocol presents a safer and more effective tool for grain quality control and food safety management because reduce the use of toxic chemical reagents.

sc.x: Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi form symbiotic relationships with over 80% of land plants, enhancing nutrient and water acquisition in exchange for plant-derived carbon. Environmental conditions strongly influence AM fungal associations, and sorghum genotypes adapted to differing soil types are expected to differ in their ability to regulate symbiosis. Limited studies have assessed how host genotype affects AM fungal community composition independent of environmental effects.

To disentangle host and environmental effects, we grew 25 sorghum landraces representing all racial groups across three contrasting environments and characterised root-colonising AM fungal communities using DNA metabarcoding. Fungal taxonomic diversity, relative abundance, and community composition were assessed using multiple diversity metrics. In one environment, an additional 94 sorghum genotypes were evaluated to further investigate host genetic effects on AM fungal composition.

Genotype, environment and genotype-by-environment (GxE) interactions all significantly influenced AM fungal community composition. Notably, GxE interactions explained more variation (R<sup>2</sup> = 20-22%) than genotype (R<sup>2</sup> = 12-14%) or environment (R<sup>2</sup> = 18%) alone, indicating that host genetic effects on AM fungal assembly are strongly dependent on environmental context. Analysis of the additional genotypes further revealed genotype-dependent differences in fungal community composition and provided evidence for a genetic basis of AM fungal taxa richness.

Together, these findings demonstrate that sorghum genotypes differentially shape their associated AM fungal communities and that these effects are strongly influenced by environmental conditions. Harnessing host genetic variation that promotes beneficial plant-microbe interactions may provide new opportunities to improve nutrient-use efficiency and crop performance in low-input agricultural systems, supporting more sustainable and resilient food production.

sc.x: Asymmetric diurnal warming linked to higher rise in nighttime minimum temperatures than the daytime maximum, is projected to intensify in future, yet field-based evidence for its independent agronomic consequences in grain sorghum is limited. A two-year field experiment at Rockhampton, Queensland, was conducted during the 2023/24 and 2024/25 growing seasons to characterize the physiological, agronomic and biochemical responses to varying thermal environment created using staggered sowing design. In the first season, the 20-day critical reproductive window (anthesis ± 10 days) in the mid-sown crops were exposed to 7-11 high nighttime temperature (HNT) events (MinT > 26 °C) without concurrent high daytime temperature (HDT) events (MaxT > 40 °C), generating near-pure HNT-stress environment. In contrast, late-sown crops in the same season experienced 5-6 HDT events without HNT events. All sowing dates in the second season were free from HNT events. Grain yield and harvest index in the HNT-exposed crops were substantially lower compared to the HDT-exposed or stress-free crops. An extreme outcome was observed in the mid-sown AVT-Sorg#1 in 2023/24, producing the highest vegetative biomass, but the lowest harvest index recorded (0.11). It confirmed that HNT can completely decouple vegetative source activity from reproductive sink realization in sorghum. Nighttime respiration (Rn) in the HNT-dominated period was approximately threefold higher than in equivalent HNT-free sowing, without such divergence in the daytime photosynthesis. It resulted the respiration-to-photosynthesis ratio (Rn/A) rising as high as 0.42. The C<sub>4</sub> photosynthetic pathway did not protect against HNT-driven nocturnal respiratory losses. Total phenolic content and antioxidant capacity were higher in the grains produced under HNT-exposed environments. The findings demonstrate that HNT during the critical reproductive window imposes greater yield penalties in sorghum than equivalent daytime heat stress, through sustained nocturnal respiratory carbon depletion and partitioning failure.

sc.x: Current climate models project that elevated temperatures and heat weaves occur more frequently - challenging crop health and thus agricultural production. Brassinosteroids (BRs) have been shown to act as hormonal regulators of plant development and with growing evidence also in response to environmental cues such as drought and temperature. This study investigates the influence of BR receptor activity on physiological and metabolic responses to elevated temperatures in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), a heat- and drought tolerant crop with growing relevance worldwide.

SbBRI1 and SbBRL1 mutants responded with either higher or lower sensitivity to 38°C as their wildtype counterpart, respectively although both showed reduced response to the hormone. A second SbBRL1 allele exhibited the opposite response in both elevated temperature and BR treatments. This was also reflected in pattern changes of primary, secondary and lipid metabolic profiles obtained by GC-MS and LC-MS.
Pathway analysis indicated BR-dependent metabolic alteration in elevated temperatures, especially primary carbon and energy metabolism, amino acid profiles, phenylpropanoid synthesis, and lipid composition in seeds, roots and leaf tissue.

We obtained EMS-mutants of sorghum BR receptors brassinosteroid insensitive 1 (SbBRI1) and BRI1-like 1 (SbBRL1) and exposed both seedlings and adult plants to different temperature treatments at 28°C, 38°C, and 48°C at seedling and adult stage measuring phenotypic variables such as root, shoot growth and photosynthesis.
Taken together, our results indicate a fine-tuned role of sorghum BR signaling in shaping the metabolic and developmental response of sorghum to high temperature.

sc.x: Sorghum is emerging as a viable alternative crop in South Carolina, especially on marginal soils. It fits well into the existing rotation system and guarantees sustainable and economical feed production to meet the needs of the livestock industry in the state. Through its recently established Center for Plant Breeding, Genetics, Genomics (CPBGG), the South Carolina State University launched a new initiative to strengthen crop improvement research to meet the local needs for new crop technologies. The Center has initiated collaboration with Purdue University to accelerate sorghum breeding activities in South Carolina.

A combined analysis of variance (ANOVA) conducted across the Olar and West Lafayette locations revealed statistically significant differences in genotypic responses between these sites. GGE bi-plot analysis was employed to assess genotype performance. The first two principal components collectively accounted for 100% of the variation, with PC1 contributing 65.26% and PC2 34.74%. The "which-won-where" polygon view identified several promising hybrids that exhibited superior performance compared to the commercial checks.

A total of 54 sorghum hybrids (including three commercial checks) were evaluated during the 2025 cropping season as an initial effort. The hybrids selected for early maturity and grain quality were evaluated for their responses to drought stress, disease pressure, and adaptation. The experiment was laid out using a randomized complete block design (RCBD) with two replications. Grain yield, disease severity, insect pest incidence, and overall plant performance was collected.

This initial study demonstrated the potential of sorghum in South Carolina and highlighted the importance of integrated sorghum breeding strategies. A farmer demonstration of the field plots created strong impression among growers, pointing a promising potential for adoption and expansion of sorghum in the state. Promising hybrids will be further evaluated across multiple environments and seasons to confirm their performance and stability.

abstracts.t: What Actually Accelerates Commercial Sorghum Breeding?A European Breeder’s Perspective on Emerging Technologies and Genetic Gain
abstracts.th: Theme 4: Emerging technologies and their application potential - commercialization opportunities for the sorghum industry

a: Alfaseed Ltd., Budapest, Hungary

sc.x: Plant breeders have access to an unprecedented range of technologies, yet technological progress does not automatically translate into faster genetic gain. From a commercial breeding perspective, the relevant question is not which technology is the most advanced, but how different technologies can be integrated into a breeding pipeline to increase genetic gain per unit of time toward relevant breeding targets. This question is particularly important for European sorghum breeding, where the target population of environments is changing together with the role of sorghum in cropping systems. Climatic trends and increasing production risks associated with heat and drought are altering crop competitiveness, while changes in sorghum acreage, market structure and cultivar availability create a continuously evolving commercial target. Spatial characterization based on soil, precipitation and temperature variables further illustrates how environmental information can contribute to identifying regions where sorghum may gain strategic importance in climate-adapted crop rotations. The genetic gain equation provides a useful framework for evaluating emerging technologies according to their effects on selection intensity, accuracy, exploitable genetic variation and breeding cycle length. Genomic and phenotypic technologies, environmental characterization, data integration and AI-assisted decision support can increase the information available for selection and potentially improve its accuracy. Controlled-environment breeding and accelerated generation strategies can reduce cycle length. Novel approaches for generating and exploiting genetic variation further expand the available breeding space. Their greatest value, however, emerges from integration rather than isolated implementation. Effective acceleration of commercial sorghum breeding therefore requires a systems-level approach linking technology, target definition, genetic gain and product development. Ultimately, the value of emerging technologies is determined by their ability to convert genetic progress into differentiated cultivars that meet future grower and market needs.

sc.x: Sorghum is an important food and feed crop in the dry lowland areas of Ethiopia. Farmers grow both early-sown long-duration landraces and late-sown short-duration improved varieties. Because timing and intensity of drought stress can vary in space and time, an understanding of major traits (G), environments (E), management (M), and their interactions (G×E×M) is needed to optimize grain and forage yield given the limited available resources. Crop simulation modeling can provide insights into these complex G×E×M interactions and be used to identify possible avenues for adaptation to prevalent drought patterns in Ethiopia. Predictive phenology models were developed for a range of Ethiopian germplasm.The aims were to (1) further parameterize and validate the APSIM-sorghum model for crop growth and yield of Ethiopian germplasm, and (2) quantify by simulation the productivity-risk trade-offs associated with early vs late sowing strategies in the dry lowlands of Ethiopia.

Field experiments involving Ethiopian germplasm with contrasting phenology and height were conducted under well-watered (Melkassa) and water-limited (Miesso) conditions and crop development, growth and yield measured. Soil characterization and weather records at the experimental sites, combined with model parameterization, enabled testing of the APSIM-sorghum model.

The APSMIM model showed good correspondence between simulated and observed data. The simulated productivity for the Ethiopian dry lowlands environments showed trade-offs between biomass and grain yield for early and late sowing strategies. The late sowing strategy tended to produce less biomass except in poor seasons, whereas it tended to produce greater grain yield except in very good seasons

This study exemplified the systems approach to identifying traits and management options needed to quantify the production-risk trade-offs associated with crop adaptation in the Ethiopian dry lowlands and further exemplifies the general robustness of the sorghum model in APSIM for this task.

abstracts.t: The effect of biomaterials coating on sensory properties of potatoes during storage
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Irbid National University, Jordan, Jordan

sc.x: Potato is the fourth most important food crop worldwide after rice, wheat, and maize, and it is the second most important crop after wheat in Jordan. During storage, potatoes undergo several quality and sensory changes that negatively affect consumer acceptance and market value. Therefore, this study aimed to improve the quality characteristics and extend the shelf life of stored potatoes using edible coatings prepared from renewable agro-food by-products.

he application of edible coatings improved the quality attributes of potato tubers compared with the uncoated control samples. Coated potatoes showed better maintenance of texture, improved visual appearance, reduced decay percentage, and delayed color changes during storage.

Whey protein concentrate, chitosan, and coconut oil were used to prepare edible coatings applied to the surface of potato tubers. Coated and uncoated (control) potato tubers were stored under different storage conditions for 120 days. Quality parameters, including texture, color, visual appearance, and decay percentage, were evaluated periodically throughout the storage period.

edible coatings based on whey protein concentrate, chitosan, and coconut oil can be an effective and sustainable approach for maintaining potato quality and extending storage life. The use of agro-food by-products such as whey protein concentrate provides a promising strategy for developing environmentally friendly preservation technologies.

sc.x: Drought stress is a major constraint to sorghum production, particularly in semi-arid regions where water availability is irregular and often coincides with critical crop developmental stages.

Drought stress significantly affected plant growth and physiology, with distinct impacts depending on the timing of water deficit. Pre-flowering stress caused the greatest reductions in plant height, leaf area index, and biomass accumulation, reflecting strong limitations on vegetative development. In contrast, post-flowering stress had a more pronounced effect on
physiological traits, including chlorophyll content and net assimilation rate, leading to impaired photosynthetic efficiency during grain filling. Growth analysis revealed reduced biomass accumulation and altered carbon partitioning under both stress conditions, with partial recovery observed when water was restored after pre-flowering stress.

This study evaluated the morphophysiological and growth responses of 20 grain sorghum hybrids subjected to drought stress at pre- and post-flowering stages under field conditions in a semi-arid environment in Minas Gerais, Brazil. The experiment followed a randomized complete block design with three replications and three water regimes: wellwatered, pre-flowering drought, and post-flowering drought. Key traits assessed included plant height, leaf area index, shoot dry weight, chlorophyll index, and growth parameters such as absolute and relative growth rates, leaf area ratio, leaf weight ratio, specific leaf area, and net assimilation rate.

Grain yield was markedly reduced by drought, with the lowest values observed under postflowering stress (~2,500 kg ha⁻¹), compared to pre-flowering stress (~4,000 kg ha⁻¹). These results indicate that sorghum is more sensitive to water deficit during the reproductive stage, when assimilate supply directly influences grain development. Overall, the study highlights the importance of evaluating drought stress at different phenological stages and identifies key morphophysiological traits associated with drought tolerance, providing valuable insights for sorghum breeding programs targeting semi-arid environments.

abstracts.t: Every DRIP Counts: Mapping the Genetic Architecture of Drought-Resilient Sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, United States

sc.x: Climate uncertainty poses critical threats to global agriculture, driving an estimated $20 billion in annual losses in the US alone. Mitigating these impacts requires the rapid development of resilient crops that maintain stable yields during extreme weather events. Sorghum exhibits superior tolerance to drought and heat stress. Its extensive natural diversity represents a powerful, untapped resource for accelerating the breeding and engineering of high-performance varieties. Elucidating the genetic networks and molecular mechanisms underlying sorghum’s innate stress tolerance requires analyzing molecular activities and the complex genotype × environment interactions driving phenotypic diversity.

At both locations, continuous, tracking of plant growth dynamics were captured by integrating multimodal HTP data from autonomous proximal and remote sensing. Association mapping across controlled and field conditions is enabling identification of time-specific and environment-dependent loci underlying the genetic architecture of sorghum drought response and WUE.

We established the DRought-assocIated Panel (DRIP), which consists of 285 diverse sorghum accessions selected from the pangenome to maximize genetic and phenotypic diversity in drought responsiveness and water use efficiency (WUE). To capture early dynamic stress responses, the DRIP was subject to a controlled drought stress experiment on an automated high-throughput phenotyping (HTP) platform where control and drought-stressed plants (80% and 40% soil moisture content, respectively) were imaged daily and dynamic morpho-physiological phenotypes extracted. We also collected transcriptome data from the entire panel in both conditions, which we used for drought-responsive expression (e)QTL analysis. Additionally, we grew the DRIP over multiple seasons in two contrasting field sites: a productive mid-western site in Missouri, and a hot, arid environment in Arizona.

Integrating candidate loci with in-house multi-omics datasets and the sorghum pangenomic framework resolves fine-scale allelic variation, helping pinpoint functionally-relevant alleles and haplotypes. Multiplexing these favorable alleles through engineering or breeding will accelerate the delivery of climate-resilient sorghum varieties.

sc.x: Sorghum grain composition and technological properties determine its value for food, feed, and industrial applications, with optimal combinations of traits varying according to end-use requirements. Understanding the genetic and molecular basis of grain quality components is therefore essential for developing breeding strategies capable of assembling diverse quality ideotypes.

We integrated molecular, genetic, and evolutionary information to identify genomic factors underlying variation in protein and starch accumulation, as well as protein digestibility in sorghum grain. First, a gene co-expression network was established from transcriptomic data collected across 10 grain developmental stages over two years in the sorghum genotype Macia. This analysis identified co-expression modules associated with grain protein and starch composition and with protein digestibility. Functional analyses using transient expression in protoplasts further highlighted SbPBF1a, SbPBF1b, and SbNF-YC1 as central regulators of genes involved in protein and starch biosynthesis. We then investigated the genetic architecture of grain quality in a panel of 300 sorghum genotypes representing the global diversity of the species. The panel was evaluated at two locations over two years in southern France, enabling the identification of genomic regions associated with variation in grain quality traits. These regions were integrated with the gene co-expression networks and evolutionary information from previous comparative and population genomic studies to prioritize candidate genes and distinguish regulatory and structural components potentially contributing to grain quality variation.

Together, these complementary approaches provide a framework for moving from phenotypic variation to biologically informed breeding targets. Our results provide new insights into the molecular regulation and genetic architecture of protein and starch accumulation and protein digestibility in sorghum, while identifying candidate genes that could be exploited to design grain quality ideotypes tailored to specific food, feed, and industrial applications.

sc.x: The response to water availability in plants is governed by a series of interconnected transcriptional cascades that form Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs). Rewiring of hub transcription factors (TFs) caused by genetic variations may alter GRN architecture and thereby physiological water use responses. In this work, we hypothesize that water-responsive GRNs architecturally differ between sorghum accessions from arid and humid climate zones. We leveraged 1) high-throughput phenotyping, 2) transcriptome (RNA-seq) and accessible chromatin (ATAC-seq) profiling, and 3) population genomics to investigate how GRN re-wiring contributes to variation in water use efficiency (WUE). Automated phenotyping in a controlled growth environment on the Danforth Bellwether platform identified four sorghum genotypes with distinct WUE patterns under drought stress. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq time-course experiments across leaf development and in crown roots revealed modules of osmotic stress related genes that were constitutively expressed at high levels in specific genotypes, but only facultatively induced upon stress in others, consistent with genotype dependent differences in GRN stability and magnitude of drought responses. We used TF-footprinting to quantify predicted TF occupancy within gene promoter regions and showed that drought-associated increases in WRKY family footprint signals in leaves varied with leaf age. ERF family footprint signals differed between leaves and roots, highlighting tissue-specific regulatory roles. We then incorporated TF-footprinting information as prior knowledge in KBoost to infer water-responsive GRNs and identified TF hubs where network centrality and regulatory connections sharply differed among genotypes. Finally, we integrated genotype-specific GRNs with expression quantitative trait loci to prioritize candidate variants associated with altered regulatory network structure. Together, these analyses identify climate-associated differences in drought responsive GRN architecture, and revealed candidate TF hubs and predicted genetic variants that may contribute to WUE variation in sorghum. sc.x: Accelerating crop improvement in sorghum for sustainable agriculture demands broadening of available genetic tools and resources. The production of bioengineered plants is a bottleneck for many plant genetics programs and sorghum is particularly recalcitrant. Here, we optimized a sorghum transformation protocol using leaf explants from the grain accession Tx430. Our leaf-based transformation protocol with exogenously expressed morphogenic regulators is efficient and enables seed to T0 plantlet in ~3 months and T1 seed in ~7 months. Cas9 is highly effective in Tx430, and a polycistronic guide RNA cassette allows for up to 8 unique targets to edit across multiple genes or for allelic series in promoters and regulatory elements. As proof of concept, we generated loss-of-function mutations in orthologs of classical maize developmental genes liguleless1 and teosinte branched1. The edited sorghum lines recapitulate the mutant phenotypes described in maize but also show some variations – such as a stronger effect on panicle architecture in the sorghum liguleless1 mutant. Our pipeline is enabling functional validation of candidate genes and regulatory elements that are prioritized based on integration of multi-omics and phenotyping data from sorghum in response to environmental stresses such as drought. T2 edited lines are then phenotyped in a controlled environment for altered stress responses. In addition, our rapid leaf-based protocol is allowing us to screen for transformability in a sorghum diversity panel, including bioenergy lines that cannot be propagated for immature embryos. In our initial phase of screening, we’ve recovered two out of 18 promising candidates for transformability, enhancing our sorghum functional genomics toolkit. This work was supported by funding from the US Department of Energy Biological and Environmental Research (DOE-BER) awards #DE-SC0023305 and #DE-SC0026032 and National Science Foundation Plant Genome Research Program award #IOS-2328611.

sc.x: This study investigates whether machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and combined models can be used to estimate grain yield in advanced sorghum trials. The specific objectives of this study were i) to develop a DL model to identify sorghum panicles in UAS imagery, named “YOLO-SORG"; ii) to test the traditional regression ML models for their ability to estimate yield using standard crop canopy features such as canopy cover, vegetation indices, and canopy height, with and without the panicle traits included; and iii) to evaluate the ML models for their ability to be implemented within a hypothetical sorghum breeding program by estimating repeatability and selection capability.

Machine learning models built on canopy features achieved the highest accuracy (R² ≈ 0.74–0.76), while panicle‑only models performed poorly, confirming that nadir‑view panicle metrics lacked predictive strength. Regularized linear models (RR, EN, LR) not only matched or exceeded tree‑based models in accuracy but also produced variance partitioning and repeatability values that closely mirrored ground‑truth data.

The study evaluated ~1,820 sorghum plots across three Texas field sites, pairing combine‑harvested yield data with high‑resolution UAS imagery collected shortly before harvest. A YOLOv11‑based deep learning model (“YOLO‑SORG”) was trained on ~25,000 annotated panicles to generate plot‑level panicle counts and bounding‑box traits. Six ML algorithms—regularized regressions, SVR, RF, and XGBoost—were tuned across 50 iterations using panicle‑only, canopy‑only, and combined feature sets to predict yield.

Simple features like canopy cover, greenness, and height consistently delivered strong, stable predictions, while panicle‑only traits from nadir imagery weren’t accurate enough to guide selection on their own. Regularized linear models offered the best balance of accuracy and biological realism, making them well‑suited for ranking entries and supporting selection decisions in real breeding pipelines.

sc.x: Sorghum is considered a minor crop in Switzerland (400 ha cultivated in 2024). Nevertheless, sorghum holds considerable potential for climate-resilient cropping systems and alternative food products. With its high drought tolerance and gluten-free grain, sorghum offers potential for more sustainable cropping systems in targeted regions and new food applications. To enhance its economic appeal, the RiSorgo project evaluates the agronomic performance of commercially available European grain sorghum varieties under Swiss conditions and their suitability for pasta production. In addition, thirty accessions from the ICRISAT breeding program were observed to capture a broader genetic diversity beyond European germplasm.

Fifteen grain sorghum varieties from four different breeding programs were tested in small plot trials in the Southern Switzerland (Cadenazzo, 2024 and 2025) and North of the Alps (Zurich, 2025). Evaluated agronomic traits were early vigour, tillering, lodging, panicle numbers, plant height, panicle emergence and yield. ICRISAT accessions were thoroughly described in both sites in 2025 using single-row plots.

Preliminary results indicate considerable variability among varieties for the agronomic traits at the different sites and years. All European varieties reached maturity and average water content at harvest was 27 ± 6 %. Mean overall yield was dt ha⁻¹, with some varieties showing promising performance under Swiss conditions. All ICRISAT accessions reached maturity, exhibiting considerable variability in phenological and agronomic traits. Grain quality analyses are ongoing.

Preliminary results show the potential of grain sorghum as a locally produced, gluten-free raw material in Switzerland. However, variety choice remains a critical factor, as performance varied considerably across locations and years. The planned continuation of field trials in 2026, along with the analysis of processing characteristics and pasta quality will provide a more robust basis for evaluating the value of cultivation and use (VCU) of sorghum varieties from field to fork.

sc.x: The effects of irrigation level and forage-sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) with low prussic acid on ruminal fermentation characteristics, feed intake, ruminal degradation kinetics, apparent total tract nutrient digestibility, and feeding behavior were evaluated.

Ruminally cannulated yearling beef (Angus) × dairy (Holstein) steers (n = 10; body weight [BW] = 450 ± 20 kg) were used in a duplicated 5 × 5 Latin square design, following a 2 × 2 + 1 factorial treatment arrangement: A) forage-sorghum hybrid (SORDAN-79 [510 ± 80 mg/kg HCN] and SWSU4804PF [prussic acid free]); B) irrigation level (dryland [360 mm, rainfall] or irrigated [360 mm rainfall + 95 mm drip-irrigation]); and C) control (OWB) (Bothriochloa bladhii; Old-World bluestem) offered on ad libitum intake throughout five-22 d periods. Feed intake and ruminal pH (wireless ruminal probes [6-min reading intervals]) were measured from d 14-22, while rumen fluid samples were collected on d 21 at 2, 4, 8, 16, 23h after feeding for ammonia analysis and at 8h for volatile fatty acids profile. On d 22, ruminal fluid (approximately 1,000 mL) was collected 4h after feeding for ex-situ assessments of ruminal total gas and methane production. Pre-dehydrated (55˚C for 72h) forage substrates (each treatment) were ground (2 mm), placed in 10 × 20 cm Dracon bags (5 g as-is), and ruminally incubated from d 17-21, while reversely removed at 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, 20, 32, 48, 64, 72, 96 h after incubation for further assessment of the substrate kinetics of degradation. A 24h observational feeding behavior assessment was conducted on d 16. Fecal samples were collected from d 17-21, twice-daily and frozen (-20˚C) for analysis and determination of the apparent total tract nutrient digestibility.
Project is ongoing and the expected final day of collection is May 26<sup>th</sup>, 2026.

sc.x: Drought associated with climate change has increasingly endangered the sustainability and potential of agriculture, notably crop production. Therefore, there is a need to develop adaptive and resilient crop varieties for sustainable crop production and food systems. Sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] is a vital crop in drought-prone areas, supporting the livelihoods of over 750 million people globally. Sorghum grain yield is low in arid and semi-arid regions, with a mean of 0.9 t/ha compared to the global average of 2.5 t/ha due to a lack of improved varieties tolerant to recurrent drought and heat and biotic constraints and desirable product profiles. Integrative breeding for early maturity, high harvest index, and water use efficiency is an economical and sustainable strategy to improve sorghum productivity and mitigate drought effects. These are crucial proxy traits that can guide sorghum improvement for drought tolerance, but current information regarding their simultaneous selection and breeding progress is sparse and scattered; hence, the review aims to address this gap.
The paper highlights innovations and advances in sorghum improvement and advancements towards early maturity, high harvest index, and water use efficiency.

The first section examines the impact of drought on sorghum production, integrative pre-breeding and breeding of sorghum, opportunities for breeding early-maturing, high-yielding, and water-use efficient sorghum varieties, and the associated breeding progress and genetic gains. Further, it outlines the opportunities and challenges of the available breeding methods for developing climate-smart early-maturing and drought-tolerant sorghum cultivars.
The information presented in this paper can guide agronomists and breeders in developing and deploying new-generation sorghum varieties with integrative traits adapted to arid and semi-arid regions.

a: Plant Stress and Germplasm Development Unit, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: We developed a large pedigreed mutant library in the sorghum inbred line BTx623, creating thousands of mutants with traits of potential breeding value, including dwarf stature, erect leaves, multiple tillers, early flowering, and multi-seeded panicles.
This resource has already revealed valuable alleles, such as loss-of-function mutations eliminating prussic acid (dhurrin synthesis), new waxy sorghum variants, and highly digestible sorghum.

To enable functional genomics, we sequenced 1,256 mutant lines and cataloged over 10 million EMS-induced mutations, covering nearly all genes in the BTx623 genome except 517 short genes. Additionally, 610,320 mutations were identified in regulatory regions of 29,790 genes. We also developed BSAseq, a pipeline for rapid identification of causal mutations. Researchers can explore mutation data through SorghumBase (https://www.sorghumbase.org) or SorbMutDB (https://www.depts.ttu.edu/igcast/SorbMutDB.php) and request seeds free of charge.

The Sorghum Sequenced Mutant Library is a powerful tool for breeding and genomic studies—but its impact depends on community use. We invite all sorghum researchers and breeders, public and private, to leverage this resource for discovery and crop improvement.

abstracts.t: Genotype × environment interaction and spatial analysis of sorghum [Sorghum bicolor(L.) moench] genotypes in the highland areas of Ethiopia
abstracts.th: Theme 1: Reduce yield gaps and enhance resilience to changing environments

a: Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia

sc.x: Sorghum is a vital for global food security, particularly in regions where abiotic and biotic stresses severely affecting its production. However, genotype × environment (G × E) interaction and spatial variation remain central problem in identifying, developing and recommending superior and stable sorghum genotypes for highland environments. Therefore, the present study aimed to identify and develop new, high yielding and stable sorghum genotypes across highland environments with desirable agronomic traits.

A total of 131 sorghum genotypes were scrutinized using a randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three replications in a row-column arrangement. Genotypic performance for grain yield, days to flowering and plant height was assessed using linear mixed model of spatial analysis to reduce spatial variation and further enhance selection efficiency.

Across the test environments, the BLUPs for grain yield ranged from 0.42 tha-1 (ETSC13383-2) at Hirna (HN21NVT) to 8.3 tha-1 (ETSC13108-3) at Haramaya (HU19PVT), with the overall mean yields ranging from 2.2 tha-1 (Adelle) to 4.4 tha-1 (ETSC13153-3). Genotype ETSC13153-3 recorded the highest mean yield (4.4 t ha⁻¹) and outperformed the standard checks Dibaba, Jiru, and Adelle by 31.8%, 38.6%, and 50%, respectively. Genotypes ETSC300067, ETSC13367-1, ETSC300072, and ETSC13139-2 also showed significant yield advantages over Adelle (≈45–46%). Spatial genetic correlation analysis revealed strong positive, negative, and weak correlations among trials.

Overall, ETSC13153-3, ETSC300067, ETSC13367-1, ETSC300072, and ETSC13139-2 were identified as high-yielding, stable, and broadly adapted genotypes suitable for recommendation in highland sorghum-growing environments. Given their outstanding performance, these genotypes are strong candidates for releasing as new commercial sorghum varieties in the near future. These genotypes hold significant potential for future sorghum improvement programs and are well suited for large-scale production in the highland regions of Ethiopia after an in-depth scrutiny of their superiority and yield stability over time across environments.

abstracts.th: Theme 6: Strengthening value chains, seed systems and market opportunities to build more resilient and profitable sorghum industries

a: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service, Stephenville, United States

sc.x: Organic sorghum acreage is increasing globally, driven by demand from organic livestock feed, food‑grade markets, and resilient production systems. Organic sorghum seed systems, however, remain underdeveloped, constraining yield stability, genetic diversity, and adoption. This presentation treats organic seed production as a systems‑level interface linking plant breeding, agronomy, and market integrity within organic value chains. The goal is to identify biological, management, and institutional levers for strengthening organic sorghum seed systems that support resilient, profitable organic markets.

Across these organic seed systems, conventional priorities often diverge from organic field realities. Early vigor, canopy and root architecture, tillering behavior, stress tolerance, and synchronized flowering emerge as disproportionately important traits for organic seed fields and users. Seed‑microbiome interactions, seedborne disease management, and post‑harvest handling are critical determinants of seed quality, stand establishment, and farmer confidence. Cooperative work with AMSD shows how farmer‑participatory selection and training can support regionally adapted organic sorghum seed enterprises and strengthen local organic seed availability.

Insights are drawn from on‑farm organic seed production, variety testing, and extension collaborations in Texas and the southern Great Plains, with farmer‑participatory organic sorghum seed development and training with the Association Malienne pour la Solidarité et le Développement (AMSD). Germplasm is evaluated under organic management with low external inputs, weed pressure, and variable fertility and moisture. Observations focus on seed‑production constraints, key plant traits for stand establishment and seed quality, seedborne disease and seed‑microbiome issues, and post‑harvest handling within organic certification requirements.

Strengthening organic sorghum seed systems is essential to building resilient, trusted value chains and expanding profitable organic industries. Treating seed as both a biological input and a trust‑based market foundation calls for collaboration among breeders, seed producers, farmer organizations, extension, and buyers, moving organic sorghum seed from bottleneck to catalyst.

abstracts.t: Title:Abstract: Sorghum’s resilience, low-input requirements, and biochemical diversity position it uniquely at the intersection of food security, animal nutrition, and bioindustrial innovation. As global agriculture pivots toward regenerative systems, sorghum can serve as a scalable platform.
abstracts.th: Theme 5: Exploring new products and novel horizons for human, livestock and industrial applications

a: Global Revive, Waco, Texas, United States

sc.x:
Objectives
1. Characterize sorghum phytochemical and macronutrient profiles relevant to human nutrition and livestock gut microbiomes.
2. Develop novel food prototypes and ingredient fractions that leverage polyphenols, antioxidants, and resistant starch for natural‑health positioning.
3. Evaluate sorghum fractions as microbiome substrates in ruminant and monogastric feed trials to measure gut health and feed conversion.
4. Optimize post‑harvest handling and processing workflows to minimize losses and maximize fraction yields for food, feed, and industrial streams.
5. Demonstrate integrated bio‑refinery pathways for biofuels and bioproducts that support regenerative farm incomes and regional circular economies.

Field and Agronomy
• Targeted variety selection and agronomic trials across moisture gradients to optimize yield and phytochemical expression.
• Regenerative practices: cover cropping, reduced tillage, diversified rotations, and compost/organic amendments.
Compositional and Analytical Methods
• HPLC and spectrophotometric assays for polyphenols and antioxidant capacity.
• Resistant starch and fiber profiling; proximate analysis for protein, fat, and carbohydrate fractions.
Microbiome and Feed Trials
• In vitro fermentation assays to screen prebiotic potential of sorghum fractions.
• Controlled ruminant and monogastric feeding trials measuring microbiome shifts (16S rRNA), short‑chain fatty acids, health markers, and feed conversion ratios.
Post‑Harvest Processing and Fractionation
• Modular processing chain: cleaning → controlled drying → milling → fractionation (bran, germ, endosperm) → stabilization.

• Life‑cycle assessment (LCA) and ecosystem service accounting to quantify carbon sequestration, soil organic matter change, and net GHG balance.
• Economic modeling of farm and platform unit economics, and scenario analysis for revenue from food premiums, feed improvements, and bio‑product sales.

Sorghum can serve as a futuristic, regenerative platform that simultaneously delivers natural‑health ingredients for humans, microbiome‑supporting feed for livestock, and feedstocks for industrial bioproducts—creating diversified, resilient revenue streams and measurable ecosystem benefits that underpin regional regenerative economies.
