abstracts.t: Genetic architecture of mesocotyl and coleoptile elongation for "deep planting" in sorghum
abstracts.th: Theme 2: Capturing sorghum yield potential leveraging advances in genomics for enhancing yield gain and stress resilience

a: Department of Agronomy, Iowa State University, Ames, United States
Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics and Genomics, University of Georgia, Athens, United States
Department of Agronomy, Iowa State University, Ames, United States
Department of Horticultural Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, United States
Department of Agronomy, Iowa State University, Ames, United States

sc.x: Sorghum germination and establishment are frequently limited by low topsoil moisture and temperature fluctuations. Deeper planting could be a beneficial management practice to improve emergence by accessing deeper soil moisture and more stable temperatures. However, increased planting depth requires sufficient mesocotyl and coleoptile elongation to ensure successful emergence. As shallow planting remains a common practice in sorghum production, elongation capacity has not been widely characterized, and the genetic basis of these traits remains poorly understood. This study aims to dissect the genetic architecture of mesocotyl and coleoptile elongation by leveraging the genetic diversity in the Sorghum Association Panel (SAP).

The image-based phenotyping pipeline was validated and proved reliable. GWAS identified nine genomic regions associated with elongation traits: six for total length, two for coleoptile length, and one for both total and mesocotyl length.

A total of 318 genotypes from the SAP were evaluated under controlled deep-planting conditions. Seeds were planted in multicell trays at a depth of 28 cm in topsoil and grown at 15 °C for 14 days under a 14-h photoperiod. Four replications were conducted using two seed sources. In each replication, four seedlings per genotype were collected and imaged with a camera mounted on a stand positioned 80 cm above the samples against a black background. RGB images were processed using PlantCV to obtain mesocotyl and coleoptile lengths. Phenotypic data were analyzed using linear mixed models accounting for replication and seed vigor effects to estimate Best Linear Unbiased Predictions (BLUPs). BLUPs were used in genome-wide association analyses (GWAS) performed in GAPIT to identify genomic regions associated with elongation traits.

These findings provide new insights into the genetic architecture of mesocotyl and coleoptile elongation. The identification of genomic regions controlling these traits could be leveraged for developing sorghum varieties with improved emergence under deep-planting conditions.

abstracts.t: Productivity and energy balance of maize and sorghum grown for biogas in a large-area farm in Poland: An 11-year field experiment.
abstracts.th: Theme 3: Managing grain, forage, and biomass sorghum production to optimize yield, quality and systems resilience to maximize economic returns

a: University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Agrotechnology and Agribusiness, Olsztyn, Poland
University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Agrotechnology and Agribusiness, Olsztyn, Poland
University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Agrotechnology and Agribusiness, Olsztyn, Poland
University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Genetics, Plant Breeding and Bioresource Engineering, Olsztyn, Poland
University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Agrotechnology and Agribusiness, Olsztyn, Poland
University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Department of Agrotechnology and Agribusiness, Olsztyn, Poland

sc.x: Grasses of the genus Sorghum are an alternative source of biomass for energy generation. Sorghum is more tolerant to varied environmental conditions, and its production is less energy intensive in comparison with maize. The aim of this study was to compare the energy efficiency of maize and sweet sorghum

The demand for energy in the production of maize biomass was estimated at 24.4–25.5 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup>. Energy consumption in the production of sweet sorghum biomass was 2.8 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup> lower on average. Mineral fertilization was the major energy input (72–73 %) in the cultivation of both crops. The average maize yields in north-eastern Poland reached 21.7 Mg ha<sup>−1</sup> dry matter (DM). The biomass yield of sweet sorghum was 4.0 Mg ha<sup>−1</sup> DM lower on average. The energy output of maize biomass ranged from 197 to 290 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup> y<sup>−1</sup>, whereas the average energy output of sorghum biomass was 61 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup> lower. The energy gain and the energy efficiency ratio of maize biomass were determined at 172−265 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup> and 7.7–11.3, respectively. The above parameters were 58 GJ ha<sup>−1</sup> and 14 % lower in sweet sorghum biomass, respectively.

The experiment was carried out in 2008–2018 at the Agricultural Experiment Station in Bałcyny (NE Poland). The experimental variables were: (i) maize (Zea mays L.) and (ii) sweet sorghum (Sorghum saccharatum L./Moench.). The study determined biomass yield and energy balance.

The yields and energy efficiency of sweet sorghum peaked in years with above-average annual precipitation. In the remaining years of the experiment, sweet sorghum was characterized by lower biomass yields and a lower energy efficiency ratio than maize. Sweet sorghum has a lower energy requirement, adapts well to environmental conditions, and can complement other substrates in biorefineries.

abstracts.t: GRAINGUARD: PREHARVEST SPROUT TECHNOLOGY
abstracts.th: Research and Innovation

a: Innovative Seed Solutions, Puerto Vallarta, Mexico
Innovative Seed Solutions, Mt. Hope, United States
Innovative Seed Solutions, Bishop, United States

sc.x:
When sorghum approaches harvest maturity and is exposed to warm, wet conditions, it can trigger germination of grain while still on the panicle, a phenomenon known as pre-harvest sprouting (PHS). Sorghum is uniquely vulnerable: its grain sits fully exposed on an open panicle, and the crop evolved in dry climates with little biological defense against moisture-induced germination at maturity. Modern producers increasingly evaluate crop and variety decisions based on risk profile, not yield potential alone. Unpredictable rainfall near harvest represents one of sorghum's most consequential vulnerabilities, constraining production confidence in traditional growing regions and limiting the crop's appeal in higher-rainfall environments where it could otherwise compete. Sprouted grain falls from the panicle, causing direct harvest loss, and grain that does reach the combine has already begun starch breakdown, rendering it unsuitable for many supply chain uses and triggering steep price discounts. Currently, nothing can prevent pre-harvest sprouting if weather conditions are conducive.

The idea is to develop a binary hybrid-specific germination suppression system, a two-gene genetic architecture that is elegantly self-limiting. Neither parent line is affected individually; the suppression technology activates only when both complementary gene components are combined in the F1 hybrid grain. The seed parent carries Gene Component A (active) and Gene Component B (inactive); the pollinator carries the reverse. Only in end-use grain, where both active components combine, does the suppression pathway engage, eliminating the risk of pre-harvest sprouting. Two stepwise research pathways are proposed: (1) discovery of native complementary gene pairs through germplasm screening, and (2) CRISPR-targeted gene editing if native pairs cannot be identified. Beyond grain quality protection, this trait reduces volunteer establishment the following season, directly simplifying stewardship obligations across herbicide-tolerant sorghum platforms, and provides an additional biological layer of intellectual property protection for seed developers. If successful, this technology could be deployed across the majority of hybrid grain sorghum acres in developed markets within a decade, with particular synergy alongside herbicide-tolerant trait platforms.

The submitting team brings plant breeding, genomics, and commercial seed industry expertise through Innovative Seed Solutions (ISS) and its established public-private partnership with the Kansas State University Sorghum Trait Collaborative Innovation Network (STRAIT KIN). Additional partners include other commercial seed companies, public land-grant universities, federal agricultural research agencies, and international agricultural research institutions.

Initial funding will be anchored by ISS, complemented by national commodity organizations, federal agricultural research agencies, international agricultural development foundations, and international agricultural research institutions.

abstracts.t: SORGHUM WASTE TO BIO-BASED FIBER
abstracts.th: New products and market opportunities for human, livestock, and industrial applications

a: Fiber and Biopolymer Research Institute, Department of Plant and Soil Science, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, United States

sc.x: The global textile industry faces mounting pressure to adopt sustainable, bio-based alternatives to petroleum-derived synthetic fibers, while agricultural residues such as sorghum stover remain vastly underutilized despite their abundant availability. This project addresses that gap by proposing an integrated biorefinery approach that sequentially isolates hemicellulose, lignin, and cellulose from sorghum stover, with a focused application on converting the extracted cellulose into Rayon textile fiber. Following organosolv fractionation, the isolated cellulose is expected to retain residual lignin (~2–7%), which may limit its suitability for high-quality applications. To address this, a mild bleaching step using 3-7% hydrogen peroxide will be implemented to achieve ~95% purity and improved whiteness. Structural analysis using FTIR, XRD will be conducted to confirm that the isolated cellulose retains characteristic functional groups comparable to commercial microcrystalline cellulose, thereby validating its quality. The purified cellulose will then be processed through the standard viscose method to demonstrate proof-of-concept Rayon fiber formation from sorghum stover. While the resulting fiber may initially require further optimization in xanthation conditions, coagulation bath composition, and drawing parameters to improve mechanical properties and reduce brittleness, the feasibility of the approach will be established. Critically, this idea does not compete with locally dominant cotton fiber production but rather complements it by valorizing an otherwise wasted biomass stream, generating a niche bio-based fiber product alongside simultaneous co-products including prebiotic livestock supplements and lignin-based composite materials, collectively utilizing over 90% of the sorghum stover feedstock across human, livestock, and industrial markets.

This project requires strong interdisciplinary expertise in biomass fractionation, chemical processing, and material characterization. Partnerships with agronomists will help in selecting the appropriate feedstock, while collaborations with textile engineers will support the assessment of fiber feasibility and processability. Additionally, experts in materials testing will help optimize fiber properties such as strength and flexibility through techniques including tensile strength analysis and advanced characterization, further enhancing the overall quality of the developed fiber.

Funding will be sought to support process optimization and material characterization. In the short term, university internal grants and competitive research awards will be pursued, alongside applications to USDA NIFA programs targeting sustainable agriculture, agricultural waste valorization, and biorefinery development. In the long term, partnerships with textile manufacturers and biorefinery industries will be explored to transition from lab-scale to pilot-scale production.

abstracts.t: GENETICS OF STAY-GREEN IN SORGHUM
abstracts.th: Research and Innovation

a: University of Nebraska, Lincoln, United States

sc.x: Sorghum is a climate-resilient crop widely cultivated in water-limited environments, making it critical for global food security. A key trait contributing to its productivity is stay-green, the ability to maintain leaf function during grain filling. However, not all stay-green phenotypes are beneficial; some genotypes retain green leaves without sustaining photosynthesis, resulting in limited yield gains. This highlights a key gap: the mechanisms underlying functional stay-green at the population level remain unclear. This project aims to dissect the molecular basis of functional stay-green in sorghum using the Sorghum Diversity Panel (900 lines). We will phenotype this diverse population under field conditions to quantify stay-green dynamics, photosynthetic traits, and yield. To capture the regulatory phase of remobilization, leaf tissue will be collected at 10–15 days after flowering, a critical transition stage when differences in senescence and assimilate partitioning emerge. We will integrate transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping to identify genes and genomic regions underlying stay-green variation. TWAS will detect genes associated with traits such as chlorophyll content and photosynthetic performance measured in the same field experiment, while eQTL mapping will leverage our lab-generated whole-genome sequence data from these 900 lines to reveal regulatory architecture. This integrative approach moves beyond descriptive phenotypes to uncover causal regulatory networks and distinguish functional stay-green from cosmetic greenness.

This idea is proposed by a graduate student with training in plant genetics, genomics, and sorghum population analysis. The project will be conducted under the guidance of an academic advisor with expertise in crop genetics and field-based research. The work will be carried out collaboratively by a team of graduate students, lab technicians, and domain experts experienced in stay-green phenotyping, transcriptomics, and association analyses, ensuring rigorous execution of both field and computational components.

This project is designed to be cost-effective and feasible within existing institutional resources. Tissue collection for RNA-seq requires precise timing and handling; our lab has experienced technicians and trained students capable of high-quality sample collection. Downstream processes, including RNA extraction, library preparation, and sequencing, will be outsourced to specialized service providers to ensure data quality and efficiency. To support sequencing costs and field operations, we will pursue external funding through competitive research grants, enabling scalability while leveraging existing infrastructure.

abstracts.t: DECODING DYE TRAITS IN GRAIN SORGHUM
abstracts.th: Research and Innovation

a: Texas Tech University, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: The U.S. shift away from synthetic dyes, accelerated by the FDA's recent ban on FD&C Red No. 3, has created strong demand for plant-based colorant alternatives. Grain sorghum is a uniquely promising source of natural pigments, namely 3-deoxyanthocyanidins like luteolinidin, found almost exclusively in sorghum and highly stable against heat, light, and pH changes, making them attractive for food, textile, and industrial use. Despite this potential, the genetic basis controlling pigment production across diverse sorghum varieties remains poorly understood, limiting efforts to breed high-pigment varieties for commercial use. This project addresses that gap by combining pigment measurement across a diverse sorghum panel with whole-genome sequencing data to identify the genomic regions controlling pigment production. Key genetic variants will be used to build haplotype maps, and candidate genes will be annotated to provide targets for marker-assisted breeding of high-pigment sorghum. The broader vision is a genomics-guided breeding pipeline that turns sorghum crop residues that are currently discarded into a scalable feedstock for the growing natural colorant market, sitting at an unexplored intersection of plant genomics, sustainable agriculture, and the bio-based materials industry.

The proposed project is led by a multidisciplinary team at Texas Tech University (TTU), namely Arin Mishra (Lead-Masters in Biotechnology student; translational research, industrial microbiology, and science entrepreneurship), Dr. Dinesh Kumar Saini (Research Assistant Professor; molecular breeding, genomics, trait mapping, and high-throughput phenotyping), Dr. Kalavathy Rajan (Assistant Professor; agricultural chemistry; biological engineering; food science), and Dr. SV Krishna Jagadish (Interim Chair and Professor; agronomist and crop physiologist providing strategic oversight and deep sorghum sector networks). The team is embedded in TTU’s agricultural research infrastructure, with active collaborations spanning plant breeding, bio-product development, and the United Sorghum Checkoff Program.

The funding strategy draws on a blended portfolio of federal and private sources, namely USDA and NSF SBIR/STTR programs, the National Sorghum Checkoff Foundation, and the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR), as well as regional grain sorghum ethanol biorefineries as industry co-investment partners. Intellectual property will be secured through TTU’s technology transfer office prior to commercialization; the Co-PIs bring a substantial combined record of competitively secured federal funding, ensuring no single phase of the project is contingent on any single funding mechanism.

abstracts.t: SORGHUM STALK ROT: A PREDICTION TOOL
abstracts.th: Innovative machinery or software tools related to sorghum

a: Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States
Kansas State University, Manhattan, United States

sc.x: Stalk rot is among the most important diseases affecting sorghum production worldwide, frequently resulting in lodging and reduced harvestability, grain quality, and yield. This disease complex is primarily caused by Macrophomina phaseolina and Fusarium spp., soil-borne pathogens commonly present in sorghum fields. These pathogens infect plants early in the season and remain in a latent phase without reproducing any visible symptoms until undergoing a switch to a necrotrophic phase triggered by severe post-flowering environmental stress, specifically water deficits, which cause the plant to remobilize carbohydrates from the stalks to fill the developing grain, ultimately leading to lodging. Despite its economic impact, growers currently lack real-time tools to anticipate disease development and lodging risk. As a first step toward this gap, we compared years with high and low disease pressure in earlier studies to identify environmental drivers suitable for predictive models. This project aims to integrate field experimentation with predictive modeling to create a data-driven decision-support tool for growers, translating real-time weather information and management data into an actionable early-warning system that predicts stalk rot severity and pre-harvest lodging risk. Ultimately, farmers would have access to a map showing when and where to prioritize harvest to avoid lodging risk at the end of the season. In addition, a smartphone app would be deployed, allowing growers to add real-time information on planting dates, growth stages, and hybrid maturity, and providing in-season alerts on disease risk to support early-season stalk rot management decisions, such as foliar applications around flowering.
This project is part of the PhD dissertation of Leticia Vieira, a Kansas State University plant pathology graduate student, under the supervision of Dr. Rodrigo Onofre.

In collaboration with the Kansas Sorghum Commission, our team has been running the Sorghum Connection for the past two years, a series of field days and winter schools designed to bring new management information directly to growers. Key collaborators include Dr. Sarah Sexton-Bowser (Managing Director for the Center for Sorghum Improvement (CSI)), Adam York (Director of Sustainability with National Sorghum Producers and the United Sorghum Checkoff Program), Andy Hineman (Kansas Grain Sorghum Producers Association board director), and other specialists involved in Kansas sorghum production and extension. These events and relationships will serve as a direct channel for conducting expert elicitation, collecting grower information, and keeping the project connected to growers, ensuring that the tool we develop actually meets their needs.

abstracts.t: RHIZOBOOST DUO: DROUGHT SEED COATING
abstracts.th: Research and Innovation

a: Rhine-Waal University of Applied Science, Kleve, Germany

sc.x: Drought, declining soil fertility, and rising fertiliser costs increasingly limit sorghum and cowpea production in dryland regions. Poor seedling establishment, restricted root growth, low nutrient availability, and reduced microbial activity often weaken crop performance under water stress. Although sorghum–cowpea intercropping can improve resource use and reduce dependence on nitrogen fertilisers, both crops are also widely cultivated as sole crops. Therefore, a practical microbial product should support sorghum and cowpea when grown individually as well as together. RhizoBoost Duo is a drought-adapted microbial seed-coating platform designed for sorghum and cowpea under water-limited conditions. Beneficial bacteria and fungi will be isolated from healthy plants and rhizospheres in drought-prone environments. Candidate microorganisms will be screened for drought tolerance, root colonisation, nutrient mobilisation, stimulation of root growth, support of cowpea nodulation and nitrogen fixation, and compatibility with other selected strains. Safety screening will exclude potentially harmful microorganisms. The innovation lies in combining crop-specific and system-level functions. A sorghum formulation will promote root development, water acquisition, and nutrient uptake, while a cowpea formulation will support nodulation, nitrogen fixation, root establishment, and drought adaptation. Each coating can be used independently for sole cropping or applied together in intercropping to support a beneficial shared rhizosphere. The concept is feasible through phased laboratory screening, greenhouse validation, and field testing. Coated and uncoated seeds will be compared under sole cropping, intercropping, well-watered, and drought-stressed conditions. Germination, root architecture, biomass, nutrient uptake, water use, nodulation, and microbial persistence will be assessed. The long-term vision is an affordable, shelf-stable, and easy-to-apply biological seed treatment that improves drought resilience and reduces fertiliser dependence.

The project brings together expertise in plant–microbe interactions, microbiology, molecular biology, soil science, root phenotyping, crop physiology, and sorghum–legume production. Breeders, agronomists, field researchers, extension specialists, farmers, seed producers, and biological-input companies will contribute to strain selection, field validation, formulation, and practical adoption.

The Sorghum Idea Challenge prize would support microbial isolation, initial screening, and greenhouse proof-of-concept studies. Further development would be funded through climate-resilience, sustainable-agriculture, soil-health, and bioeconomy grants. Partnerships with seed and biological-fertiliser companies would support formulation, shelf-life testing, regulatory approval, commercial production, and affordable local distribution.

abstracts.t: SORGHUM ON-THE-GO: JUST ADD HOT WATER
abstracts.th: New products and market opportunities for human, livestock, and industrial applications

a: Nu Life Market LLC, Scott City, KS, United States

sc.x: Consumers increasingly seek convenient foods that provide whole-grain nutrition, fiber, and protein. As a gluten-free, non-GMO grain, sorghum aligns with these trends, yet opportunities remain to position it as a primary grain in convenient, everyday meal formats. Sorghum On-the-Go presents a convenient, whole-grain sorghum meal in a single-serve cup designed to be prepared with hot water in minutes, similar to instant rice, oats, or pasta-based meals. The concept aims to increase sorghum consumption by positioning sorghum as the primary grain in a convenient, ready-to-prepare meal format. The cup could support both sweet and savory applications, with dried fruits, vegetables, and seasonings adapted to different consumption occasions, including breakfast, lunch, and quick dinner. Combining the convenience of an instant meal format with the nutritional attributes of whole-grain sorghum, while creating an additional use for sorghum bran Extrusion will be used to precook the sorghum and develop two complementary components: (1) small, grain-like pieces produced from whole sorghum meal with pea protein isolate to increase protein content, and (2) thin, strand-like structures produced from a sorghum meal–bran blend. The second component is designed to valorize sorghum bran as a milling by-product by transforming it into a functional component of the meal while contributing dietary fiber and the antioxidant potential of pigmented sorghum, while providing visual and textural differentiation. Separating the components allows each structure to be developed for its intended functional and textural role while creating contrast in the final meal. Key technical challenges include balancing hydration rate, expansion, starch gelatinization, structural integrity, and bran inclusion, particularly in a high-fiber extrusion matrix.

The concept was developed by Victoria Lopez, R&D Scientist at Nu Life Market. Nu Life Market provides access to sorghum ingredients, product development resources, and single-screw extrusion capabilities, with technical input from personnel in extrusion, food safety, and sales to support preliminary development.

Preliminary development and initial extrusion screening could be conducted using Nu Life Market’s existing ingredients, R&D resources, and extrusion capabilities. External funding would be pursued through applied research programs, such as Sorghum Checkoff opportunities and competitive research grants, to support further process development with specialized extrusion partners. This could include evaluation of twin-screw extrusion for the high-fiber, bran-containing component, followed by product and analytical evaluation to optimize formulations, establish processing conditions, and define a pathway toward scale-up and commercialization

abstracts.t: NUTRIENT-ENRICHED SILAGE SORGHUM
abstracts.th: Research and Innovation

a: 1Department of Plant and Soil Science, Institute of Genomics for Crop Abiotic Stress Tolerance (IGCAST), Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA, Lubbock, United States
1Department of Plant and Soil Science, Institute of Genomics for Crop Abiotic Stress Tolerance (IGCAST), Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA, Lubbock, United States

sc.x: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is a water-efficient and drought-tolerant alternative to maize for silage production in semi-arid regions. However, its broader adoption as a high-quality silage crop is constrained by relatively low protein and starch digestibility. To overcome this limitation, we are pyramiding high protein digestibility (HPD) and waxy (low amylose) alleles to develop nutritionally enhanced silage sorghum. Using an EMS mutant population, we have identified the causative alleles underlying the two traits and developed molecular markers.

It will be a doctoral dissertation project; all experiments, data generation, and analysis will be conducted by the graduate student. Our breeding utilizes marker-assisted backcrossing to introgress these two recessive alleles into five elite silage sorghum backgrounds, enabling precise allele tracking while minimizing reliance on labor-intensive biochemical assays. Initial crosses between F1 donor plants carrying both alleles and elite silage lines have been completed, launching the introgression pipeline.

This project is awarded by the Southern SARE grant for the graduate student category.
Subsequent backcrossing and selfing will produce homozygous double-recessive lines, which will be systematically evaluated for grain composition, digestibility, seed development, biomass yield, and overall agronomic performance. By integrating targeted allele stacking with elite germplasm improvement, this project aims to deliver high-biomass, nutrient-enriched sorghum cultivars that enhance feed efficiency and livestock productivity. These improved silage varieties will strengthen sorghum’s role as a resilient forage crop for water-limited production systems worldwide.
